The migration was not the cause. `write_userns_maps()` wrote `deny` to `/proc/<pid>/setgroups` before `gid_map` unconditionally — the documented recipe for the **unprivileged** case, which `user_namespaces(7)` requires only when the writing process lacks `CAP_SETGID` in the parent namespace. cixd is real root and has it, so the deny was never needed, and it cost every container the ability to call `setgroups(2)` for its whole lifetime. dnsmasq calls `setgroups()` before `setgid()` when told to run as a user, so it died with `failed to change group-id to root: Operation not permitted`, exit 5, **and nothing on stderr** — it logs to syslog unless told otherwise, so the container just exited 5 in a restart loop with no diagnostic anywhere. `gid_map` is now written first and setgroups is denied only if the kernel refuses, which keeps the unprivileged path correct instead of assumed. **What made this a real outage rather than a latent flaw was a default.** User namespaces were opt-in when the deny was written; ADR-0207 made them the default for newly created containers, converting a sharp edge on an unused option into "a container recreated for any reason will not start". A `container-storage` migration recreated `dns-1` and `dns-2`, and neither came back. **Two things found on the way that were also real**: the `dns-1`/`dns-2` container recipes staged `/etc/dnsmasq-servers` but not `/etc/dnsmasq-hosts`, even though the command line passes `-H /etc/dnsmasq-hosts` — that file only ever existed because DNS-server registration wrote it into the container's writable layer at runtime, so anything resetting that layer lost it and dnsmasq then could not start, and because it could not start `dns_server_sync_all()` (which only touches *running* containers) could never put it back. Both recipes now stage it, alongside `capture_output: true`, because a service that dies silently with an exit code is exactly what that field is for — it turned an unexplained exit 5 into a one-line answer. The other container recipes here (`ldap-1/2`, `ntp-1/2`, `syslog-1/2`, `jump`) run real service software and none has been started since userns became the default; they are likely affected the same way and should be brought up and checked rather than assumed fine.

- **`/etc/resolv.conf` pointed at a shadowed inode, so the host could not resolve anything (found live, v2.23.1).** Moving state to the config partition exposed an ordering bug that had been harmless for as long as state lived elsewhere. `boot_init()` created `STATE_DIR` and `resolv.conf` inside it, bind-mounted that file onto `/etc/resolv.conf`, and **only then** mounted the config partition over `/config` — so the file it had just created lived on the *root filesystem's* bare mountpoint, and mounting the real partition over the top shadowed the exact inode the bind mount still pointed at. The symptom is issue #138 again by a different route, and it is the same deeply misleading shape: `GET /v1/system/resolv` reported the right nameservers, `PUT` wrote them to the right path, `dns-1`/`dns-2` were running — and every lookup failed. Caught by the next deploy's own fetch: `curl: (6) Could not resolve host: git.home.arpa`. The config mount now happens before anything under it is read or written. **Verified by the error changing**: the same repo sync that failed with curl exit 6 (could not resolve) now fails with exit 22 (an HTTP status), which means the name resolved and the connection was made. **Getting the fix onto the box needed the fix**, since the box could not fetch its own source — resolved by serving that one tarball over plain HTTP by literal IP from the LAN, this project's documented unblock for a host that cannot resolve, with `pkg_sha256` as the gate that makes a plain-HTTP source safe. `cix@v2.23.3`'s recipe records that URL and why it is dead, rather than leaving a future reader to work it out.

- **State lives on the config partition, and `state-storage` is retired ([ADR-0232](docs/adr/0232-state-lives-on-the-config-partition.md), #250, #251).** Two problems, one decision. `cix-config` held `net.conf` and nothing else — 15360 bytes of 64 MiB — while the platform's own definition of itself sat on the containers partition beside images and packages: networks, DNS/DHCP/NTP/LDAP, syslog targets, the CA and every issued certificate, container definitions, device maps, site identity. The layout implies three tiers and only two were in use, with the configuration tier as the empty one. Meanwhile the role that was supposed to protect that content **could not do the one thing that justified it**: `treecopy_recursive(source, target)` copies *current* state onto the disk and never adopts state already there; `storage_placement.json` — the record of which disk holds state — lives on the OS disk, the disk being protected against; and boot resolves placement from that record alone. After an OS disk failure the reinstalled box does not know the state disk exists, and the natural recovery copies fresh empty state **over** the real one. So `STATE_DIR` now defaults to `/config/state`, and the role, the `STORAGE_KIND_STATE` placement, `GET`/`POST /system/state-storage(/migrate)`, `cixctl storage state` and the dashboard panel are all gone — 273 operations where there were 276. **The migration copies and deletes nothing.** `migrate_state_to_config()` runs at boot only when the destination is absent and the legacy directory present, and renames the source to `state.migrated-<timestamp>` *after* the copy succeeds; a failure at any point leaves the original exactly where the previous build expects it, so booting the other slot recovers the machine, and failure is non-fatal because refusing to boot over a migration is worse than running from where the data already is. **One near-miss caught in review**: `diskrole_init()` rejects an unknown role by returning `-1`, which refuses the boot — so an upgraded box with `state-storage` assigned would have been bricked by retiring it. That entry is now skipped with a log line, the disk untouched. Durability is `GET /system/backup`, which is what it always actually was.
- **The storage guide covers the system partitions as roles too, and protection is its own column.** Asked for: *"storage guide should have all role types even the ones that are system native"*, and *"a protected indicator should be clear on webui and cli (not (protected) but a different column)"*. The guide now opens its roles section with the five OS-disk partitions — ESP, both root slots, config, containers — each with its job and whether it is yours to change, because "what is this partition for" is the same question the assignable roles answer, and leaving them out made the role list look like the whole story when it covers only disks you add. It also records that `cix-containers` is deliberately *not* protected. In the CLI and the dashboard, protection is now a column of its own rather than a parenthetical on the role or label — where it was previously invisible for any partition that had a role at all.

- **`cix-config` is sized 512 MiB instead of 64 (#250).** The partition was sized for what it held — one file, `net.conf`, using 15360 bytes — rather than for what it is *for*. The layout implies three tiers (immutable roots, host configuration, container data) and the configuration tier held a single file while the platform's own definition of itself (networks, DNS, DHCP, NTP, LDAP, syslog targets, the CA and every issued certificate, container definitions, device maps, site identity) sat on the containers partition instead. Moving that where it belongs needs somewhere to put it. **512 rather than 256** because PKI is the one part with real growth — a file per issued certificate — and this is sized once at install and cannot be enlarged afterwards without repartitioning the OS disk; 448 MiB is noise against any disk this installs on, and it takes the question off the table permanently. **One thing followed from the size**: `mkfs.btrfs --mixed` was passed for this partition *only* because 64 MiB is below btrfs's ~109 MiB minimum for separate data/metadata profiles. At 512 MiB it gets the normal layout like every other filesystem here — `--mixed` was never desirable, only necessary. The parameter is kept, because "this filesystem may be tiny" is an honest thing for a helper to be able to express. Takes effect on the next install; existing boxes keep the 64 MiB they were built with.

- **Storage gets its own guide, and `format` defaults to btrfs.** Asked for directly: *"I want a doc that specifically talks about disk formats and why and snapshots and so on, and one that shows each disk role and how it's used and by what ... this should be accessible to users so they understand what to create disks for"*. [`docs/guides/storage.md`](docs/guides/storage.md) is that doc — the OS disk's five fixed partitions and which four are protected and why; the two-step role-then-format shape and why it is two steps; **all six roles** (`container-storage`, `state-storage`, `rebuildable-storage`, `log-storage`, `swap`, `backup`) with, for each, whether it is a per-host singleton, what actually lives there, and which call puts it there; a plain "so what should I create a disk for" section ordered by how often it is worth doing; btrfs versus ext4; how snapshot-backed container rootfs works and why per-container storage is nearly free; quotas; partitioning; and how to move a placement afterwards. `administration.md` kept only the two-step shape and now points at it rather than carrying a second copy — its own storage section had gone stale in exactly the way that predicts, still describing the role vocabulary as *"`container-storage` or `backup` — a small, fixed vocabulary"* when there are six. **And writing it surfaced a real defect rather than just documenting one**: `POST /disks/{name}/format` still defaulted to **ext4**. ADR-0207 made btrfs the sole substrate for this platform's own writable storage and put ext4 on a retirement path, but nothing moved the default with it — so an operator formatting a data disk without saying otherwise got the one filesystem that cannot snapshot, and every container later placed on that disk got a full copy of its image instead of a copy-on-write clone. Nobody chose that; the default simply outlived the decision. It is btrfs now, in the daemon and in `openapi.yaml` together, with `--fs-type=ext4` still available for the case where something outside Cix has to read the disk.

- **Attached disks stop mounting inside the data directory ([ADR-0231](docs/adr/0231-attached-disks-do-not-mount-inside-the-data-directory.md)).** Reported while trying to delete `vda5`: *"why are the mount points sitting under another mount point ... I am very confused"*. An assigned-role disk mounted at `<data-dir>/disks/<device>`, and on a real host the data directory is `/var/lib/cix` — the OS disk's own `cix-containers` partition. So every attached disk's mountpoint was a directory inside that partition's filesystem, and the kernel will not unmount a mountpoint that still carries other mounts. `cix-containers` was therefore permanently unmountable, unresizable and unreclaimable the moment any disk was attached, reporting only that *"something on this disk may still be busy/in use"* — which reads like a stray process rather than a structural fact. **Nothing decided this**: `disks/` was created alongside `state/`, `containers/`, `logs/` and `volumes/` because that is where subdirectories went, but those hold data and a mountpoint is not data. It was the odd one out in that list, and that was the whole bug. Disks now mount at **`/mnt/cix/<device>`** on a **tmpfs**, with `--disks-dir=PATH` to override and one rule when it is absent: a non-default `--data-dir` keeps disks inside it (which preserves the test suite's isolation without editing every daemon-linked test), anything else uses `/mnt/cix`. **The tmpfs is the part that matters, and it is about a property the platform does not yet have**: the root slot is currently mounted `rw`, so plain directories on the root would work today and would be wrong the day the A/B roots become genuinely read-only, which is what they exist for. `/mnt/cix` ships in the image (`mkbootroot`) so even creating it never writes to the root, and the tmpfs mount is non-fatal like the config partition's — a disk mountpoint is not worth refusing a boot over. **No migration**: nothing persists an absolute path under it (placements and container records store a disk *name*; the assembly path is rebuilt each boot), and a mountpoint is worthless across a reboot, so the next boot simply lands everything in the new place. One near-miss worth recording — the first cut used `ensure_dir()`, a bare `mkdir(2)`, and `/mnt` is not in the root image, so it would have failed `ENOENT` and **refused the boot**; `persist_mkdir_p()` and the shipped directory both exist to make that impossible.

- **The dashboard called `cix-containers` part of the fixed OS layout, and refused to manage it.** Reported directly: *"we're protecting cix-esp, cix-root-a/b and cix-config right? anything else should be changable."* That is exactly what the daemon implements — `DISKPART_OS_PROTECTED_PARTITIONS` is **4**, and `GET /v1/disks` reports `vda5` (`cix-containers`) as `"protected": false`. The **web UI** was the only thing disagreeing, and it disagreed because it asked the wrong question: it gated on `is_os_disk`, which every partition of the OS disk inherits, instead of on the `protected` field the API already returns. **This is #9 surviving one layer up.** The daemon had exactly this bug — role assignment, format and unmount each keeping their own blanket `is_os_disk` refusal — and fixing it there left the dashboard reimplementing the old rule in JavaScript, which is what an operator actually sees. Eleven call sites moved to `protected`: the role tab's refusal note (which also named five partitions when the rule covers four), the row action cell, the role-assign selector, the format-status poll, the three role-filtered device pickers, and the container storage-placement picker. `is_os_disk` stays only where it states a fact — the OS-disk badge, the partition-table tab, the "Add a partition…" action #140 legalised — and the detail pane no longer claims a non-structural partition is "never modified". **One more thing the same test was hiding**: `refreshDiskFreeSpace()` returned early for the OS disk, so the free-space figure was never fetched for the one disk whose partition-table tab explicitly tells the operator that new partitions can be added there. **And the unmount error now names what is actually holding the mount.** `umount2(2)` returns `EBUSY` for a mountpoint carrying other filesystems, which is indistinguishable from an open file if all you are told is that something "may still be busy/in use" — and on this platform it is *always* submounts for the containers partition, because the rebuildable-storage and container-storage disks mount under `<data-dir>/disks/`. The daemon now lists them and returns 409 rather than a bare 500, asked only after the real call has failed so the kernel stays the judge of what was possible.

- **`cixctl pkg build-log` can name the build it wants (#245).** The command took no arguments at all, so when two builds overlapped the daemon refused it with `400 multiple builds in progress -- specify ?name=&image=` — advice the CLI had no way to follow. That is not a rare corner: **a recipe publish causes it by itself**, queueing a rebuild for every image tracking that package rolling, so the moment an operator most wants to watch a build is exactly the moment the command stopped working. The contract was never the problem — `GET /v1/pkg/build/log` has accepted `?name=` and `?image=` since ADR-0157 Phase 2, documented with both parameters; `cmd_pkg_build_log()` was simply dispatched with no `argc`/`argv` to put them in. Now `--name=` and `--image=` map straight onto those parameters, `--image` without `--name` is refused with a message rather than silently ignored (the daemon ignores it in that combination), and a value that could terminate or extend the query string is rejected **before** it is sent — package and image names are already constrained to that character set by the contract, so a rejection means a typo, not a limitation. Sending no query at all when neither flag is given keeps the request byte-identical to what every earlier client sent, so the "one build in progress" fallback is untouched. Two stale doc claims fixed in the same change: the contract said "up to two package builds can genuinely be in flight", which has not been true since `max_concurrent_jobs` became configurable (10 by default), and neither the API narrative nor the CLI reference mentioned the parameters existed. **Found by using it** — while watching a tcc rebuild that a recipe publish had queued alongside it.

- **The compiler reports C11, because C11 is what it provides (#235, tcc 0.9.28rc-17).** `__STDC_VERSION__` said `199901` while `_Static_assert`, `<stdatomic.h>`, `<stdalign.h>`, `<stdnoreturn.h>`, `_Generic` and `_Thread_local` all worked. That is not a missing feature — those are expensive — but a compiler describing itself inaccurately, which is cheap to fix and silently expensive to leave: portable code **cannot** probe for C11 atomics, there is no way to, so it reads the version macro, takes a worse path for no reason, and every such failure then looks like a missing feature rather than a mislabelled one. `python` has looked like "TCC cannot do atomics" on exactly this basis. **Two edits, correct only together**: the default `cversion` goes to `201112` (which `-std=c11` already set, so the default now matches a mode the compiler already had), and upstream's `__STDC_NO_ATOMICS__` define is deleted — upstream emits it whenever the version is `>= 201112`, so bumping the version alone would announce C11 and deny atomics in the same breath, and that pair is precisely what CPython's `pyatomic.h` reads. `__STDC_NO_COMPLEX__` and `__STDC_NO_THREADS__` stay, because `<threads.h>` genuinely is not shipped and the entire point is accurate self-description. Both sed anchors were checked against the pinned source **before** the build rather than after a failure. Gated at the first build and again at stage 3 — the binary that ships — on the macro **and** on atomics computing the right answer. **Three earlier revisions carried this change and failed, and it was never the cause**: written for rc-11, carried through rc-12 and rc-13 beside the constructor-priority patch, and rc-14 dropped it and failed identically, which is what cleared it. #219 has since been root-caused independently by reading the pinned source — tcc has no sorting *or* merging for `.init_array.NNNNN`, and neither `__init_array_start`/`_end` nor `DT_INIT_ARRAY` covers those sections, so the whole suffixed-section approach could never have worked — so this landed alone. Verified on 192.168.15.95 by `probe-tcc-conformance/21` against the compiler the build environment actually resolves: `201112`, `__STDC_NO_ATOMICS__` not defined, atomics correct, all five C11 features still working. **`python`'s recorded gcc reason is not edited on the strength of this** — ADR-0226 makes a toolchain reason a measurement with a date, and whether python now builds under `CC=tcc` is a real build nobody has run yet.

- **procps builds again, and gettext turned out not to be the problem (#220).** procps could not be rebuilt at all: the composer correctly refused it with `declared build tool "gettext" is not installed anywhere`, and gettext does not link here -- unresolved `libtextstyle_cr_*` references from its bundled libcroco. The obvious reading is that fixing gettext is the prerequisite. It is not. procps only needed gettext because the recipe fetched a GitLab **tag archive**, which ships no generated `configure`, so it had to run `autogen.sh`, which calls `autopoint`, which is part of gettext. procps-ng also publishes an ordinary release tarball carrying `configure`, `aclocal.m4` and every `Makefile.in` already generated -- verified by listing the archive before switching to it, and checksummed identical across two independent fetches. `procps@4.0.6-9` builds from that instead, so no autotools regeneration runs, `autopoint` is never invoked, and **gettext leaves `pkg_build_depends` entirely** -- taking with it the perl-shebang wrappers for `aclocal`/`automake`/`libtoolize`, which existed for no other reason than surviving `autogen.sh`. The generated files are touched after extraction, because the failure mode to design against is make deciding one is stale and reaching for automake's `missing` script, which would quietly reintroduce exactly the dependency this removes. **Every other gap the recipe documents is a configure-or-compile gap and carries forward untouched** -- the `regex.h` VLA prototype, `__GNUC__`/`_GCC_LIMITS_H_`, the `__dso_handle` stub, `--disable-pidwait`, `--disable-numa`. One of them is now unconditional rather than incidental: this tarball's `configure` came from a newer autoconf that tries C11 *before* C99, and tcc passes the C11 probe since ADR-0223, so the C99 block that would have set `ac_cv_prog_cc_c99` is skipped outright and `configure.ac`'s own check then reads it unset -- the upstream inconsistency was always there, the newer autoconf just guarantees you meet it. Built and installed from source on 192.168.15.95 with no artifact tier consulted: 18 files, including `ps`, `free`, `pgrep`, `vmstat`, `sysctl` and `libproc2.so.1`. gettext's own link failure stays open as a real defect in a catalogued package, retitled to drop the claim that it blocks procps, because it no longer blocks anything.

- **Which image can build what is a contract now, not a convention (#182, ADR-0230's CI domain).** `cix-builder` builds the control plane, `kernel-builder` builds kernels, `iso-builder` builds ISO tooling — enforced by **nothing**. `pkg_hostbuild_start()` validated `build_image` only as *"exists"*, never as *"may build this"*, so naming the wrong one passed every check at the API boundary and then failed minutes later deep inside a build container, with a compiler error instead of "that is not what that image is for". A recipe now declares `pkg_build_image=`, and the daemon holds the caller to it: an omitted `--build-image` **resolves** to the declared one (so `cixctl pkg hostbuild cix` just works, rather than the operator having to remember), and a caller naming a different image is refused immediately with both names in the message. Still required for a recipe that declares none, and ordinary package recipes are unaffected. The early "must be non-empty" check had to move after recipe parsing for the resolution to be possible — a malformed name is still rejected on sight, because that is a bad request whatever the recipe says.

- **The API contract was not valid YAML, and nothing noticed because the only thing reading it did not mind.** Two descriptions carried an unquoted colon — `description: The daemon's own settings: bind address, TLS and connection throttle.` — which YAML reads as a nested mapping, so every standard reader rejected `openapi.yaml` outright. `apigen` has its own parser and tolerated them, so the contract this project treats as its source of truth was parseable by exactly one tool in the world. Found while validating an unrelated edit. Both quoted; the whole spec now parses, reporting **184 paths and 276 operations** — which independently confirms the operation count the build gate asserts. **A gate came with the fix**, because fixing two lines fixes an instance and not the class: `test_apigen` now rejects any plain scalar containing `": "`, tracking folded and literal blocks so prose is left alone (it flagged a quoted error message on its first run, which is exactly the false positive that would have made it useless). Proven in the failing direction — the violation was reintroduced, the gate caught it, and it passed again once restored.

- **The platform's five lifecycle domains are named, and control-plane assembly finally has its own status ([ADR-0230](docs/adr/0230-the-five-lifecycle-domains.md), #182).** Cix has a complete delivery pipeline and no *shape*: everything is reachable through two flat namespaces that group by implementation, so `/system/iso` (make media), `/system/update` (stage a control plane) and `/system/reboot` are siblings. #182 asks for three things to be settled before any endpoint moves, and this settles them. **The five domains** — catalogue, CI, CD, host lifecycle, media. **They are named in the CLI, dashboard and docs, not as URL prefixes**: a prefix is clearer to a reader of the URL list, who is the person this helps least, and costs a breaking change across 275 operations, every generated helper and route, the whole CLI tree and every guide — for a gain confined to the least operator-visible surface. There is a quieter reason too: a lifecycle domain is a *view* over resources (assembly touches packages, artifacts, the ESP and the slots), so several endpoints would belong to two domains at once and the prefix would be a lie in the URL rather than an ambiguity in the docs. What would change that answer is written down: a second consumer that reads the contract before the documentation. **And the rule for status**: it belongs to the thing that is happening, never to a neighbour that happens to know about it. `GET /v1/system/assembly` is the first application and #182's own sharpest symptom — assembly had no endpoint at all, and its progress was two generation counters on `/system/boot`, an endpoint whose subject is *what booted* reporting on *what is being built*. Moved, not duplicated, with its one consumer updated in the same change.

- **Published artifacts carry this host's architecture (#183, first concrete step of #179).** `pkg_artifact_build_request()` emitted `<name>-<version>.tar.gz`, so every artifact this host published arrived at the cache unlabelled and was stamped by hand afterwards — two were caught doing exactly that either side of a stamping run in one session. The cache has made architecture part of an artifact's identity since its own ADR-0008 and **deliberately never infers one**, because "everything here was built for this" is something an operator knows and a parser must not guess. It is now added at the single point that builds the request URL for **both** fetch and push, so the two directions cannot drift apart. `uname(2)`'s machine field, asked once; a failure falls back to `unknown` rather than to a bare name **on purpose** — an artifact published as `<name>-<version>-unknown.tar.gz` is visibly wrong and can be deleted, while a bare one is indistinguishable from a correct single-architecture artifact and will be served to a machine that cannot run it. Safe to start requesting stamped names immediately: the cache resolves a bare name for GET/HEAD while exactly one architecture is published, and returns `409` naming the problem once two are, rather than picking one. The **local** cache keeps its unstamped `<name>-<version>.tar.gz`, because a host has one architecture and stamping it would claim a distinction that does not exist there.

- **A recipe can declare the capabilities its build needs, and the gate reached 33 tests — but the capability is worth exactly one of them (#224).** `pkg_build_caps` lets a recipe say what its build container requires; the `cix` recipe declares `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, and with cgroup delegation a build container can now `unshare(CLONE_NEWNET)`, `unshare(CLONE_NEWNS)`, `unshare(CLONE_NEWCGROUP)`, `mount` a tmpfs, `mount cgroup2` and create a cgroup — every syscall the ungated tests need, all measured. **And the full suite goes from 35 of 86 passing to 36.** That number is the finding, and it re-diagnoses the issue: privilege was necessary and is not the binding constraint. With every syscall available the remaining 50 fail on **fixtures** — a real kernel image, dnsmasq, a staged `ld-linux`, the seeded artifact floor — plus one nested `container_create` failing `EINVAL` rather than `EPERM`, which is a wrong spec rather than a forbidden one and is unexplained. Recorded in the Makefile beside the list so the next person doesn't repeat the investigation expecting a bigger prize. The remaining work is provisioning a test fixture image, which is a different and more tractable problem than "find a privileged place to run".

- **A container trusted with `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` now owns its own cgroup subtree, which is what nested containers need (#224).** The route to running the ~50 remaining tests was measured rather than designed: an ordinary container with `cap_add: ["CAP_SYS_ADMIN"]` can already `unshare(CLONE_NEWNS)`, `unshare(CLONE_NEWCGROUP)`, `mount` a tmpfs and `mount cgroup2` — all confirmed on a real host — and then **cannot create one directory inside that cgroup tree**, because the cgroup belongs to real root while the container's root is a mapped uid (`uid_map: 0 3507872 65536`). The kernel's answer is delegation, and it is a chown rather than a capability: the directory plus `cgroup.procs`, `cgroup.subtree_control` and `cgroup.threads`, exactly the set the kernel's delegation guidance names, which is also what systemd does. **The resource-limit files are deliberately not delegated** — `memory.max`, `pids.max` and `cpu.max` are the budget this platform imposed, and a delegatee that can raise its own limits has not been limited; the kernel's model is built around that split. Applied implicitly with `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` rather than as a second knob, because the alternative is incoherent: that capability already grants the mount and the namespace, so withholding the chown leaves a container able to mount the tree and unable to write in it. Only for **userns** containers, and that is the safety argument — the subtree goes to a mapped uid that owns nothing on the host, so "root of its own cgroups" is not root of anything else. Non-fatal if the host refuses: the container still runs, it simply cannot nest. **Three corrections were needed to get here and each was a wrong reading of a real observation**: `CAP_NET_ADMIN` is already granted by default so requesting it is correctly refused; `mount` and cgroup failures were `ENOENT` (missing `/run`, unmounted `/sys/fs/cgroup`) rather than `EPERM`; and the "leaked host bridges" were devices inside the container's own netns, since `/sys/class/net` is not per-netns while `/proc/net/dev` is.

- **The build gate went from 15 tests to 28, and the number came from a measurement (#224).** Two-thirds of the suite was written, committed and executed nowhere — which is not an abstract debt: it is why a contract change to `POST /v1/pkg/recipes` was deferred earlier the same day rather than made, and why the installer seed's refusal path shipped unverified. #224 said the question was *where* they should run and that option 1 "costs one probe to settle", so it was settled. **What a composed build container can do, asked of the kernel rather than assumed**: it is uid 0 with `CapEff 00000000b884fdff`, and `unshare(CLONE_NEWNET)`, `unshare(CLONE_NEWNS)`, `mount()` and creating a cgroup all **fail**. Building the whole suite there and running every binary: **35 of 86 pass**. **Six of those 35 are still excluded, and that is the part worth reading.** A build container shares the host's network namespace and filesystem, so a test can "pass" by mutating the machine it is built on — the probe run left `cix-ctnet0`, `cix-ctnet1`, `cix-test0`, `vt-a` and `vt-b` behind on a real host. Doubling coverage by leaking bridges onto the build machine is not a trade worth making, and CLAUDE.md already records leaked bridges breaking later runs. So `test_network_interfaces`, `test_routes`, `test_daemon_bind_ip` and `test_storage_placement` (shared netns) and `test_esp`, `test_boot_console` (real boot paths) stay out. One more was caught by the gate itself: `test_dual_console` passed when the probe ran it alone and failed inside the build, so it is non-deterministic there rather than unsupported — #224 already had a "needs real consoles" bucket and it belongs in it. **13** join, taking the gate to 28. The rest are confined by construction — each forks its own `cixd` against a fresh `mkdtemp` data directory — and every one was observed passing in that exact environment before being listed. The remaining 51 need #224's option 2 or 3 and the issue now says precisely which and why.

- **gcc fetches from a mirror, because ftp.gnu.org stopped answering this site (#244).** Measured: `ftp.gnu.org` accepts our TCP connections on both 443 and 80 and then sends nothing — 12 s to an empty reply — while `mirrors.kernel.org` and `www.kernel.org` answer from the same host in under a second. Not DNS, not IPv6, not the internet; that one server is not talking to this egress, and **29 recipes' latest revisions fetch from it**, essentially the platform's whole GNU base. It only bites on a source build, which is why it surfaced as `gcc@toolchain` failing a rolling rebuild. `gcc@16.2.0-15` moves to the mirror with `pkg_sha256` unchanged, so nothing about what gets built changes — verified byte-identical (`e6738e29…`). **This should not have been filed as a decision.** `glibc` and `m4` have fetched from that same mirror for some time, and gcc's own recipe header already recorded the tarball as verified byte-identical across both mirrors; the answer was in the repo, in that file, before the question was asked. The remaining 27 are latent — none is blocked until it needs a source rebuild, and each moves to the mirror the next time it bumps a revision, which is the convention those recipe headers already describe.

- **The compiler supplies `__builtin_bswap16/32/64` (#208, tcc 0.9.28rc-16).** The 0.9.28rc upgrade fixed twelve of the fifteen builtins this project had found missing — `ffs`, `clz`, `clzll` and `popcount` all work, measured — and left the three byte-order ones, which are the dangerous ones: TCC emits an ordinary undefined external rather than implementing or rejecting them, and **an undefined symbol is legal in a shared library**, so a `.so` builds, installs, publishes and stays broken until something calls it. That is exactly how libblkid (#176) and libnl shipped. Supplied as real functions in `libtcc1.a`, the same shape as this recipe's own `atomic_compat.c`, so no codegen patch is carried (ADR-0223). **The recipe's gate caught a subtly wrong first attempt, which is the argument for having written it**: the runtime alone is not enough, because with no declaration in scope TCC applies the implicit `int f()` rule — `bswap64`'s 64-bit result gets read as a 32-bit int and truncated, and `bswap16`'s return carries junk in the upper bits. Declarations now sit in `tccdefs.h` beside the `__ATOMIC_*` predefines; **declarations only, never definitions**, which would hand every translation unit an unused static function to warn about under the `-Wall -Werror` this project builds with everywhere. Verified on 192.168.15.95: all seven builtins link and run, and `bswap32` in a shared object reads `resolved`.

- **A rebuild whose install keeps failing is no longer retried forever (#243).** `pkg_try_start_queued_rebuild()` popped an image from the queue **only when every entry in its manifest was already satisfied**. A started-but-*failed* install therefore left the image at the front, still unsatisfied, to be started again on the very next pass — no attempt count, no backoff, no memory of the failure. A package that cannot install at all became an unbounded retry loop that never drained and never yielded the single job slot. Measured on 192.168.15.95: `toolchain` tracks `gcc` rolling, `gcc`'s upstream was unreachable, and the log carried **219 consecutive fetch failures** with `GET /v1/pkg/rebuilds` pinned at `depth 1` and every other package operation refused `409 another package install is already in progress` — which is how it surfaced, by blocking an unrelated probe. **Cancelling does not help, and the reason is worth keeping**: `POST /v1/pkg/cancel` frees the slot correctly (#239) and the drain immediately starts the next attempt on the same still-queued image; the log shows `cancelling fetch (pid 4714)`, `fetch cancelled by operator`, and a fresh fetch moments later. The only escape was a reboot — to work around a network timeout, on a shell-less host. A failing image is now dropped from the queue on **any** failure, not only one leaving the package uninstalled: an upgrade failure keeps the old version installed, which is exactly the gcc case, and the image is no more satisfiable for it. Nothing is lost — the failure is durably recorded on the package entry, and a later publish re-queues the image naturally, which is why the queue is deliberately not persisted in the first place.

- **The rebuild queue is visible, and publishing says what it started (#236).** A publish is documented and implemented as a metadata write, and also queues an image rebuild for every image tracking that package `rolling`. Nothing reported it — not the request, not the response, not any endpoint — so the host committed itself to real work an operator could neither see nor count, which before the event loop stopped blocking on it made the box unusable for minutes. `GET /v1/pkg/rebuilds` now reports the queue (`queued`, `depth`, `capacity`), `cixctl pkg rebuilds` renders it, and queueing logs what it queued **by name** so the consequence appears at the moment it happens rather than only as a pending count afterwards. `depth == capacity` is called out explicitly, because at that point further rebuilds are being **discarded**. **The response body is still empty and that half is deliberately not done**: `POST /v1/pkg/recipes` returns 204, and nine assertions across three daemon-linked test files depend on it — tests that cannot run from the dev sandbox and are not in the build's own selftest set, so changing the contract would mean editing them blind with no way to verify. Recorded on the issue rather than half-changed.

- **Installer media carries a package seed, so a fresh box can name the network (#135, [ADR-0229](docs/adr/0229-installer-media-carries-a-package-seed.md)).** Bringing up a freshly installed host was circular: no recipes without a git forge, no forge without DNS, no DNS without a recipe. The last real bring-up got through it by pushing 298 package and 20 image recipes one at a time from a developer machine, serving the toolchain over plain HTTP from a laptop by literal IP, and pointing the repo URL at an IP — which then failed TLS because the certificate names the host. **Both halves of the fix already existed and neither was used**: `mkinstalleriso` stages `<seed>/recipes` and `<seed>/artifacts` onto the media and `cix-install` copies them into the installed box, while the daemon passed `""` with a comment saying a real seed "changes what the media DOES ... and that is a product decision, not a repair". This is that decision. **Recipes: all of them** — small text, and the complete set is what lets the box build anything afterwards. **Artifacts: only enough to reach DNS** (glibc, zlib, dnsmasq, ~57 MB of which glibc is 56.8) because everything else follows once `dns-1`/`dns-2` resolve the forge — which is exactly the acceptance test #135 states; staging the whole local cache would put gcc, the kernel and the toolchain on the media for no bootstrap benefit. **An explicit list rather than a derivation, deliberately**: deriving it from the `dns` image's manifest would silently change what the media carries whenever an unrelated image changed, and on a host not running DNS would yield an *empty* set — shipping media that claims a seed and cannot bootstrap. A list is visible in a diff. And a missing artifact **fails the whole build**, naming it: incomplete media reveals itself only on the installed box, which is the same silent-success class as an assembly reporting success or a loader file standing in for a C library. ISO grows ~71 MB.

- **Two corrections to the loop metric, both found by using it (#229, follow-ups).** First, the worst-pass high-water was gated on the slow threshold, so a healthy box always read `0` — **indistinguishable from the measurement being broken**, and that ambiguity appeared immediately: zero after a full package install on a real host could not be told apart from a bug. A number that only ever appears once something is wrong cannot be trusted at the moment it finally appears, so every pass is tracked; idle now reads `worst_pass_ms: 3`, and twenty passes of the 1.8 MB `/v1/pkg` read **131 ms**. Second, `worst_pass_activity` was permanently empty: `activity` is cleared the moment a request finishes dispatching, and a pass is booked at its *end*, so the one field answering "what was it doing" always found it wiped. A per-pass copy fixes it, and empty now genuinely means the pass served no request — which is the informative case. Verified: `{"worst_pass_ms": 118, "worst_pass_activity": "GET /v1/pkg"}` against the endpoint actually driven.

- **The loop can now report being alive and useless at the same time (#229).** `stallwatch` asked one question — is the loop going round — and a daemon can be entirely unusable while the answer stays yes. Measured on 2026-09-01: a publish went unanswered for **247 seconds** and the stall store recorded **nothing**, correctly by its own definitions. The loop never went quiet and no single request was in flight long; it spent seconds of *every pass* starting a rebuild, with every other client waiting to be accepted. A field for the second question (`activity_started_monotonic`) had already been added, with a comment naming this exact problem — and the monitor never read it, so half the mechanism sat there doing nothing. Each pass is now timed, counting work and **excluding the epoll wait**, because that duration is the latency floor every waiting client is subject to. `GET /v1/system/stalls` gains `loop`: `worst_pass_ms`, `last_pass_ms`, `slow_passes`, the threshold, and `worst_pass_activity` — where **empty is informative, not missing**: it means the loop was busy with work no client asked for, which is precisely the case that used to be invisible. A rate-limited `slow-pass` record is appended too, kept as a distinct event from `stall` because "what is it blocked on" and "what is it spending itself on" are different questions with different answers.

- **The dashboard can no longer show green while nothing is answering (#231).** Reported directly: *"when the server died several times, I have no reachability (diode) and tx rx stay green and blink occasionally."* The cause was not the lamps. `fetch()` has no timeout of its own, and during the #237 outages the daemon still **accepted** the connection and simply never answered — so the promise neither resolved nor rejected, neither branch of `refreshHealth()` ran, the reachability state kept whatever it last had, and TX went on blinking on every doomed poll. An indicator that cannot go red while nothing answers is worse than none, because it is trusted. Health checks now carry a 1.5 s `AbortSignal.timeout` (under the 2 s poll interval, so two can never be in flight arguing about the same lamp), and a timeout is reported as what it is — "not answering", distinct from "unreachable", because accepting a connection and then saying nothing is a different fault with a different cause. TX blinking during an outage is left exactly as it was and is correct: a transmit lamp flashes on transmit, and against a red panel with RX dark it reads precisely right. Verified against a stubbed fetch across all three outcomes: healthy → ok, hangs → degraded → error, refused → degraded → error with its own message.

- **The default image never got a real C library, because "runnable" was inferred from a file existing (#241).** Every container made from `base` died instantly with `` /usr/bin/bash: /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.38' not found ``, while `POST /v1/containers` still answered `201 "running"` — which only ever proved the child `execve()`'d. Controlled against storage placement (identical failure with default placement), so not a disk problem. `base` had **46 packages and no glibc among them**: `pkg_seed_default_image_libc()` decided the image was "already runnable" by `stat()`-ing the dynamic **loader file**, and `pkg_seed_image_baseline()` stages a loader and a libc into every image — so the file was always there, the check always short-circuited, and the glibc *package* was never installed. The image then carried a baseline libc for life, and the first binary needing a newer one failed at runtime. It now asks the question it means: is the glibc **package** in this image's manifest. Installing it is idempotent, and the existing guards still refuse cleanly when there is no recipe or no cached artifact. **The pattern is the one this project keeps re-finding** — an assembly that reported success, a `201 running` that meant `execve` returned, a stall store that said the loop was alive: a proxy standing in for the property actually wanted. Verified on 192.168.15.95: after installing glibc into `base`, a container runs and prints `uname -a`.

- **A cancelled fetch says it was cancelled (#239, follow-up).** The first verified cancel freed the chain slot correctly and then recorded `failure_kind: fetch` with `"fetch failed (curl exit status -1)"` — because killing the child produces a real nonzero status and the cancel flag was checked *after* the curl-shaped explanations. An operator could not distinguish their own cancel from the network breaking, and the contract promises `cancelled`. Checked first now, because the operator's intent is the cause and curl's exit status only its consequence.

- **The disk-resize path can explain its own failures (#163, follow-up).** `run_tool_argv()` sent every filesystem tool's stdout and stderr to `/dev/null`, so a missing shared library, a filesystem the tool refused and a failed mount all reached the operator as one identical sentence — the same guess-as-diagnosis failure `g_sfdisk_last_error` was introduced for on the sfdisk path. It captures now, and `DISKPART_ERR_RESIZE_FS_FAILED` carries the reason. It paid for itself on the next attempt, which said `could not create the scratch mount point /run/cix-resize-vdb1: No such file or directory`: `/run` exists in this project's minimal container **images** and not on the host's own squashfs root, so an image fact had been applied to the host. One shot instead of a guessing round. (Note `run_sfdisk_capture()` could not be reused for this — it hardcodes `execve(DISKPART_SFDISK_BIN, ...)` and ignores `argv[0]`, so calling it for another tool silently runs sfdisk with that tool's arguments.)

- **A btrfs partition can be grown, and the platform can finally maintain the filesystem it is built on (#163).** `diskpart_resize()` refused any filesystem but ext4, and the reason given was real: `btrfs filesystem resize` needs the filesystem MOUNTED, the exact opposite of `resize2fs`, while the table rewrite needs it unmounted. So it is a different flow, and it is now written: the entry grows unmounted, then the partition is mounted at a private scratch point under `/run` (these images have no `/tmp`), `btrfs filesystem resize max` runs, and it is unmounted again on every outcome — leaving it exactly as it was found. **Investigating it turned up something larger**: Cix's own `btrfs-progs` package shipped **only `usr/sbin/mkfs.btrfs`**. On a platform whose storage substrate is btrfs (ADR-0207), nothing could grow, scrub or query a filesystem it had created — there was no `btrfs` binary anywhere on a host to call. `btrfs-progs 7.1-8` builds and installs it (`make mkfs.btrfs btrfs`, still two named targets rather than a bare `make`, keeping the recipe's deliberate economy), and `mkbootroot` stages it — the same "declared `_BIN` macro that was never staged" gap that made `sfdisk` and `mkfs.btrfs` each fail at `execve()` on every installed host once before. **One extra guard, because the failure this path exists to prevent is silence**: after the table grows, the kernel's own reported size is re-read, and if it has not changed the filesystem is deliberately *not* grown and a 409 explains why — `resize2fs` and `btrfs resize max` would both otherwise grow to the OLD bound and exit 0, telling an operator the resize worked when nothing was gained.

- **A stuck fetch can be cancelled, instead of holding the box hostage (#239).** `pkg_cancel()` accepted a fetching entry, set the cancel flag and did nothing else, on the stated reasoning that "a fetch is a host-side subprocess, not a container — there is simply nothing for the caller to kill", leaving the flag to be honoured by "whichever completion path runs next". That has a hole: **if the fetch never completes, no completion path ever runs.** Confirmed live during this session's own work — `gcc@toolchain` sat in `fetching` for over half an hour retrying an unreachable `ftp.gnu.org`, held its chain slot, made every install and hostbuild return `409 another package install is already in progress`, and `POST /v1/pkg/cancel` returned **200 having changed nothing**; a reboot was the only way out, which on a shell-less host is a heavy remedy for a network timeout. It blocked a deploy. The fetch is a real forked child, so the chain now records its pid and cancel `SIGKILL`s it — which makes its pidfd readable, which drives the ordinary completion path, which honours the flag. The existing machinery finishes the job; cancel only has to end the child.

- **A partition's GPT label could be read off the wrong disk (#240).** `disk_enumerate()` chose *which disk's GPT to open* from `parent_name` before `disk_name_from_partition()` had computed it — and `parent_name` is declared inside the loop, so the read used **uninitialised stack**, in practice whatever the previous iteration left there. Attaching a second GPT disk to 192.168.15.95 and creating `cix-cstore` on it produced: `vda1 label='cix-cstore'`, `vdb1 label='cix-esp'` — each disk's partition 1 wearing the other's label. **It was invisible for the platform's entire life because a Cix host had exactly one partitioned disk**, so the leftover value was always the OS disk's name and the wrong-by-construction read was always accidentally right; it needs two GPT disks to show. Nothing was ever written to the wrong disk (`read_gpt_partition_name()` is `O_RDONLY` and `sfdisk` only ever ran against the requested device), but `strlen()` on that buffer can run past its 32 bytes and the resulting partition number is arbitrary, so this is a real memory bug and not only a reporting one. Fixed by computing the parent before using it. **The wider point**: CLAUDE.md already recorded `part_label` as a late-arriving attribute that can read empty after boot, and #140 deliberately keyed its protected-partition rule on the partition *number* because "a protection a rename can lift is not a protection" — both judgements were better founded than they knew, because a label could not merely be stale, it could belong to another disk. It has **no unit regression guard**: `disk_enumerate()` reads `/sys/class/block` through a compile-time constant with no injectable root, and this sandbox has no block device nodes at all. Making that root injectable is worth doing and is not done here.

- **The OS disk's reserved free space is finally usable (#9).** #140 made appending a partition to the OS disk legal — the whole point being that an operator who sized `cix-containers` smaller than the disk could use the remainder. But role assignment, format and unmount each kept their own blanket `is_os_disk` refusal, and **a partition inherits `is_os_disk` from its parent**, so the appended partition could be created and then never given a role, never formatted and never mounted. Confirmed on 192.168.15.95: appending `vda6` into 83.6 GiB of free space returned `201` with every existing partition byte-identical and the kernel aware of it without a reboot, and then `POST /diskroles` and `POST /disks/vda6/format` both returned `400 this disk holds the fixed OS layout`. Reserved space that could be carved and not used — the same bug #140 fixed, surviving one layer down. All three guards now ask `diskpart_os_layout_untouchable()`, one rule shared with the delete and resize paths rather than three spellings of the question: the OS disk **as a whole** stays refused, so do its first four structural partitions, and nothing else relaxes — a format still demands a role, an unmounted target and a matching `confirm_disk_name`.

- **Starting a rebuild no longer makes everything else wait (#238, [ADR-0228](docs/adr/0228-build-environment-composition-runs-in-a-forked-child.md)).** Composing a build environment (ADR-0199) walks and copies every file of every declared build tool -- for `toolchain`, gcc, glibc and binutils -- and it ran inline in the event loop. Measured on 192.168.15.95: publishing eleven recipe revisions back to back, ten took **8-57 ms** and one took **247,591 ms**, with the audit log bracketing the gap exactly (23:28:02 -> 23:32:12). Composition now runs in a forked child watched on a pidfd (`CONN_PKG_BUILDENV`), exactly as the fetch child already was, and the install resumes when it exits. **The resume carries no state at all**: it re-derives the recipe from the chain and calls the same preparation function, which reaches `buildenv_image_for()`'s existing already-composed fast path -- indistinguishable from a first call that found the environment ready. That works only because image state lives on disk (`image_current_version()` re-reads `manifest.json` every call, no cache), which is now a load-bearing property rather than an incidental one. Two details cost real thought: the child **closes every inherited descriptor**, because unlike the fetch child it never `execve()`s so `SOCK_CLOEXEC` does nothing for it and it would otherwise hold live client sockets open for the whole composition -- reintroducing #237's symptom through the fix meant to prevent it; and a **failed composition deletes its image**, because the already-composed check skips an empty one, so a leftover would be re-forked on every attempt forever. **The instrumentation recorded nothing for those four minutes**, and that is the finding worth keeping: the loop kept heartbeating because it kept going round doing seconds of work per pass -- alive by the only measure it has, unusable by every other. That is #229 with a real case attached, and it is also how the first write-up of #238 came to claim, wrongly, that nothing else was served during the window; that claim was inference rather than measurement and was corrected on the issue.

- **The daemon can no longer be frozen by a client that stops reading (#237, [ADR-0227](docs/adr/0227-responses-are-buffered-and-drained-never-blocking.md)).** This was the actual cause of the "the box hung, I reset it" episodes, and it is not the one that had been chased. `cixd` wrote every response by putting the client socket back into **blocking** mode and writing the whole body inline, in its single event loop. So one client issuing an ordinary GET and then not reading held the entire control plane off for as long as it liked — unauthenticated, no misbehaviour needed beyond being slow. Measured on 192.168.15.95 with one client requesting `GET /v1/pkg` (**1,798,212 bytes** on that host) and never reading it: health went from **7 ms** to **hard timeout on eight consecutive samples**, and back to **14 ms** the instant that socket closed. Responses are now built into a per-connection buffer and drained on `EPOLLOUT`; the common case (the whole thing fits in the socket buffer) closes exactly as before, and a peer that makes **no** write progress for 30 s is dropped so it cannot pin a connection forever — the deadline is measured from the last byte that actually moved, so a genuinely slow reader keeps resetting it and is never punished for being slow. `tls_write_some()` is the non-blocking counterpart of `tls_write_all()`, existing as a real function because OpenSSL requires a `WANT_WRITE` retry to repeat byte-identical arguments. The HTTP layer gained a response **sink** hook rather than a direct call, since the buffer lives on `main.c`'s `struct conn` which that layer must not know about — with no sink installed it behaves exactly as it always did, which is what leaves WebSocket and exec writers untouched. Every `struct conn` is now `calloc`'d, not `malloc`'d: the new fields are only correct if they start zeroed, and 25 sites setting fields by hand is a defect waiting for the next field. **Two things are worth recording beyond the fix.** First, the dashboard polls `/v1/pkg` — so on a phone or a slow link the operator's own browser was the slow reader, and the thing wedging the control plane was the thing built to watch it, which is exactly why reachability died while TX/RX kept blinking. Second, `stallwatch` had been naming the cause correctly for days: `{"state":"S","wchan":"wait_woken","activity":"GET /v1/pkg"}` — a socket wait, on a request that is not a build — while the investigation went to the rebuild queue and build-environment composition instead. Those were real costs and worth removing (#236 above), but they were not this. `test_slow_client` now reproduces the original failure exactly and additionally asserts the write deadline fires.

- **Composing a build environment copies by reference now, not by byte (#236).** The innermost cost behind the publish hang: composing an environment copies **every file of every declared tool** — for a toolchain, gcc, glibc and binutils, thousands of files and hundreds of megabytes — through a 4 KB `read()`/`write()` loop, in the daemon's own event loop, so every byte moved is a byte during which nothing else is served. Every image lives on one btrfs filesystem (ADR-0207), so those copies can be **reflinks**: `FICLONE` shares extents instead of duplicating them, and the result is a full independent copy semantically, with copy-on-write handling later divergence. The read/write loop stays untouched as the fallback and takes over cleanly wherever cloning is unsupported or crosses filesystems — which is the dev sandbox and any non-btrfs deployment — so nothing depends on which path ran. `FICLONE` is spelled out rather than pulled in from `<linux/fs.h>`, which is exactly the kernel-uapi-beside-glibc header fight CLAUDE.md warns about, and the value was verified against a standalone TCC compile: `0x40049409`, the kernel's own.

- **Publishing a recipe stopped hanging the daemon (#236).** `POST /pkg/recipes` called `try_start_queued_pkg_rebuild()` **before writing its response**, so a client publishing a recipe waited while the daemon forked a build container and composed a build environment. Measured at **10,981 ms for a single metadata-only publish**, with the single-threaded event loop blocked throughout; twenty-one of them made the host unusable for long enough to need a manual reset, twice. Two independent faults, fixed separately because they are separate. **The ordering**: publishing is a write, and its response should not be gated on build work the publish merely made *eligible* — the response is now written first and the queue kicked after. **The cost**: the queue walk re-derived every rolling entry's target version with a directory scan plus a full recipe parse, per package, per call — and it runs over every entry of every queued image, with `toolchain` alone declaring 27 packages rolling. It now goes through `recipe_latest_version()`, which is that same pair memoised against the package directory's own mtime and size. "Re-derived fresh every call" is preserved exactly, because the cache is invalidated by the directory changing, which is precisely when a new version appears. **Worth recording that `stallwatch` reported nothing throughout, correctly**: the loop never stopped, it was doing real work. The daemon was unusable and healthy by its own definition simultaneously — which is #229's measurement gap, not a missed event. **Corrected after measuring the first attempt**: moving the kick to *after* the response did not help the client, because every response carries `Connection: close` and the socket is not closed until the handler returns — so a publish still took **12,257 ms** for `glibc`. And the cost is not only the walk: making an image unsatisfied starts a real install, which composes a build environment. The drain is now off the request path entirely — the event loop starts a queued rebuild on its next pass, guarded by a cheap depth check, since calling an expensive drain speculatively every pass would be worse than the bug. Publishing answers immediately; the rebuild begins within one loop pass. **The loop is still blocked while a rebuild is being started** — a real remaining cost, stated rather than implied fixed.

- **The dashboard no longer has two things scrolling on a phone (#233).** `.tree-panel { max-height: 40vh }` made the tree its own scroll container at mobile width, because its content is taller than 40% of a phone screen. Two scrollables stacked vertically is the classic trapped-gesture bug: a drag starting over the tree scrolls the tree, a drag two pixels lower scrolls the page, and neither is what the finger meant — the desktop layout is an app shell where exactly one inner region scrolls, and carrying a piece of that into a document that scrolls as a whole gets the worst of both. **Diagnosed by measurement, not inspection**: a script injected into a headless render reported every element that overflows and every nested scroll container, naming `NAV#tree` directly; after the fix only `BODY` remains, which is the document scroll itself. Two honesty notes. The horizontal scrollbar visible in the first phone-sized screenshot was **an artifact of headless clamping the viewport to 500px** inside a 390px window, not a real defect — it would have been easy and wrong to report it. And this leaves the tree occupying the top of every page, which is not the right final answer: a phone probably wants it behind a disclosure, and that is a design change needing a real device to judge, so it stays recorded rather than guessed at.

- **The dashboard uses the Cix palette and typography (#232, first pass).** The brand's ten material colours — carbon, ferrite, machined, paper, nickel, copper, phosphor, bus blue, amber, fault — are now defined **once**, and the semantic tokens map onto them, so "what colour is a warning" and "what is Amber" each have exactly one answer and the two cannot drift. All four theme states (bare `:root`, the `prefers-color-scheme` media query, and both `data-theme` stamps) were updated together and asserted to define the same set, which is the trap that leaves one state rendering a half-changed palette. Dark now sits on carbon with ferrite panels and machined borders instead of generic grey; light uses warm paper rather than sterile white, which the guidelines ask for by name. Two signal colours get a derived darker sibling for use as *text* on a light ground — phosphor and amber are tuned to glow on carbon and do not carry contrast on paper — while staying exactly as specified wherever they are a lamp. Typography names Inter and JetBrains Mono with the guidelines' own fallbacks, resolved locally and never fetched: this daemon is not going to load a font from someone else's CDN, and the dashboard has to work on a disconnected machine. Verified by rendering both themes headless and looking at them, rather than by reading hex values. **Not done, and not claimed**: the 8px spacing base, the 12-column grid, the shipped SVG icon set, and the editorial-voice pass over interface copy.

- **A failed request now tells the status lamps immediately (#231).** `refreshHealth()` polls every two seconds and owned the lamp colour outright, so a click that failed *right now* left the panel showing the previous poll's answer — green, while the thing the operator had just watched fail had already failed. The evidence was there and was being discarded. A `fetch()` that throws is now counted into the **same** consecutive-failure tally rather than a second one, so a real outage still needs two failures before going red and a single blip still reads as degraded; this adds evidence to that count rather than inventing a second opinion about reachability. **TX deliberately still blinks before the request is sent**: a transmit lamp flashes on transmit whether or not anything answers, which is what the panel this imitates does — the missing half was that a failed exchange left no trace at all. Worth recording that the original report was mostly #230: the current stylesheet already recolours *both* lamps to `--error` and pulses them, so the "stayed green" behaviour was a stale cached `app.js`, and the panel was never as wrong as it looked.

- **The dashboard was served with no caching information at all, so a deployed change could stay invisible (#230).** No `Cache-Control`, no `ETag`, no `Last-Modified`, and assets referenced without a version marker — a browser given nothing is free to invent a freshness lifetime and keep what it has. That cost real time: a stale `app.js` made LED behaviour look broken while the source said otherwise, and the report was investigated against code the browser was not running. Shipping a dashboard change here costs a hostbuild, an A/B slot write and a reboot, so a change that then cannot be seen wastes all of it. **Fixed with validation rather than expiry**: every static response now carries an `ETag` and `Cache-Control: no-cache`, which does not mean "do not store" but "store, and revalidate before reuse". The browser keeps the file and asks whether it still holds; an unchanged file is answered with a **304 carrying no body**, so being always-correct costs a round trip instead of a download, and no build step or content-hashed URL is needed. The tag is mtime and size rather than a content hash, deliberately — hashing would mean reading every byte of every file on every request to answer a question that is almost always "unchanged", and the case it misses (two files sharing an mtime to the second *and* a byte count) does not arise for an asset rewritten wholesale by an install. A weakened validator (`W/"..."`, which an intermediary may substitute) is accepted too: not doing so would silently re-download a file the client already had, and a correct-looking 200 is exactly the kind of failure that stays invisible.

- **A gate that read comments as calls (#234).** `test_api_surfaces` checks two things about each operation and only one of them ignored comments: the path check skips a line whose first non-space characters open a comment, while the exposure check substring-searched each client file whole. So a comment *naming* an operation's generated constant was indistinguishable from a call to it — and a comment written to explain why the CLI must **not** call an unexposed operation failed the build for calling it. The explanation had to be reworded around the checker, which is the wrong way round: a gate should not make correct code harder to explain. Fixed by blanking whole comment lines before the search, so both halves apply the same rule — not an exception, the rule the other half already used. Deliberately line-leading rather than a real comment parser, for the reason the path check gives for the same choice: a parser must know that `/*` inside a string literal is not a comment and that the `//` in an `https://` URL is not one either, and `web/app.js` contains both. The change is **self-verifying** — the reworded comment was restored to name the constant plainly, so the build passing is the proof, and it was simulated against the real files first (the token present before blanking, absent after, with real calls still detected).

- **The disk allocation chart now works for a disk with no partitions.** It bailed on `parts.length === 0`, so the OS disk drew a full donut while `sda` — the whole-disk btrfs that actually carries images and artifacts, and the one that fills up as packages are built — drew nothing at all. A partitioned disk is carved up by its partition table, so its segments are partitions; an unpartitioned one is carved up by its own filesystem, so its segments are used and free, from `statvfs` figures the daemon already reported (ADR-0142). **No daemon change was needed** — `used_bytes` and `free_bytes` were already in `GET /v1/disks`; I had claimed otherwise off a response I truncated at 400 characters, which cut them off. Filesystem overhead is shown as its own segment rather than folded away, because a chart whose parts do not add up to the whole is the small wrongness that makes someone distrust the rest of the page: on `sda` that is used 18.9%, free 79.3%, overhead 1.79%, totalling exactly 1.0000 of the disk.

- **A fresh box can seed its own build image in one command (#141).** `cixctl image materialize NAME` creates the image, declares its manifest from the image recipe, and installs every package in it. Measured against a brand-new image: the full 27-package toolchain, **gcc included, in 32 seconds, with no compilation at all**. The capability turned out to already exist and only the shape was missing — the decisive line is in `pkg.c`, where an artifact-tier install verifies against the recipe's own checksum and `_exit(0)`s straight to staging **without composing a build sandbox**, so a host with no compiler can install any approved package. What stood in the way was coverage: of the toolchain's 27 packages, 26 were approved after the earlier backfill and the last gap was `tcc@0.9.28rc-9`, missed because my version sort ranked `0.9.27-14` above it by comparing "27" against "28rc". This is deliberately **client-side**: every endpoint it uses already existed, so it needs no daemon change, no A/B slot write and no reboot, and the API-First rule stands exactly as written. It also removes the reason `pkg bootstrap`'s host-`/usr`-copy mode exists (#168, ADR-0225). One bug found by running it: a package pulled in as another's build dependency answers 409 *already installed*, which the first version reported as failure — so a run that worked perfectly announced "5 of 27 package(s) did not install".

- **#224 diagnosed to one named blocker, and it found two real bugs on the way.** Five probes on a real Cix host, because the issue said option 1 costs one probe to settle. A build container turned out to be entirely capable — uid 0, `CapEff 00000000b884fdff`, writable data dir, fork/waitpid — with loopback down (fixed, above), and after that a `cixd` starts and answers HTTP inside one. Two bugs surfaced that nothing could have caught: **`test_pkg.c` had never compiled** (six string literals broken by real newlines; the cix recipe builds eight named binaries and `make selftest` fourteen, so it is in neither), and **`test_dns` staged Debian's dnsmasq closure** — twenty hardcoded libraries including libsystemd, for a binary whose Cix build declares exactly two, with a failure message advising `apt-get install dnsmasq`. `elfcheck_needed_libs()` now reads `.dynamic` so the test stages what the binary declares rather than what another distribution's did. The tree compiles clean on a Cix host: **112 binaries, 0 errors**. What remains is one mount: `mountns_pivot()` gives a container `/proc`, sysfs, tmpfs `/run` and devpts and never mounts cgroup2, so a container that creates containers cannot make a cgroup — correct for an ordinary container, wrong for a build sandbox running this suite. Three costed options are recorded on the issue; the choice changes what a container can do, so it is a decision rather than a fix, and is left as one.

- **The 67 daemon-linked tests could not run in the build gate for one reason: loopback was down (#224).** The issue named three possible homes for them and said the first cost one probe to settle, so `probe-daemon-tests` measured it on a real build container instead of reasoning about it. The answer was better than expected — **uid 0, `CapEff 00000000b884fdff`, a writable temp dir, fork and waitpid all fine, and both test binaries compiled** — with a single blocker: `bind: Cannot assign requested address` on `127.0.0.1`. A fresh network namespace has `lo` present but **down**, and the bring-up lived inside `container_net_child_configure()`, which `container.c` calls only when `net_count > 0`. Every package build sandbox is deliberately network-isolated, so it had no working loopback either — invisible until something binds it, and then it fails as what reads like a configuration mistake rather than a missing interface. `container_net_child_loopback_up()` now runs for any container with its own netns. **Loopback is not network access**: it reaches nothing outside the namespace, so a build sandbox stays exactly as isolated from the network as before; what changes is that it stops being isolated from *itself*, which no real Linux system is and no software expects to be. Along the way every child exit code got a name — 123 was in use for the direct-rootfs bind with no entry, noticed only because reusing it for the loopback failure would have made the table state the wrong cause, and 125's three volume-mount cases were unnamed too. There are now none left undecoded.

- **Two things the first running-config build got wrong, both found by fetching the real document from a real host.** It compiled cleanly, every gate passed, and the daemon served **1.8 MB of JSON that was malformed 914 bytes in**: `backupconfig_write_json()` writes bare members for a caller to splice into an object it already opened, not a value, so the document contained `"backup":,`. It is the only one of the 33 writers shaped that way — audited, not guessed — and it is wrapped at the new call site rather than changed, because its existing caller depends on that shape and the cost of a second caller belongs to the second caller. And the document was **99.7% one section**: `packages` rendered 1806 KB, of which **1756 KB was `files[]` manifests**. A package's file list is the *result* of configuration, not configuration, and neither is a build error or whether an artifact was cached. `pkg_write_json_config()` renders what a config document means by a package — name, image, version, state — which is the difference between something you read, diff and paste into a review and something you scroll past. Extracting it needed the state-to-name switch, so that is now one `pkg_state_name()` both callers share rather than a second switch over the same enum, which is the pair that drifts the next time a state is added.

- **`show running-config`: the whole configuration as one ordered, redacted document (#150, ADR-0206).** An operator asking *what is this box configured to do?* had no answer short of visiting a dozen endpoints and assembling the picture by hand. `GET /v1/config` renders **33 sections** — identity, resolver, time, sysctl, kernel modules, swap, disk roles, volumes, backup, routes, networks, DHCP, DNS, PKI, LDAP, syslog, packages, images, containers — and `cixctl show running-config` renders them Cisco-style. Three properties are the design, not details. **Derived, never stored:** a kept rendering would be a second source of truth for every setting and would drift, which is what `One Source of Truth` exists to prevent. **Order is the contract:** a section never depends on one below it, so the document reads in the order the state would have to be built, and containers come last because they consume everything above. **Secrets are never rendered** — checked rather than assumed: every reused subsystem writer was read first, and the ones holding a secret already emit `auth_token_set`/`bind_password_set` rather than a value. **The section list has exactly one definition.** ADR-0206's fifth point is the owner's hard requirement — the schema generates the vocabulary, nothing hand-maintains a second copy — so `tools/apigen.c` now reads the `ConfigDocument` schema and emits an X-macro that `daemon/src/config.c` expands into its renderer table: a section in the schema with no renderer does not compile. Adding a configurable subsystem to this platform is a schema edit plus a renderer, and forgetting either fails the build rather than shipping a document that looks complete and is not. The presentation is deliberately the CLI's (ADR-0205) — the text is never parsed back, so its format is not a contract, which is what lets it change without a daemon rebuild, an A/B slot write and a reboot. `POST /v1/config` (apply) and `/config/diff` are deliberately not in this change; they are the half that mutates state. The dashboard renders the same document its own way — its own leaf in the tree rather than a tab, because it is not a facet of one subsystem but every subsystem at once — with a Copy button, since being pasted into a ticket is the point and is also exactly why it is redacted first. **Both gates fired on the first build and were right to**: `test_apigen` refused a route count that changed without the number being updated deliberately, and `test_api_surfaces` caught `getConfig` declaring `x-cix-expose: [web]` with no dashboard caller — the API-First mandate noticing a declared surface that did not exist. The honest fix was to build the view, not to downgrade the declaration.

- **A recipe comment that can go stale now cannot go unnoticed (#226).** Every artifact-approved recipe explains itself with `# With it set, an install fetches <artifact base_url>/zlib-1.3.2-9.tar.gz` — a **hardcoded** filename, copied forward verbatim on each version bump and never updated. 113 recipe revisions name a file that is not theirs; `bison@3.8.2-7` still said `bison-3.8.2-2.tar.gz`, five revisions on. Nothing breaks — the checksum, the load-bearing part, was always right — but a comment that exists only to explain was telling the reader the wrong thing. **None of the 113 can be fixed**: a published revision is immutable and `pkg_recipe_add()` permits exactly one edit, adding an absent checksum; correcting a comment alongside it was refused with HTTP 409, which is the rule working. So `test_recipe_hygiene` is a guard rather than a cleanup, and it scans only each package's **latest** revision — 39 of them — which is what lets the number fall as packages bump. The convention going forward is to stop hardcoding the name at all (`<name>-<version>.tar.gz`), which the test accepts and which cannot drift.

- **A successful install kept reporting the previous attempt's failure (`failure_kind`).** `pkg_fail()` sets both `error` and `failure_kind`, but only `error` was ever cleared — not on a fresh attempt, not on success. So `efivar@iso-builder` sat at `state: installed`, `version: 39-5`, `error: null`, `failure_kind: "build"`, and anything keying on that field read a healthy package as failed. Found by being bitten: the loop draining package drift branched on it and declared a successful build a failure. Cleared at both sites that already clear `error`.
