- **efivar stopped building, and it was glibc getting more precise rather than efivar going wrong (#187).** Retiring `libc-dev` did not merely swap a package — it moved the build from glibc 2.36 headers to **2.44**, which carry a C23 const-generic `bsearch`: with a `const` BASE the macro yields `const void *` instead of `void *`. efivar searches two const tables and assigns the result to a plain `struct efivar_guidname *`, so `guid.c:88` and `:205` became *assignment discards const qualifier* — errors, not warnings, because `ERRORS` defaults to `-Werror`; `-D_GNU_SOURCE` is what turns ISOC23 on despite `-std=gnu11`. **Neither site writes through the pointer**, so const-correcting `:88` properly would change `_get_common_guidname()`'s out-parameter and ripple into its callers — an upstream API change, not a packaging decision. 39-5 appends `-Wno-error=discarded-qualifiers` through `ERRORS_GCC`, which is upstream's own extension point (`ERRORS ?= -Werror $(call family,ERRORS)`), so it lands after `-Werror` and touches nothing else; overriding `CFLAGS` would discard OPTIMIZE/DEBUGINFO/WARNINGS wholesale and `CPPFLAGS` would work only by ordering accident. The failure was invisible until the drift sweep tried the upgrade, since 39-3 stayed installed and working throughout.

- **The artifact cache was nearly inert, and 75 approvals fixed it.** `pkg.c` enters the artifact tier only when a recipe declares `pkg_artifact_sha256`, so an unapproved package is recompiled from source on every host even when its verified bytes already sit in the cache. **152 of 725 recipe revisions carried an approval**; the newest revision of 75 packages did not, including `gcc`, `binutils`, `perl`, `isotools` and `openssl` — 683 MB of already-built artifacts nothing would ever fetch. Each checksum was computed by streaming the artifact through `sha256sum` and cross-checking it against the value the cache advertises; all 75 agreed, which is the point of keeping the checksum in git rather than trusting the server. Proof it engages: `openssl` 3.0.20-2 → 3.0.20-3 in `cix-builder`, formerly a full source build, installed with `artifact_cached: true` **before the first status poll returned**; `isotools` 2.14-9 → 2.14-14 took one second. **A wrong issue was filed and closed along the way (#225)**, claiming the approval was impossible under recipe immutability — the mechanism already existed: `recipe_adds_only_artifact_sha256()` permits exactly one edit to a published version, adding an absent checksum, and refuses replacing one (the #145 failure, where an edited checksum silently sends every install down the source path). The daemon's own error text covers only the refused case and I read it as covering both, without checking the registration path. The rule then proved itself: an attempt to correct a stale comment *in the same change* was refused with HTTP 409, and the corrections were dropped rather than the rule bent. That stale comment turned out to be **113 recipes naming the wrong artifact file** (#226), copied forward across revision bumps — harmless, since the checksum was always right, and fixable only at each recipe's next bump.

- **Every TCC-built package was rebuilt against the new compiler, and only one broke.** #216's fault was *silent* — where two aliased locals are only read and written, it corrupts values and the program exits 0 — so every binary the old compiler produced was suspect, not merely the ones that failed. That makes a full rebuild remediation rather than housekeeping. **A rebuild in place turned out to be impossible**, and not as a matter of taste: installing an already-installed version returns 409, and even delete-then-reinstall is deduped away, because an image version is a hash of the package MANIFEST (ADR-0155) — the same set of `name@version` pairs resolves to the pre-existing directory and the freshly built tree is discarded. So each package took a revision, which is what a distribution does for a toolchain rebuild and which also gives provenance: the version now says which compiler produced the binary. Artifact checksums were dropped from every bumped recipe, since those bytes came from the old compiler. **102 package-image builds across six images; one genuine failure.** `libcap` writes `__attribute__((constructor (300)))`, and the new compiler does not parse a priority argument at all — the only third-party regression the upgrade caused. Measured before choosing a fix (`probe-tcc-conformance/13`): the *bare* attribute works correctly, only the prioritised form is rejected, and gcc handles both. The priority is dropped as a declared loss under ADR-0222, defensible here because a priority orders a constructor against *other* constructors, libcap has one of each, and tcc cannot express a priority on any constructor — so the ordering was never enforceable in a TCC-built system. Filed as its own issue rather than buried, since it is a regression against 0.9.27 and the next package to use that form will hit it too. **Two silent-failure modes surfaced and were filed rather than worked around**: nothing aggregates the daemon's own per-package `available_version`, so drift accumulates unseen — **34 of 139 installed packages were behind their recipes** and nobody knew, found by accident while generating bumps (#217) — and an image rebuild that is deduped away reports `installed` while discarding what it built (#218). Both were also self-inflicted here: the first rebuild pass under-scoped by classifying packages on the *installed* recipe, which for twelve pre-#206 packages declares no build tools, silently dropping sixteen; and the driver's own success check tested `state == installed` without checking the version advanced, so it logged libcap's failure as OK. Caught only by re-reading `available_version` afterwards instead of trusting the driver's tally.

- **The compiler is now a pinned upstream snapshot, and that one change closed four issues (ADR-0223, #216).** `tcc.recipe` builds `mob` commit `2ba12e83` (0.9.28rc) instead of the December 2017 0.9.27 release. The trigger was #216: 0.9.27 gives two simultaneously-live locals the **same stack slot** when a `case` label of an enclosing `switch` sits inside the block declaring them, which is why `miniperl` segfaulted — `regexec.c:8131/8132` put `SV *ret` and `REGEXP *re_sv` both at `-0x820(%rbp)`, so `re_sv = NULL` destroyed a value assigned three lines earlier. Root-caused from the real binary rather than by reading: `keep_on_failure` (ADR-0175) preserved the build container, the crashing `miniperl` was pulled off the box, and the faulting address was mapped through `.dynsym` — the binary is stripped, but `-rdynamic` leaves 805 `Perl_*` addresses — then reduced to thirty lines whose only variable is whether the `case` label is inside the block. **The severity was never the crash**: where two aliased locals are only read and written, the fault corrupts values and exits 0, which this project has shipped twice (#122's `tar` listing one member per archive; squashfs byte-swapping every field). perl crashed only by luck of a dereference landing next to the clobber. **No patch existed to take** — Debian carries four tcc patches and none touches codegen, there has been no release since 2017, and Debian itself pins a git snapshot — so the choice was maintaining a codegen patch by hand forever, or pinning. Measured before committing (`probe-tcc-conformance/8`, `/9`, `/10`, all on a Cix host): #216 fixed, **#212 gains real C11**, **#209's `-pthread` accepted** instead of silently dropping the source file, **#208 down from 15 missing builtins to 3**, and #211 handled natively so our patch retires. Five of six local patches are gone, each verified individually. **Every gate is kept, including for bugs the compiler no longer has** — and that judgement paid on the first build: dropping `lib/atomic.c` was *wrong* (upstream defines only the size-suffixed `__atomic_test_and_set_N` and no `__atomic_clear`) and the gate caught it rather than a package doing so months later. Nine revisions, each a real finding: the `__ATOMIC_*` sed targeted a call mob does not have (its own guard failed the build rather than shipping a compiler missing the macros); the `__dso_handle` gate asserted NULL, true only of our own stub, and failed against upstream's *more* correct self-referential value; the bootstrap snapshot pointed `-B` at a directory `make clean` empties; **the bootstrap compared two builds made by different compilers**, so it only ever passed because earlier revisions barely changed codegen, and across a 2017-to-2026 jump it failed and blamed the compiler for not reproducing itself — it does, the comparison was wrong, and it is a real three-stage now; and the library-path fix reached only the first of three configures while its verification grepped for a string that `/usr/lib/<triplet>` matches as a substring, so it **passed vacuously** — a gate that cannot fail is worse than none. **Two latent bugs in our own code** surfaced from the stricter compiler and are fixed: an `enum` used 350 lines before its definition (C has no forward-declared enums; GCC and 0.9.27 tolerated it for five releases), and four files using fixed-width types with no `<stdint.h>` in scope, found by scanning the tree rather than fixing the one the build reached. **Deployed:** `cixd v2.8.2`, built entirely by the new compiler, is running on 192.168.15.95 — booted into slot B with the three-try counter armed, counter cleared afterwards, and verified past `/v1/health` with a real DNS create/read/delete round-trip. One migration hazard recorded in `CLAUDE.md`: inline linkage reverses, bare `inline` starts working and `extern inline` starts failing, so `static inline` is the only durable spelling. perl stays on gcc — its `miniperl` is fine now, but a TCC build fails later linking an XS module with tcc itself crashing; `-shared` was proven sound in general (five cases) before trusting the upgrade, so that is narrow and tracked separately.

- **`perl` builds and installs, on gcc, with the TCC gap declared rather than hidden (#214, #216).** Three revisions built perl with TCC and each found a real gap: `perl.h`'s `PERL_DIAG_STR_(x)` expands to a *parenthesized* string-literal concatenation used as a `char[]` initializer, which TCC's array-initializer parser rejects; `hints/linux.sh`'s `-Wl,-E` needs TCC's own `-rdynamic` spelling, and is load-bearing — stripping it linked fine and then every XS module failed at runtime with `undefined symbol: Perl_croak_nocontext`. The wrapper written for that then translated a **bare `-E`** as well, which is a different flag entirely — preprocess-and-stop, not export-dynamic — so Configure's preprocessor probe got handed a link flag, concluded no C preprocessor existed, and stopped to ask a human to name one. **That is #214, and it is why two builds sat for 110 and 125 minutes holding both slots.** With it fixed the build finally ran through Configure and the whole Unicode table pass, and then `miniperl` segfaulted — deterministically, same address across separate processes. The kernel's own `Code:` bytes decode to a pointer loaded from a local slot, `+0xc`, dereferenced; checked against real perl source rather than memory, `sv.h` puts `sv_flags` at offset 12 and defines `SVs_GMG` as exactly the `0x200000` the next instruction masks, so the trap is **`SvGMAGICAL()` on a NULL SV** (#216). That is codegen, not a recipe problem. perl joins `kernel`, `openssl` and `gcc` on the Tier 3 exception list under **ADR-0222** — a declared capability loss, and explicitly *not* a provenance compromise, since Cix's gcc is its own three-stage bootstrap with stage 2 proven byte-identical to stage 3. The recipe records the whole trail and says perl returns to TCC once #216 is fixed, so the exception cannot quietly become permanent. Two gates now run the perl that was just built rather than trusting `make`'s exit status: one loads a real XS module (the only actual test of that export-dynamic linkage), one runs `crypt()` against a known salt. The second earned itself immediately — `-4` had **no `libxcrypt` declared**, so it was absent from the composed sandbox (ADR-0199) and the build died on its last line trying to `cp` a `libcrypt.so.1` **that no Cix package ships at all** (libxcrypt provides `.so.2`); had the host happened to have one, it would have been staged into the package with no provenance. `-5` declares the dependency, drops the copy, and installs 2766 files with 48 XS modules and zero copied libraries.

- **Uninstalling a package wedges the whole daemon for the duration (#215).** `DELETE /v1/pkg/perl@iso-builder` returned **204 immediately** and 192.168.15.95 then served no HTTP at all for ~16 minutes — the log store shows the entire window silent between two requests. It was not a crash: the box pinged, port 80 completed a TCP handshake, and `cixd` is PID 1 so a death would have panicked the kernel. Uninstall drives `image_produce_new_version()`, which copies the image tree synchronously on the single epoll loop. Two things make it worse than slow: the 204 goes out **first**, so the API reports success and then disappears, and anything monitoring by port check or ping sees a healthy host throughout. Filed rather than fixed here; the build path already forks a child and reports progress, and uninstall needs the same.

- **An in-flight build can be stopped, and only because a person asked (#213).** A build that will never finish held its chain slot until the daemon restarted, because nothing could stop it — found when `perl`'s own `Configure` sat on `No dice. I can't find a C preprocessor. Name one:` for 66 minutes, reading a stdin that would never produce anything. `POST /v1/pkg/cancel`, `cixctl pkg cancel`, and a dashboard action now exist. Deliberately **not** an automatic timeout on silence: `gcc`'s bootstrap goes quiet for long stretches and a large link produces nothing for minutes, so a threshold tight enough to catch a real hang eventually kills a legitimate build mid-way through — and the asymmetry decides it, since failing to kill a hung build costs a slot while killing a live one costs the whole build. `last_output_seconds_ago` has existed since #58; what was missing was the verb to act on it, and a person can tell `gcc` linking from `perl` waiting on stdin where a threshold cannot. The outcome records `failure_kind` **`cancelled`**, not `build` — issue #101 made the kind a required parameter precisely so a failure says what happened, and "an operator stopped this" and "this did not work" call for opposite responses. **Four defects surfaced while building it, three of them only findable by running it, and one would have been genuinely dangerous.** A cancel arriving during build-environment composition — the window after the fetch and before the container exists, which ADR-0199 makes wide — set a flag nothing honoured, so the build went on to succeed and the cancel silently did nothing. `registry_remove()` kills and reaps directly, so the exit never reaches the epoll path that is the *only* place `pkg_build_completed()` is normally called: the container really died and the entry sat in `building` forever still holding its slot (`handle_stop()` had found and documented this exact case for a manual stop, so this uses the same remedy rather than a second one). And the cancel branch recorded the cancellation and then **fell through to the success path**, merging a stopped build's half-finished tree into the image and leaving it `installed` — the operator's cancel overwritten a moment after being written, for want of a `return`. Worth recording how each was found: every diagnosis reasoned from reading the code was wrong, and each one that landed came from making the system report what it observed — the container list, and the entry's own JSON.

- **keepalived has all three firewall backends back, from packages Cix built itself.** `ipset@7.24-8` ships `libipset.so.13`, its 19 headers and `libipset.pc` — 26 files where the previous revision shipped one. The library was never missing: ipset built it on every run and the recipe discarded it, on reasoning that was half right (its own CLI links libipset statically, so no `libipset.so` appears in `ldd src/ipset`) and drew the wrong conclusion (that nothing else could want it). keepalived did, and reported `Use libipset: No` for four revisions while the library sat unshipped in the build tree — the same shape as elfutils withholding `libelf.pc`: a package that genuinely has the thing, and a consumer correctly reporting that it cannot find it. `keepalived@2.3.4-6` now measures **`Use iptables: Yes`, `Use nftables: Yes`, `Use libipset: Yes`**, closing the regression `2.3.4-2` opened. The whole arc is worth reading as one thing: the original 2.3.4 had all three by copying **eight** of Debian's libraries into the package, which looked complete and was not self-hosted; rebuilding from source lost all three; and -3/-4 (nftables), -5 (iptables) and -6 (ipset) each brought one back as its dependency became a real package. That sequence was only possible because each loss was recorded — a build that had silently kept the features using another distribution's libraries would have had nothing to pay back and no record that anything was owed, which is the argument ADR-0222 makes in the abstract. One honest limitation: keepalived **dlopens** libipset rather than linking it, so it does not appear in `DT_NEEDED` and the recipe's linkage assertions cannot see it; the dependency is real and declared, but verified through configure's own summary rather than the binary.

- **`iproute2` builds from source, with `ip vrf` removed and declared — closing #207 (ADR-0222).** The last of the six. It ships 173 files and **zero copied libraries**, where 6.18.0 copied four of Debian's (`libelf-0.188`, `libmnl`, `libcap`, `libz`) straight into the package; `ip` now links `libelf.so.1`, `libmnl.so.0` and `libcap.so.2` from real Cix packages. Blocked on a genuine TCC bug rather than a packaging gap: `ip/ipvrf.c` builds a BPF program from an array of designated compound literals, which TCC miscompiles by using a struct field's byte offset as an array index (#211, twelve-line reduction). Per **ADR-0222** the command family is removed and *declared* — `ip vrf exec/identify/pids` and `ipnetns.c`'s `vrf_reset()` call are gone, `ip link ... type vrf` is untouched, and the recipe asserts both directions so neither half can be wrong silently. Getting from "compiles one object short" to "installed" took six further revisions, and every one was a real gap: `strdupa` is gated on `__GNUC__` which TCC does not define, so it silently became an undefined symbol at link (mapped to `strdup`, declared — stack to heap cannot dangle, and the leak is bounded by a CLI process); `-Wl,-export-dynamic` is unsupported, and `SHARED_LIBS=n` removes it at **no** cost here, checked rather than assumed (the previous build produced zero `.so` modules, so there was nothing to dlopen); `bison` and `flex` were undeclared, needed only by `tc`'s ematch grammar — which is why they surfaced only after `ip` had already linked, a reminder that a build reaching its last directory has proven only the tools the earlier directories needed. **And `HOSTCC` arrived from the build environment as `gcc`** while `config.mk` set only `CC:=tcc` — netem's host tools would have been built by a compiler the recipe never asked for, and it failed *loudly* here purely because gcc is not among this recipe's declared tools, which is ADR-0199's composed environment doing its job. Now pinned. Two of the six were self-inflicted and both were repeats of documented traps: backticks inside a double-quoted `pkg_changelog` (so the shell ran the command being described), and a capability check that read the binary's symbol table — the binary is stripped, `nm` reported **0** entries, so the "removed" half passed vacuously while the "retained" half failed. It now checks the build inputs, which are deterministic.

- **Compiler claims must be measured on Cix's own compiler, not a dev sandbox's (#208–#211).** Four TCC conformance issues were filed in one sitting, every one of them probed against this dev sandbox's `/usr/bin/tcc` — which is **Debian's** tcc 0.9.27, not Cix's `tcc@0.9.27-10`. Nothing built locally was ever published, so the Build Provenance Mandate held; the failure was of *validity*, not provenance — the answers were about the wrong compiler. Two proofs of divergence had already appeared in the same session and were not acted on: Debian's tcc rejects anonymous unions in the kernel's `bpf.h` that Cix's parses, and compiles a `bpf_insn` reduction that Cix's rejects. `recipes/package/probe-tcc-conformance` now re-runs the lot on a Cix host, following `probe-gcc-headers`' pattern — a scratch recipe that deliberately exits nonzero so its diagnostics are kept in the build log. **Two claims did not survive.** #208's builtin list was short by seven — `memcpy`, `memcmp`, `memset`, `memmove`, `alloca`, `offsetof` and `ctzl` are *also* missing on Cix's tcc, and all seven were reported present by Debian's, which is why they were never listed; `iproute2` had been assessed as "all host-side builtins supported" on that basis and uses six of them, so the reasoning was unsound rather than merely lucky. And the CLAUDE.md note on inline linkage, **wrong twice now**: it originally said `static inline`, was corrected to `extern inline` from the bad probe, and Cix's tcc says neither — `static inline`, `static` and `extern inline` all come out file-local and link, while bare **`inline`** is the one that collides, which is consistent with the m4 evidence all along since gnulib's `_GL_INLINE` expands to bare `inline`. #209, #210 and #211 reproduce exactly and are unchanged, and #211's twelve-line reduction turns out to reproduce on Cix's tcc too, which makes it usable as a regression gate.

- **`iptables` builds from source with the nftables backend on, and `keepalived` gets both firewall backends back (#206, #207).** 1.8.13 passed `--disable-nftables` for a correctly-diagnosed reason — `configure.ac` requires `libnftnl >= 1.2.6` and the ambient Debian one was 1.2.4 — and that constraint expired the moment `libnftnl@1.2.9-2` became a Cix package. `iptables@1.8.13-4` now produces `xtables-nft-multi` and the full nft binary set alongside the legacy ones, 184 files and 121 extension modules. It also **ships headers and pkg-config files**, which the old recipe deleted as "not runtime-needed" — that deletion was the entire reason nothing could build against `libxtables`/`libip4tc`/`libip6tc`. Note configure treats libnftnl as a *probe*, so a missing or too-old one silently yields a legacy-only build that installs cleanly (the #113 shape), which is why the recipe asserts the version up front and asserts `xtables-nft-multi` exists afterwards. `keepalived@2.3.4-5` then measures `Use iptables: Yes` and `Use nftables: Yes`, closing the capability regression its own `-2` introduced. Worth stating plainly, because -2 through -5 read as a sequence of retreats: the original 2.3.4 had all three features by copying **eight** of Debian's libraries into the package, and every revision since has paid that back one real dependency at a time. Two revisions were spent on this project's own gaps rather than iptables' — **#209 filed** (TCC does not split GCC's `-Wp,a,b,c` comma lists, so every `libxt_*.oo` failed), and one assertion of mine that looked for `libxtables.pc` when the pkg-config *module* is named `xtables`.

- **`libnl` and `libnftnl` are packaged, and `iw` stops shipping Debian's libnl (#207).** `libnl@3.11.0-4` builds all six library families with correct SONAMEs; it took four revisions and three of the failures are worth keeping. The version-script guard used `grep -r --include=`, which this build image's grep reads as a *filename*, so the guard failed on its own error before `make` ran. Then configure, make and `make install` all exited 0 and **the #176 install gate refused the result** — `libnl-route-3.so` carried an undefined `__builtin_ffs`, the first time that gate has fired on a real package rather than a test, and the origin of **#208**. Then the compatibility shim included `<strings.h>`, and a `-include` header is processed before the TU can define `_GNU_SOURCE`, so it latched glibc's feature-test macros early and hid `struct ucred`: `field 'nm_creds' has incomplete type`, an error naming nothing to do with builtins. `libnftnl@1.2.9-2` was inspected *before* building rather than discovered a revision at a time, which caught its needs up front — and still cost one revision to a subtly wrong `sed`: `[^ ]*` excludes only a literal space, so it ran through the TAB and line-continuation backslash after `libnftnl.map` and deleted both, producing `recipe commences before first target` four directories deep. **`iw@6.17-3` fixes a live provenance violation**: 6.17 did not build its netlink dependency, it copied the build host's Debian libnl in with `cp -a`, and the artifact checksum verified perfectly throughout. It now declares `pkg_depends="libnl"` and ships **one** file where it shipped four. `ipset@7.24-7` got the same treatment — that one was *not* shipping a Debian binary, since ipset has libmnl as a build dep, but the copy is indistinguishable from the contaminated case by inspection, which is reason enough.

- **Two dependencies were blocking a third invisibly, and one would have shipped a silently crippled binary (#206, #113).** Both found while converting `iproute2`. **`libcap@2.78-10`**: its build runs its own `progs/mkcapshdoc.sh`, which starts `#!/bin/bash`, and the bash package ships exactly `bin/sh` and `usr/bin/bash` — no `/bin/bash`. The kernel's ENOENT is for the missing *interpreter*, so the shell reports it against the *script* (`cannot execute: required file not found`, exit 127), which reads as a missing file when the file is present and executable. It surfaced while installing **iproute2** and was reported against libcap, a package nobody had asked for. The guard around the fix was then wrong twice — a whole-file `grep` where the `sed` only rewrites line 1, flagging heredocs in `quicktest.sh` that write a test script at run time, and a follow-up that blamed `grep --include` on evidence from a different package entirely. **`elfutils@0.192-11`** is the one that mattered: the recipe installs libelf with `make -C libelf install`, but `libelf.pc` is installed by the *top-level* `config/Makefile`, so a completely installed libelf was invisible to pkg-config. iproute2's configure *probes* for it, printed `ELF support: no`, and would have shipped an `ip` with no BPF program loading, exiting 0 the whole way. The only reason it was caught is that iproute2's recipe reads configure's own `config.mk` back and fails when a declared dependency did not turn on. Copied individually rather than by `make -C config install`, which would also install `libdw.pc` and `libdebuginfod.pc` for two libraries the package does not ship — a false claim being worse than a missing one.

- **libmnl is packaged — Cix's first netlink library — and `ipset` builds from source against it (#207).** Six recipes could not be rebuilt without netlink development files, and the project packaged none of them; those six are the networking tools, and they are exactly the ones the old shared sandbox could build because Debian's netlink libraries sat there ambiently. `libmnl@1.0.5-2` is built from netfilter.org's own release tarball on a Cix host, and `ipset@7.24-6` now links `libmnl.so.0` — confirmed by reading its `DT_NEEDED`, not inferred. Getting there cost three real findings, each now written into `docs/guides/writing-recipes.md` so the next person does not pay for them again. **TCC cannot honour `--version-script`**, which broke both libraries at the link step; stripped from the *generated* Makefile with a `grep` guard, because a `sed` that silently matches nothing leaves the original failure to be rediscovered at link time. The trade costs symbol versioning and nothing else, and `nss-pam-ldapd` and `zlib 1.3.2-6` already make it. **`PKG_CONFIG_PATH` must be set explicitly** to consume another Cix package's `.pc` — this was the first recipe here to need one, and a genuinely-installed `libmnl` still reported `checking for libmnl >= 1... no`, which reads like a packaging failure rather than the search-path one it is. And the **contrast in how packages fail** is worth keeping: `libmnl` and `ipset` failed *loudly* at the link step, where `zlib`'s configure merely probed, printed "No shared library support", built a static library and installed cleanly — which is #113 in one sentence, and why `libmnl`'s `pkg_install` asserts its `.so`, header and `.pc` rather than trusting that `make` exited 0.

- **Seven of #206's 37 recipes now rebuild from source, and the remainder split into two very different piles.** A batch conversion using the derived-baseline method: `bzip2@1.0.8-2`, `iputils@s20180629-2`, `net-tools@2.10-3` and `sysklogd@2.7.0-3` built **first time**; `linux-pam`, `openldap-client` and `nss-pam-ldapd` earlier. Every failure named its own gap — `pkg-config: command not found` (→ `pkgconf`), `cmp: command not found` (→ `diffutils`, which is why 18 recipes already declare it). **But two failures were a different kind entirely**, and finding that out is the more useful result: `iw` and `ipset` failed on `Cannot find development files for any supported version of libnl` and `Package requirements (libmnl >= 1) were not met` — and **`libnl`, `libmnl` and `libnftnl` have no recipe in the catalogue at all**. Six of the 37 need them: `iw`, `ipset`, `iptables`, `iproute2`, `hostapd`, `keepalived`. Those are the networking tools, and they are exactly the ones the old shared build sandbox could build because Debian's netlink libraries were sitting there ambiently; under a composed environment that supply is correctly gone and nothing replaced it. So #206 is really two problems — about 31 recipes that need a declaration, and six that need packages written first (#207). The unbuildable `iw` and `ipset` revisions were **withdrawn rather than shipped**, on the same reasoning as the earlier `linux-pam`/`openldap-client` withdrawal: a recipe revision nobody has built is indistinguishable from a correct one until someone needs it.

- **The first two of #206's 37 unbuildable recipes are rebuilt from source, and the method is evidence-driven rather than guesswork.** The issue warned that guessing a tool set is the failure mode. It does not have to be guessed: each recipe's set is derivable from three real sources — a **baseline** the ~50 already-declaring recipes converge on (`tcc make linux-headers bash coreutils sed grep gawk binutils`), the **extra tools its own `pkg_build()` demonstrably invokes** (`autoreconf`, `python`, `perl`, `bison`, `m4`, `go`, `cargo`), and the **libraries it already declares** in `pkg_depends`. Profiling all 37 that way: **24 need only the baseline.** And the failure loop is self-correcting, which is what bounds the cost — both first attempts failed naming exactly what was missing: `tcc: error: undefined symbol 'crypt'` (glibc 2.44 moved `crypt()` to **libxcrypt**) and `/bin/sh: find: command not found` (**findutils**, which openldap's own `shtool mkln` shells out to). `linux-pam@1.6.1-4` and `openldap-client@2.6.14-3` now build through the ordinary install path. **Three issues moved at once:** #206 gains a proven method and two conversions, #174's blocked remainder is done (both now ship `pam.pc`/`pam_misc.pc` and `ldap.pc`/`lber.pc`), and one of #113's two live cases is resolved — the freshly built `linux-pam` has **10 shared objects and 0 GCC-built**, where `1.6.1-2` had GCC-built `pam_*.so` throughout. Worth recording that the platform caught a mistake mid-flight: an attempt to *update* the already-published `-3`/`-2` revisions was refused with `409 versions are immutable`, which is exactly right, so the work moved to `-4`/`-3` and the never-successfully-built attempts were removed rather than left as dead revisions. `nss-pam-ldapd@0.9.13-3` followed and built **first time, no iteration** — its derived set needed no correction, which is the method working rather than luck, since it was derived the same way. Its `libnss_ldap.so.2` and `pam_ldap.so` are both TCC-clean, so **no current revision carries a GCC-built shared object any more** and #113's live exposure is closed.

- **A GCC-producer detector for TCC-pinned recipes — and a correction to the first version of it (#113).** GCC stamps its identity into an ELF `.comment` section, so a `GCC:` marker in output from a recipe pinning `CC=tcc` looks like proof the build did not go the way the recipe says. The first cut of this check reported **seven current recipes as GCC-built**. That was **wrong**, and the error is worth recording: Cix's own glibc ships `crt1.o`/`Scrt1.o` carrying `GCC: (GNU) 16.2.0` — correctly, since glibc is built with Cix's GCC — so **every executable TCC links on this platform inherits that marker**, whatever compiled the package's own code. The check looked sound only because *Debian's* `crt1.o` happens to carry no marker: a property of one dev sandbox, generalised to the platform. `xz/5.8.3-6` was the clearest refutation — rebuilt locally from the identical recipe it came out fully TCC-clean, with `configure` correctly recording `CC = tcc` and zero `gcc` in the build log; its only flag had been `usr/bin/xz`, an executable. **Corrected:** the detector now returns `ELFCHECK_GCC_INCONCLUSIVE` for any executable (ET_EXEC, or ET_DYN carrying a PT_INTERP) rather than a clean "no" — *cannot tell* and *no* are different answers, and collapsing them is exactly how the wrong conclusion was drawn. Restricted to shared libraries, which link `crti.o`/`crtn.o` but not `crt1.o`, the honest number is **86 artifacts checked, 10 with GCC-built shared objects, only one of them a current revision** (`nss-pam-ldapd/0.9.13-2`; `linux-pam/1.6.1-2` is the other live one but is already blocked by #206). That the set includes `zlib-1.3.2-1/2/3` — the exact case this issue was filed about, fixed in `-6` — is what corroborates the narrower method. The test now builds a GCC executable on purpose and asserts it comes back *inconclusive*, so the mistake cannot return quietly.

- **Deleting a partition now tells the kernel too, closing a hole that could have overlapped two partitions on the same sectors (#140).** Found by deleting the test partition appended to the live OS disk. `sfdisk --delete` updated the table correctly — free space returned to exactly its previous extent — and the kernel went on exposing `/dev/vda6` for a region now marked free, while the API returned **204**, reporting complete success for a half-done job. That stale node is not untidy, it is dangerous: the space it maps is free, so the very next append hands the same sectors to a new partition while the old node still points at them — two device nodes, one region, and whichever is written first loses. `BLKPG_DEL_PARTITION` is now part of deleting a partition rather than a cosmetic follow-up, and a failure to remove it is **reported**, telling the operator not to create another partition on that disk until it has been rebooted. `ENXIO`/`EINVAL` are treated as success, since both mean the kernel does not have the partition — the desired end state — for the same reason `EBUSY` is success on the add path. This is the exact mirror of the gap the append path had, and it only surfaced because the append test was carried through to its cleanup instead of stopping at the interesting half. **Verified on the live boot disk:** a full append→delete cycle on 192.168.15.95 now leaves both views agreeing — append gives `201` and the kernel sees `vda6` at once; delete gives `204`, the kernel forgets it immediately with no reboot, and on-disk free space returns to exactly its original extent (`89723485696` bytes at sector `34473984`). Before the fix, the identical delete left `/dev/vda6` mapping sectors the table had just marked free.

- **A partition can be appended to a disk that is in use, including the OS disk (#140).** Testing the append on real hardware found sfdisk refusing outright: it runs a pre-flight `BLKRRPART` check and rejects any disk carrying a mounted filesystem. That check is right for a *repartition* and wrong for an *append*, which by construction does not read, move or modify an existing entry. So the append now passes **`--no-reread`** — suppressing that one check — and deliberately **not** `--force`, which would overrule every other guard sfdisk makes as well. `--no-tell-kernel` goes with it, so sfdisk never touches the kernel's view at all: that makes behaviour identical on a busy disk and an idle one instead of "sometimes the kernel already knows", and the kernel is then told about **exactly** the new partition via `BLKPG_ADD_PARTITION` — the same mechanism `partx(8)` uses, and the reason adding a partition to a running system is ordinary rather than a reboot. The new partition's start and length are **read back from the table** rather than taken from the requested size, because sfdisk aligns to the disk's own granularity and registering the requested bounds would leave the kernel disagreeing with the table — a discrepancy that would not surface until something wrote near the end of it. A failure to register is reported, not swallowed: a partition that exists in the table with no device node consumes the space while nothing can use it, which is worse than either outcome alone. `EBUSY` from BLKPG is treated as success, since it means the kernel already knows. **Verified on real hardware, on a live boot disk with root, `/boot`, `/config` and `/var/lib/cix` all mounted:** a 1 GiB append returned 201, partitions 1-5 stayed byte-identical, `vda6` appeared at sector 34473984 — precisely where the free extent began — the kernel saw it **immediately** without a reboot, and on-disk free space fell by exactly 1073741824 bytes. Then the machine was rebooted, came up on slot a, all six partitions persisted at the same offsets, and both DNS containers returned. That reboot was the point of the exercise: an append that quietly broke booting would be the worst thing to discover later.

- **The dashboard offers what the OS disk can actually do, and its refusals stopped lying (#140, dashboard half).** Three bugs, all the same blanket `is_os_disk`. The **add-partition form was hidden outright** on the OS disk — the operator's literal complaint, since they had sized the containers partition smaller than the disk precisely to keep the remainder usable. The **context menu returned nothing** for the OS disk *and every partition on it*, so a right-click did nothing at all, with no explanation — which is what "the UI simply fails" meant. And the note claimed the layout "is fixed and is never repartitioned", which is now false. Only the table-rewrite button stays hidden there, because rewriting is the one operation that can destroy the ESP and root slots. **The daemon now reports `protected` per partition** rather than each client re-deriving the rule from `is_os_disk` — the dashboard was doing that in five separate places, which made the policy a second source of truth living outside the code that enforces it, and "no option is offered at all" is only implementable if the client is *told* which partitions those are. The refusal messages were split too: `IS_OS_DISK` now says only the table cannot be rewritten (it used to claim the disk "can never be repartitioned", which was the more misleading half of the old policy), and a new `PROTECTED_PARTITION` explains that this particular partition is one of the four the machine boots from *and that its neighbours further along are ordinary*. One message covering both situations would be wrong about one of them. Verified by headless render — 0 JS errors, and the DOM checked to be the real dashboard rather than a browser error page, a distinction that has already produced one worthless "pass" in this project. A disk's Partitions tab also gained an **allocation donut**: a table of sizes answers "how big is each" but not "how much of this disk is spoken for", which is the question an operator asks before adding a partition — and the question that started this issue, since the free space existed and the platform would not use it. **Unallocated space is a segment in its own right rather than an absence**, because free space you cannot see is free space you do not know you have; protected partitions are drawn desaturated so "cannot be touched" reads without consulting the legend. Hand-drawn SVG, since the dashboard ships no dependencies and this is one circle with dash offsets. Verified against a real disk view rather than just a page load: four segments drawn, legend showing each partition's size and share plus `unallocated … available`.

- **The OS disk's free space is usable (#140, daemon half).** Every partition-table operation refused the OS disk outright. The reasoning was sound in isolation — `vda` carries the ESP, both A/B root slots and `/config`, and a bad table rewrite makes a machine unbootable with no remote recovery — but it was far too blunt: the operator had deliberately sized `cix-containers` **smaller than the disk** so the remainder stayed allocatable, and the platform refused to let them use the space they had reserved. **The distinction the old check missed is between rewriting a table and appending to one.** `sfdisk --append` adds an entry and does not read, move or modify the existing ones, so appending after the system partitions cannot harm them — while `create-table` genuinely can, and stays refused on the OS disk permanently. Mounted partitions are likewise no obstacle to appending, and refusing on that basis is precisely what made the reserved space unreachable, since the OS disk always has mounted partitions. Delete and resize now protect **only** partitions 1–4 rather than the whole disk. The policy is keyed on the partition **number**, not the label: the number is what `sfdisk` and the kernel operate on, whereas a label is cosmetic and editable by any tool that writes the table — a protection a rename can lift is not a protection. It **fails closed**: a partition on the OS disk whose number cannot be determined counts as protected, because being wrong that way costs an operator some manual work and being wrong the other way costs a bootable machine. The predicate is exposed and unit-tested across thirteen cases an operator can actually hit, and mutation-tested twice — reverting to the blanket policy fails four cases, and flipping the fail-closed guard fails its own. **Not yet exercised on real hardware**: doing so means writing to a live boot disk's partition table, which is the one thing this issue is about not getting wrong.

- **Composed build environments are reclaimed now, by last use rather than by reachability (#112, ADR-0221).** Nothing ever removed them, and because a recipe version is immutable, *correcting* a tool list is the normal way to work — so abandoned environments are the common case rather than the exception, each a full rootfs, growing without bound. The issue asked "when is an environment dead?" and proposed reachability over the recipe catalogue, then correctly noted that is not the same as unreachable, since an older recipe version can still be rebuilt. **The reframing that settles it: look at what being wrong costs.** Composition is cheap and deterministic, so deleting one that turns out to be wanted causes a *recomposition*, never a failure — this is a cost question with automatic recovery, not a correctness question, and precision buys nothing. So: every build stamps the environment it used, an environment an in-flight build holds is **never** touched (the one hard rule, and a question about a live process rather than a prediction), and anything idle past the window is reclaimed at daemon start. Age also resolves the case reachability cannot see at all — an environment nothing will ever want again is indistinguishable from one merely idle, and last-use handles both without telling them apart. Deliberately **not** folded into cache pruning, as the issue argued: prune the cache and a build gets slower, reclaim an environment and a build *recomposes* one; identical in a size figure, different in meaning. A **missing** stamp reports "used now" rather than "never used", so the first daemon carrying this change does not discard every pre-existing environment at once — an upgrade should not spring that, and being conservative costs one window. The retention window is fixed rather than configurable: the penalty for reclaiming too eagerly is one recomposition, so there is no operator decision here worth a knob.

- **A network's allocation window can be changed after creation (#137 follow-up).** Setting it was only possible at `POST /v1/networks`, which put it out of reach on exactly the network that most needs it: the management network **cannot be deleted while it is the management network** (409, correctly — it is how the daemon is reached), so "delete and recreate with a pool" was never a route that existed. A real bridged LAN therefore had no way to gain the pool that keeps auto-allocation off live equipment. `PUT /v1/networks/{name}` + `cixctl network set-pool` closes that. **Only the window is mutable** — subnet, prefix and host address define the network's identity and its bridge, and changing them under running containers would invalidate addresses already handed out; the window constrains only *future* auto-allocation, so narrowing or widening it is safe with containers attached. Absent and explicit-null are kept distinct (leave alone vs clear), and a partial update validates the pair it will **end up with** rather than the pair it was handed — sending only an `alloc_end` below an existing `alloc_start` is rejected, which it would not be if the unchanged bound were treated as absent. Clearing both on a bridged network deliberately returns it to failing closed rather than to allocating from the bottom of the subnet. Verified against a live daemon across all five paths: set, end-below-start, outside-subnet, null-clears-one-bound, and unknown-network.

- **A storage migration's outcome now reaches the log store (#172, last remaining piece).** The issue reported two defects; checking found both already fixed — `treecopy` handles device nodes with `mknod` and fails loudly on any type it does not understand (the silent skip would have produced an image store whose every rootfs lost `/dev/null` and `/dev/ptmx`), and the copy child's stderr is captured into the reported error. Its regression test was confirmed to genuinely execute rather than skip: as an ordinary user it prints `SKIP: cannot create a device node here`, and as real root it runs the device-node case for real. But the issue's own words were "writes **nothing whatsoever to the log store**", and that was still true: `storagemigrate.c` had no `logstore_write` at all, and the completion handler wrote only to stderr — which this daemon never mirrors into the log store, so on a real installed box with no shell it went nowhere. The reason was reachable only by polling `GET .../migrate`, and an operator working out what happened to a host hours later reads the log store, by which time nobody is polling. Both outcomes are logged now, success included — "did that migration ever actually finish?" is a real question about a job that moved 15 GB, and silence is a poor answer. **Not verifiable in this sandbox**: reaching the completion handler needs a migration that actually forks a copy child, which needs a real block device, and this container has none — a `404 no such disk` is rejected long before any child exists. Verifying it needs a real migration on real hardware.

- **A compiler builtin that was never implemented can no longer reach an image (#176).** TCC does not implement every GCC builtin and does not fail on the ones it lacks — it emits them as ordinary undefined external symbols. `libblkid.so` shipped that way with an undefined `__builtin_clz`: it compiled, installed and published without a single error, and only broke much later when something tried to link against it. Same shape as the do-while miscompile that truncated every tar listing (#122) — a clean exit and a wrong artifact — except this one is mechanically detectable. **The sweep the issue asked for is done and complete: 156 of 156 published artifacts, exactly one hit** — `libblkid-2.42.2-2`, the already-known case. The three artifacts too large for the first pass were checked separately and are clean, so the issue's own caveat ("not safe to assume it is the only affected package") is now retired rather than carried. Nothing pins the broken revision and 192.168.15.95 runs `2.42.2-3`, so there is no live exposure. **The durable half is a build-time gate** in `merge_tree()` — the single funnel every built file passes through, for image installs and hostbuild harvests alike — checking the *source* before anything is copied, so a rejected build leaves nothing of itself behind. It reads the ELF dynamic symbol table directly rather than shelling out to `nm`, which is not guaranteed present on a Cix host; and it reads fields explicitly out of a byte buffer rather than casting onto `<elf.h>` structs, because "ELF64 is naturally aligned so it's probably fine" is precisely the reasoning the `struct epoll_event` packing bug (ADR-0008) was hiding behind. Failing the install outright — rather than warning — is safe because **no compiler ever defines a `__builtin_*` symbol**: a builtin is expanded inline by definition, so a hit is never a false alarm. `test_elfcheck` builds a real shared object carrying an undefined builtin rather than committing a synthetic fixture. `test_pkg`, `test_images`, `test_pkg_cache` and `test_image_recipe` all pass with the gate live, which is the check that matters: a gate over every installed file must reject nothing legitimate.

- **Uninstalling a hostbuild now takes its bytes with it (#165), and stripping a `.pc` file got a rule instead of a habit (#174).** `pkg_delete()` removed the package record and left the entire artifact directory on disk. Not untidy — dangerous: those paths are consumed **by path, not by package** (an ISO build reads `<artifacts>/kernel/bzImage` directly), so an uninstalled hostbuild stayed fully deployable and bootable while `GET /v1/pkg` showed nothing to explain where the bytes came from. The removal runs **before** the record is cleared, deliberately: if it fails, the package stays installed and still describes the bytes that are still there, rather than producing exactly the state this bug is about. A `FAILED` hostbuild is cleaned too — a build that died partway still wrote output, and output from a build on record as having failed is the same bug in its worst form. Regression test asserts on the **file**, not the API's answer, and mutation-testing confirms both assertions fire when the fix is reverted.
- On **#174**, the issue's framing turned out to be wrong in a useful way. It named four recipes stripping their pkg-config files on the stale premise that nothing here uses pkg-config — the premise really has expired (20+ current recipes use it), but only **three** of the four are wrong. `procps` deliberately ships a **runtime only**: the same line deletes `usr/include`, the static lib and the `.so`. Restoring its `.pc` would make pkg-config *succeed* and hand a consumer include paths and a link line for files that are not in the package, surfacing much later as a confusing compile error instead of an honest "not found" — **a false claim is worse than a missing one**. So `docs/guides/writing-recipes.md` gained the rule rather than a list to memorise: *ship a `.pc` exactly when you ship the dev files it describes.* `xz@5.8.3-6` is rebuilt and proven — `usr/lib/pkgconfig/liblzma.pc` now ships alongside the headers it describes. The other two could **not** be verified and were deliberately not shipped: both predate ADR-0199, declare no build tools, and cannot be built at all — which is how #206 was found.

- **`cixctl console` was advertised but unroutable, and `container console` hung forever in silence (#108, both operator-reported).** Two bugs, one of them worse than it looked. The first was a dispatcher gap: `cmd_console()`'s own usage string has always printed `usage: cixctl console NAME`, so an operator typing exactly what the CLI told them to got `unknown command`. Routed as an alias, the same shape `logs` already has. The second was the real one. `exec_into_container()` handed the daemon a valid grandchild pid **before that grandchild had tried to `execve()` anything**, so a command missing from the container looked like complete success: the daemon sent its 101, the client attached to a pty whose process was already dead, and waited forever with no banner, no error, and no exit. Reproduced exactly against a live container whose image has **no shell at all** — `/usr/bin/bash` and `/usr/bin/sh` both absent — where a raw upgrade returns `101` and then nothing, ever. The daemon's ordering was already right (it attempts the exec *before* upgrading, and builds a 500 naming `strerror(errno)`); it was being lied to. Fixed by reporting the failure back through the pipe that already exists: `pipefd` is `O_CLOEXEC`, so a **successful** `execve` closes it and the daemon reads a clean EOF — the absence of bytes is what makes it a trustworthy success signal. The old code's comment claimed the failure diagnostic reached "the console's own client, which is the right audience"; that audience does not exist yet at that moment, which is precisely why the message went nowhere. The sibling `exec_into_container_piped()` was checked and is genuinely fine — its failure message lands in a pipe the caller really does read. Regression scenario added and mutation-tested: reverting the fix fires all three new assertions.

- **Index completeness is enforced by the build now, and it found a fourth drift on its first run (#201).** Three index drifts were found by hand in one evening, all the same shape — the substance shipped and the pointer to it did not. The Documentation Map already assigns every document an owner and a mutability rule, and that Map is what made them findable *once someone went looking*; what a rule cannot do is notice. `test_docindex` enforces the same thing ADR-0199 said about build tools: sufficiency is enforced by the build, minimality is review. It checks that every ADR has a row in the ADR index, that every `docs/` subdirectory has a row in **both** `docs/README.md` and CLAUDE.md's Documentation Map (both, because `docs/brand/` really did sit in one and not the other), that every guide is listed, and that no index row links to a file that does not exist. **On its first run it failed**, naming ADR-0168 — the container capability bounding-set drop, sitting unlisted between 0167 and 0169, a fourth drift nobody had found. Row added. All four checks were then mutation-tested: each was made to fail by reintroducing exactly the bug it exists to catch, with a distinct message, because a gate never seen to fail is decoration. Matching is deliberately on the link target (`0168-...md`, `(keys/)`) rather than a bare number or name, so a directory mentioned in passing prose cannot satisfy a check — that is how this class of gate goes green while the row it enforces is missing.

- **The release public key is published, so the signatures are actually checkable (#193 part 5).** Signing an ISO and then keeping the public key only on the build host verifies nothing for anyone — until now the key existed on 192.168.15.95 and in a scratch directory, which is exactly as useful as no signature at all. It is now committed at `docs/keys/cix-release.pub`, and the committed copy was proven against a genuinely published artifact (`cix-installer-2.5.1-1-x86_64.iso` → `Signature and comment signature verified`) rather than assumed to match. **It lives in git and deliberately not in the artifact cache:** the cache serves the bytes, so a cache that also served the key would be vouching for its own payload — git is a different system, different credentials, different path, and an attacker who can replace an ISO there still cannot replace the key you check it against. That same argument is why no per-ISO checksum belongs in git: a checksum committed beside the recipes travels the same path as the recipes and proves nothing they did not already claim. The new `docs/keys/` directory carries its own README (pinning, why re-fetching defeats it, why there is no expiry or revocation lookup, what happens when a key is retired) and its rows in both documentation indexes, since "not in the map" is not a valid state for a document here. Auditing #193's part 3 alongside it found nothing to fix: the installer makes no self-check at all, so there is no claim of "signature verified" to correct — satisfied by absence rather than by wording.

- **A restart no longer forgets an ISO that is sitting on disk (#205).** Found by publishing one for real: the reboot into v2.5.0 left a finished, signed ISO on disk while `GET /v1/system/iso` reported `state: none` and `POST /v1/system/iso/publish` refused it with "no ISO has been built on this host" — a false statement about a file the daemon could see. Any restart between building and publishing stranded the artifact with no route out but a full rebuild. The cause was narrow: `ISO_OUTPUT_PATH` was derived *only inside the build handler*, so nothing knew where an ISO would be until a build ran in that process. It is now computed once at startup and the state is **recovered from disk rather than persisted** — a stored claim about the ISO would be a second source of truth able to disagree with the filesystem, and the thing it describes is already on the filesystem. **The recovery creates a hazard the fix has to answer:** old ISOs becoming publishable means an operator could publish a stale one as current. So `built_version` is read back out of the trusted comment inside the ISO's own signature — a signed claim about the artifact, not a label about whatever is running — and a mismatch is called out at boot. Verified across all four paths: signed recovery (`built_version: v2.5.0`), unsigned recovery (publish refused, naming the missing release key), the boot log lines, and no-ISO. **One thing nearly shipped broken:** the first cut called `iso_recover_state()` before `logstore_init()`, so every one of its log lines went nowhere — this project's own recorded lesson about stderr never reaching the log store, learned a third time, and caught only because the line was checked for rather than assumed.

- **The installer ISO can now reach the artifact cache — signing was necessary but not sufficient (ADR-0220).** With #197 done, .95 built an ISO that signed itself, and it still could not be published: `POST /system/iso` writes to local disk and reports a *filesystem path*, `publish_hostbuild_artifact()` covers packages only, and no endpoint returns an ISO's bytes. So the artifact existed, correctly signed, with no route off the box at all — not even a manual one. `POST /v1/system/iso/publish` closes that. **The signature uploads first, and the order is required rather than tidy:** the cache refuses an ISO with no signature beside it, which is correct — an unsigned installer is exactly the artifact that must not be downloadable — so failing between the two uploads leaves a signature with no ISO (harmless, overwritten next attempt) rather than a bootable image nobody can verify. An unsigned ISO is refused *here*, naming the missing release key, rather than letting the cache answer 409 and describing the symptom while hiding the cause. Deliberately not routed through pkg.c's package push queue: that queue publishes fresh builds keyed by `name@version`, and an ISO has neither — no recipe stands behind it and nothing resolves it by version, which is why the cache counts installers separately from packages in the first place. `publish_state`/`published_name`/`publish_error` are reported separately from `state` because a built-but-unpublished ISO is a perfectly usable local artifact and folding the two together would make one look broken. **Proven end to end on real hardware:** v2.5.0 on 192.168.15.95 built and signed an ISO, published it as `cix-installer-2.5.0-1-x86_64.iso` (the cache went `installers: 0` → `1`), and downloading it back out and checking it with **stock minisign** gives `Signature and comment signature verified / Trusted comment: cix installer iso, v2.5.0` — while flipping one byte gives `Signature verification failed`. A downloader running no Cix software can now tell a genuine installer from a substituted one, which is the entire point. Doing it for real also surfaced #205: the ISO build state is in-memory, so the reboot into v2.5.0 left a finished signed ISO on disk that the daemon reported as `none` and refused to publish.

- **libc-dev is gone (#187, ADR-0217) — and finishing it meant finding six recipes the earlier phases had missed.** The package recipes were migrated in phases 1-3, but every **image** recipe still pinned `libc-dev` in its manifest: `chrony`, `cix-builder`, `kernel-builder`, `iso-builder`, `dev`, `gcc-tcc-bootstrap`. Purging the package with those in place would have left six registered, live recipes naming something unresolvable — trading one piece of debt for a worse one. Each gets a new version pinning `glibc:2.44-12` instead; same job, different provider (libc-dev was Debian headers and CRT objects repackaged, glibc is the one this project builds from source), and named explicitly because glibc is implicit only for a composed build environment and for the default image. `dev` and `gcc-tcc-bootstrap` were migrated on the assumption both were superseded; checking afterwards showed that was right for `dev` (ADR-0208 renamed it to `iso-builder`, and both still exist) and **wrong for `gcc-tcc-bootstrap`**, which the current gcc recipe still names as its own `--image` target and which ADR-0208 deliberately kept. The gcc chain having landed does not retire the image that builds gcc. Migrating both was the correct action either way — a recipe that cannot resolve is a worse resting state than one merely unused — but the reasoning given for half of it was a shape-based guess, and the follow-up issue has been rescoped to `dev` alone. **The blocker cleared first:** `kernel 6.18.40-18` built and installed on `kernel-builder` with `glibc` as the implicit libc and no libc-dev anywhere, which is what made the purge safe to perform rather than merely desirable. **The cache artifacts are gone too, after one wrong turn worth recording.** DELETE against `libc-dev-2.36-8.tar.gz` returned 404 while GET returned 200, and that inconsistency was read as a missing DELETE route — a bug was filed against the cache server on that basis. It was wrong. The cache resolves an *unstamped* name for GET/HEAD only; the canonical name carries the architecture (`libc-dev-2.36-8-x86_64.tar.gz`), and DELETE against that returns 204. `GET /api/v1/artifacts` gives the canonical name for every artifact and would have shown this immediately. All three removed, `POST /api/v1/gc` freed 59.9 MB, store went 155 → 152 packages, every fetch path now 404. The filed issue was closed as invalid. This repo had already absorbed three bogus reports of one already-fixed cache bug; this made four, from the same root cause each time — asserting a server defect without checking the server's own API first.

- **The release key became a REST surface, and an ISO now signs itself (ADR-0220, closes #197).** `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE /v1/system/release-key`, contract first as ADR-0218 requires — and the order proved itself twice on the way: the generated dispatcher refused to link until the three declared operations had handlers, then `test_api_surfaces` refused to pass until the CLI and dashboard actually called what the spec said they exposed. Neither gap needed noticing; both were structurally impossible to leave behind. `POST /v1/system/iso` signs its output when a key is installed and reports `signature_path`; **a missing key does not fail the build**, because an unsigned ISO still installs and most hosts able to build one should hold no signing material at all — the absence is reported (`signature_path` stays null) rather than inferred from success. A signing failure *with* a key present is logged as an error, which is the case an operator must not ship past. `PUT` refuses an RSA key at install time — the realistic mistake, given the Secure Boot pair stored right beside it — and that check was mutation-tested: disabling it makes `test_signing_keys` fail, so the guard is known to bite rather than assumed to. The public key comes back in full, deliberately breaking the never-return-key-material rule that governs every other secret here: a signature nobody can verify is not a signature, and REST reporting it was checked against the stored key with `openssl` independently, not taken on trust.

- **Installer ISOs can be signed, and the signature was proven against the real verifier before a line of C was written (ADR-0220, #197 unblocked).** #197 could not be built as written: it specified the **existing platform key** *and* **Ed25519**, but that key is the Secure Boot key handed to `sbsign` and UEFI mandates RSA, while minisign is Ed25519-only. Different algorithm, not different encoding — it would have failed at the first signing call. The answer is a **separate Ed25519 release key**, and that is better regardless of the clash: sharing one key means whoever can sign a download can also sign a bootloader, and the two have very different blast radii (firmware re-enrolment on every host, versus republishing a public key). **The whole scheme was prototyped against stock `minisign 0.11` first** — legacy `Ed` mode over the raw ISO (OpenSSL's Ed25519 is PureEdDSA, so the daemon needs no BLAKE2b), a key id derived from `SHA-256(pubkey)` so the public key file and every signature agree by construction with no stored id to drift, and the **global signature over `signature ‖ trusted comment`**, which is the piece naive implementations omit and minisign then rejects. `test_releasekey` uses stock minisign as its oracle, never a verifier written here — this is the artifact that gets *booted*, so the last check between a substituted ISO and a machine should not be code from the project that produced it. Four negative cases, and they are the point: a tampered byte fails, an **edited trusted comment** fails (proving the global signature is load-bearing rather than decorative), a different key fails, and an **RSA key is refused at install time** rather than at signing time on a real release. Extracting `pki_run_openssl()` into `opensslrun.c` came with it — a second subsystem needed a subprocess-with-capture primitive, and duplicating it would have been a parallel implementation while linking `pki.c` for it drags DNS validation and the container registry into a signature-format unit test.

- **Layer 3: an API call in code nothing reaches now fails the build (ADR-0218 complete).** Layers 1 and 2 prove a helper exists and is referenced; neither proves a person can reach it, and a generated helper called from a function nothing calls satisfies both perfectly while the operator still cannot do the thing. The check walks the CLI's call graph from `main()` and fails on any API call outside it — proven by orphaning one dispatcher line, which correctly reports `cmd_files_get() is unreachable but calls the API`. **Its first version cried wolf on working code**, which is why the implementation is careful: it treated every `type name(` line as a function *definition*, forward declarations included, so a prototype claimed the byte range of everything after it, every later boundary shifted, and six live commands were reported dead — `cmd_files_get` among them, called two lines from where the checker said nothing called it. A definition now requires a body (`{` ending the signature or alone on the next line), and the walk is deliberately **conservative**: an unrecognised construct marks a function reachable, never dead, because a false pass is a missed warning while a false failure is a broken build for correct code. It also refuses to pass when it finds implausibly few functions, since a clean result from a broken parser means nothing. Today's answer: 436 definitions, 312 reachable, **zero** API calls stranded — the value is not that number but the day someone declares an operation exposed and wires it to nothing.

- **The two real gaps ADR-0218 layer 2 exposed are now closed.** Declaring exposure turned "nobody offers this" from an accident into a visible fact, and two of the fifteen were genuine holes rather than design choices. **`cixctl pkg artifact-publish NAME`** publishes an already-built artifact without rebuilding it — the endpoint existed since #171 and had no interface on either channel, which is why this session's own backfill of `cix v2.2.0-rc35` had to be driven by hand with `curl`; the local cache does not survive a reinstall and a rebuild of `cix` or `kernel` is the most expensive thing this platform does, so a push that failed or predated the artifact server must not cost one. **`cixctl dhcp remove --network=NAME` and a Remove button in the dashboard's DHCP table** delete a network's configuration outright — distinct from `disable`, which stops serving and keeps the range. Every other DHCP operation was `[cli, web]`; this one could be created and edited from both channels and taken back from neither. Both channels for DHCP, CLI-only for publish, matching the artifact-export family beside it. Thirteen operations remain unexposed and all are now deliberate: single-item GETs both channels reach by listing, plus the image export/rename family, each a recorded decision rather than an oversight.

- **`x-cix-expose` is declared for all 264 operations and enforced both ways (ADR-0218 layer 2).** The contract now records which presentation channels must offer each capability — **212 both, 33 CLI-only, 4 web-only, 15 neither** — and `test_api_surfaces` fails if a channel omits something declared for it *or* offers something the contract does not expose, because each direction catches a different mistake: a promise the channel does not keep, and a capability the channel granted itself. **This is only checkable because of layer 1.** Enumerating a channel's operations used to mean reconstructing URLs from string concatenation, which produced three different answers in three attempts; now every call site names its operation, so it is an identifier scan, and identifiers are not built by concatenation. Two defects surfaced while building it, both found by reading the output rather than trusting a green result. The check first used `strstr()` and credited channels with operations they never call — `getVolume` matches inside `getVolumeBackups`, `getNetwork` inside `getNetworkPorts`, `getPkg` inside `getPkgRecipe` — six phantoms, all a longer name swallowing a shorter one; it now matches whole identifiers. And the negative check only scanned `cli/src/main.c`, missing `client/src/console.c`, where both WebSocket paths (container console, `pkg build/log`) were still hand-built — **a channel is not one file**, and that gap made an operation the CLI has always used look exposed by nobody. Both are converted, and a WebSocket upgrade is treated as what it is: a declared API operation whose path drifts like any other. The 15 unexposed operations are now a *recorded* state rather than an accident — mostly single-item GETs both channels reach by listing, but they include real gaps worth deciding on separately (`POST /pkg/{name}/artifact/publish` had to be driven by hand with `curl` during this session's own artifact backfill, and `DELETE /dhcp/networks/{network}` has no interface at all).

- **The dashboard can no longer invent an API path either (ADR-0218 layer 1, step 3b) — and a browser caught what four green checks did not.** All **218** `apiRequest` sites plus the WebSocket console, the raw backup/restore transfers and the build-log `fetch()` now call `CIX_API.<operationId>()` helpers generated from the spec. Parameters are `encodeURIComponent()`'d **once, in the generator**, rather than at ~226 call sites that did it inconsistently. The same composed-path defect the CLI had turned up here too: `STORAGE_KINDS` held `endpoint: "state-storage"` and built `"/v1/system/" + k.endpoint`, a path no generated helper covers and a silent 404 the day an endpoint is renamed — each kind now carries its two contract paths. **The part worth recording is the failure.** A first conversion pass used regexes whose expression capture stopped at the first `)`, so it swallowed the *closing paren of the call itself* — 33 sites lost a paren and gained a double-encode. `test_web` passed. The negative check passed. `test_api_surfaces` passed. The dashboard was **completely broken**: `Uncaught SyntaxError: missing ) after argument list`, found only by rendering the page in headless Chromium. Static checks confirmed the paths were no longer hand-written and had nothing to say about whether the file still parsed. Redone with a balance-aware parser instead of regexes, gated by `node --check`, and verified by rendering: zero JS errors, and the DOM grew 144,904 → **213,429 bytes** — ~68 KB of content the SyntaxError had been suppressing — with `"No containers"`, `v2.2.0` and the boot slot all fetched live through the generated helpers. The generated map lives at `web/api.js` rather than under `build/`, the one deviation from ADR-0218's "generated files live in build/" and for a real reason: the file is **served**, so it must be in the web root the daemon and the `cix` recipe both read. The property that matters — never committed — is kept by `.gitignore` instead, and the recipe's existing `cp -r web/*` picks it up because `pkg_build()` runs `make` first.

- **`POST /v1/system/iso` had been broken on every real host since the package seed landed, and its error message was made of documentation (#202).** `mkinstalleriso` grew a 14th argument in #189 part 2 (the seed directory) and checks `argc != 14`; the daemon still passed 13 and a `NULL`. Every server-side ISO build printed the tool's usage text and exited 2, surfacing as `mkinstalleriso failed (status 0x200):   delivery mechanism and not a trust boundary` — a **fragment of that usage prose**, caught mid-sentence because the daemon reports the tail of the child's stderr. An error made of documentation reads like anything except a wrong argument count, and it sent the investigation to signing keys and artifact paths first. Fixed with `argv[13] = ""` — "no seed", the same convention `mkbootroot` already uses for an absent optional input — deliberately *not* a real seed, because staging one changes what the media **does** (it would install a host that runs containers with no network) and that is a product decision, not a repair. **Why it survived is the part worth keeping:** `test_installer` calls `mkinstalleriso` **directly** with all 14 arguments, so it stayed green throughout — it exercises the tool and never this call site. A caller and callee that only ever meet in production. Found only because ADR-0217's libc-dev removal used an ISO build as one of its "does this image still do its job" checks.

- **libc-dev is uninstalled, and each image was verified by building the thing it exists to build (ADR-0217 phase 3).** `linux-headers` went into `kernel-builder` first — libc-dev was that image's only source of kernel UAPI headers, a prerequisite found while planning rather than mid-execution. Verification is *doing the job*, not inspecting the result: `isotools 2.14-9` and `kernel 6.18.40-18` are fresh revisions carrying **no `pkg_artifact_sha256`**, so each must build from source and cannot hit a cached artifact and prove nothing. `isotools` built clean on a libc-dev-free `iso-builder`, its C headers now from `glibc` and its UAPI headers from `linux-headers`. That verification also corrected itself en route: an ISO build was the first attempt, but `POST /system/iso` consumes the *isotools artifact*, not the `iso-builder` image — rebuilding `isotools` **on** that image is the test that actually proves anything. Phase 2's mass upgrade of 41 packages was deliberately skipped per the ADR: build dependencies only matter on rebuild, 30 of the 39 targets have never been built anywhere, and each picks up its current recipe the next time it is genuinely built.

- **The CLI can no longer invent an API path (ADR-0218 layer 1, step 3a).** All **247** call sites now take their path — and their verb — from `CIX_API_<operationId>` constants that `apigen` regenerates from the spec each build; a mistyped path used to compile and fail at runtime, and a wrong constant name simply does not build. The conversion was mechanical and safe precisely because the emitted form is a *substitution of the string* (`%s` per parameter, in spec order) rather than a new calling convention, so the existing `snprintf` sites kept their shape. **All 145 distinct literal (method, path) pairs resolved to an operationId with none left over** — the CLI's usage already matched the contract exactly, which is worth knowing on its own. Three sites were genuinely hand-composed and got real thought rather than a mechanical edit: `cixctl storage {state,logs,rebuildable}` shared one code path by interpolating a URL segment (`"/v1/system/%s"`), which is a path no generated constant can cover and would 404 silently the day an endpoint is renamed — the three contract paths are now passed in, keeping the shared shape with no client-side synthesis. **The keeping-it-that-way half is the negative check** (`test_api_surfaces`), and its design is the interesting part: enumerating which paths a channel builds was attempted three times during ADR-0218's own research and gave three different answers, one supporting the confident and false claim that the dashboard cannot stop a container. Asserting a channel builds **none** needs no understanding of the code at all, which is exactly why it can be trusted. Its first run flagged a help message that merely *mentions* `POST /v1/system/iso`; the rule was sharpened (a path being built is a literal that *starts* with `/v1/`) rather than given an exception list, since a check accumulating exceptions stops being one. Proven in the failing direction by putting one hand-typed path back: it names the file, line and the constant to use instead.

- **The dispatcher is generated from the API contract, and the two can no longer disagree (ADR-0218, step 2 of the plan the ADR carries).** ~1,900 lines of hand-ordered `strcmp`/`strncmp` chains in `dispatch()` are gone; every one of the **264** operations in `docs/api/openapi.yaml` now dispatches through a table that `tools/apigen.c` regenerates from the spec on every build, into `build/generated/api_routes.h` — under `build/`, so a stale committed copy is not merely forbidden but impossible.
