The on-disk presence of `<base>/rootfs` is the storage-mode marker (the filesystem is the one source of truth; revival keys off it, so a restart can never silently re-provision away a container's writes). Quota moves to qgroups in **exclusive** bytes — a snapshot references its whole image from the first instant, and the quota owed is the container's own divergence. File staging, stopped-container file access, disk-usage reporting and deletion all follow the marker; cross-disk storage migration of snapshot containers is refused loudly until phase 4's tooling. A copy-based `--test-direct-rootfs` mode gives the sandbox full coverage of everything but the snapshot ioctl itself.
- **Overlay's code retirement moved from phase 2 to phase 4, for measured reasons** recorded as a dated correction in the ADR: the sandbox cannot host btrfs at all, the staged test toolchain is ~1GB and `test_pkg` creates a build container per install — a full-copy fallback means 15–25GB of copying per suite run — and hardlinks are unsafe for a writable rootfs. Overlay remains the non-btrfs path (what every unmigrated ext4 host actually runs) and dies together with ext4.
- **Phase 3 (#160) — user namespaces by default, opt-out.** A container created without an explicit `userns` field now takes the platform default (`daemon-config.userns_default`, **on** for fresh installs — the secure-by-default posture the owner set); an explicit true/false always wins, and the platform sets `userns:false` on its own build containers, stated in code rather than inherited from a memset. **The resolved mode is pinned into the persisted definition at creation, image_version-style** — without the pin, flipping the platform default would have silently swapped every pre-existing container's isolation mode (and storage layout) on its next restart; the regression test flips the default while a container is stopped and proves revival stays pinned. On btrfs a userns container's rootfs is the same O(1) snapshot a non-userns one gets — host-0-owned, extent sharing intact — presented through `MOUNT_ATTR_IDMAP` applied by the parent on the fork-shared detached fd between map-write and child-release (no fd passing, no per-inode chown); volumes get the same id-mapped treatment, closing ADR-0179's EOVERFLOW gap. Non-btrfs hosts keep the live-proven phase-2b copy+chown path; revival reads which presentation a rootfs needs from its own ownership. The dev sandbox's LSM forbids `uid_map` writes outright, so the fixture seeds `userns_default:false` through the ordinary config channel and the kernel-side proof belongs to `.95`. The `userns` API contract — which had zero `openapi.yaml` coverage since ADR-0179 — is documented in both contract files.
- **Upgrade migration: a definition persisted before the default flip is pinned to `userns:false` at load** (`migrate_pin_userns_absent()`, same one-shot shape as issue #76's `ldap_login` migration). Post-flip creates always carry the pin, so an absent key means the def predates the flip — and non-userns is the mode it actually ran with. Without this, `.95`'s existing containers would flap to userns on their first post-upgrade revival. The regression test strips the pin from the persisted file between daemon restarts, sets the default to true, and proves revival stays non-userns (bug reintroduced under full rebuild to prove the test catches it).
- **`libc-dev` stages what a libc development environment *is*, by name (2.36-6, closes #169).** It used to run `cp -a /usr/include/.` — the build container's entire include tree, which via the bootstrap is the build *host's* — so every image installing it received another OS's headers: valgrind, Erlang, the host gcc's C++ headers. Now it copies 106 named glibc headers, glibc's own directories, the kernel UAPI trees, and the multiarch entries **named individually** (that directory also holds libstdc++, libffi, lua and openssl headers, so wholesale copying is precisely how contamination got in). Result: **1,405 files / 11 MB, down from 6,128 / 99.8 MB**, with real Cix sources still compiling against it. A build-time gate now fails the recipe if any known-foreign tree appears, so a regression shows up as a failed build rather than a shipped artifact — and that gate immediately caught a bug in my own allowlist: top-level `sys/` on this host is libcap-dev's, not glibc's, so it is now staged only when it genuinely contains glibc's `sys/types.h`.
- **Two structural contamination paths found and filed (#168, #169), and the `kernel-builder` artifact withdrawn because of them.** `cix-builder` *is* the shared build sandbox (`PKG_BUILD_SANDBOX_IMAGE`), `pkg bootstrap` copies the host's whole `/usr` into it, and every successful install folds into it forever — so it held ~8 GB / 88,798 entries of a developer workstation (rustup, cargo, chromium, node, go, qemu, sudo, several gcc trees), **93% belonging to no package in its manifest**. Separately, `libc-dev.recipe` does `cp -a /usr/include/.`, carrying the build container's entire `/usr/include` — Debian's Erlang, valgrind and gcc-12 C++ headers — into *any* image that installs it. The image artifact published today was built on a Cix host but contained those foreign headers, so it was withdrawn from the cache and its checksum removed from the recipe: built-on-Cix is only half the rule.
- **`kernel-builder` built on 192.168.15.95** (artifact withdrawn pending #169). 19 packages including a Cix-built `gcc 16.2.0-11` pulled from the artifact cache, and `kmod` — whose absence from `dev` was half the reason the documented self-hosted kernel build could never have worked. Two packages (`bzip2`, `m4`) arrived as genuine transitive dependencies and are now named in the manifest, because an image's version *is* the hash of that list: a manifest short of reality computes an artifact URL that does not resolve.
- **`elfutils` stops guessing which gcc it is patching (0.192-8).** Its `pkg_build()` wrote a `syslimits.h` correction to a hardcoded `.../12.5.0/include-fixed/` path — the gcc present when the fix was written — so any image with a different gcc failed with a bare "No such file or directory" naming a path nobody had thought about since. It now asks gcc its version, and says so in a sentence when there is no gcc at all. The correction itself is unchanged and still needed.
- **Every build image now has one job (ADR-0208).** These manifests were never designed — each recipe says so in its own header (*"Captured from 192.168.15.95"*), so a package list was whatever a box happened to hold when it was snapshotted. That is how `cix-builder`, the image that exists to build TCC-only code, came to carry `gcc:9.5.0-6`: nobody chose it, a capture took it. It is not inert either — an available gcc is exactly how a `configure` without an explicit `CC=tcc` silently picks the wrong compiler, which is how an `sshd` once shipped with `-lpam` on its link line and no PAM in the resulting ELF. `cix-builder` 3.0.0 drops gcc and pins the patched `tcc 0.9.27-9`. New `kernel-builder` holds the real GCC toolchain plus `kmod`/`bc`/`bison`/`flex`/`elfutils` the kernel genuinely needs — it is the **one** image legitimately holding gcc. `dev` is renamed `iso-builder`, with `grub`/`sbsigntools`/`xorriso`/`mtools` in its manifest rather than installed by hand afterwards: "dev" named no job, so it got prescribed for kernel builds it could not perform, and an image called "iso-builder" without the ISO tools would not be one. Every operator-facing reference moved with the rename; the ADRs and ROADMAP keep their historical text.
- **Build environments are composed, never inherited (ADR-0209, ADR-0210, closes the mechanism half of #168).** Four things went at once, because each depended on the others. A recipe that declares no build tools now **fails**, naming itself — there is no fallback environment, so a build can never quietly run against something fuller than it asked for. Nothing folds into a shared sandbox any more: `cix-builder` stops being the accumulating union of everything ever installed on a host. `pkg bootstrap`'s live host-`/usr` copy is refused permanently — not narrowed, because copying another operating system's files is the wrong thing, not the amount. And a composed environment is destroyed when its build ends, so `__buildenv-*` images stop piling up; it is kept only while a `keep_on_failure` container still needs it as its lowerdir, which the suite caught me getting wrong.
- **`base` stops being privileged (ADR-0210)** and the baseline shrinks to the glibc floor — `libtinfo` and `libgcc_s` are ncurses and gcc, packages we build ourselves and were pointlessly copying Debian's versions of. What remains is named in the code as the last unclosed link in the bootstrap rather than left implicit.
- **The default image is created by the daemon, and now actually exists (ADR-0210).** `cix-install` copied a C runtime into `images/base/rootfs`, and `mkinstalleriso` staged a `payload/cix-runtime` tree on every ISO to supply it, on the stated grounds that nothing else ever would. That path stopped being read when ADR-0107/0108 made images versioned — container creation resolves strictly through `image_current_version()` — so the seeding wrote to a directory nothing consults. Removing it exposed the bug it was masking: a fresh daemon reported `{"images":[]}` and refused a container on `base` with `"image rootfs does not exist"`, because nothing created the default image except a first `pkg install` doing it as a side effect. **A freshly installed box could not create a container at all.** `ensure_default_image()` now materializes it at boot from an empty manifest through the same `image_create()` every other image uses, idempotent by construction. Verified live before and after against a fresh data directory (`{"images":[]}` and a refusal, then `base` present at the empty manifest's own hash with a container actually running on it), and end to end by `test_installer` — a real install plus two independent QEMU boots, its assertions rewritten to prove the *replacement* works rather than deleted, scanning for the version directory instead of hardcoding a hash that would fail for the wrong reason later.
- **A storage migration would have silently gutted every image, and its failures were undiagnosable (#172).** Moving a real host's 15 GB image store onto a second disk failed twice with `bulk copy failed` and *nothing whatsoever in the log store* — the copy runs in a forked child whose stderr nothing captured, so the reason died with it. That is the #125/#132 pattern again, on an operation that moves a host's entire image and package store. `storagemigrate` now pipes `treecopy_last_error()` out of the child, and every `treecopy` failure names its operation and path (`mkdir: /x/usr: No such file or directory`) instead of returning a bare `-1`. **The worse half was hidden behind it:** `treecopy` skipped device nodes *silently*, justified by a comment asserting they are "never expected under any of this project's own storage-placement trees" — true for state- and log-storage, false for the image store, which is exactly what this endpoint moves. `pkg_seed_image_baseline()` stages `/dev/null`, `/dev/zero`, `/dev/full` and `/dev/ptmx` into every image rootfs (ADR-0150 added ptmx so `posix_openpt()` works), so a migration that *succeeded* would have produced an image store whose containers fail on `/dev/null` and cannot allocate a PTY — surfacing days later, nowhere near the cause. The comment was not merely wrong, it was load-bearing: it justified skipping silently rather than failing. Device nodes and fifos are now copied with `mknod`, anything else fails loudly, and the **mode is preserved explicitly** because `mknod()` applies the umask — a 0666 `/dev/null` lands at 0644, unwritable by any container not running as host root, which is the default since ADR-0207 phase 3 (verified source 666 → copy 666; without the fix, 644). `test_treecopy` covers both halves and was confirmed to catch the original bug by restoring the silent skip.
- **Image versions can be reclaimed, and until now they could not (`POST /v1/images/gc`, ADR-0209).** Every install produces a new immutable version (ADR-0107/0108), a container pins whichever was current when it was created, and *nothing anywhere in the API ever removed one*. Not theoretical: 66 versions of an 8 GB rootfs filled a 16 GiB partition, and the disk filling up is how it was found. A version is kept if it is its image's `current_version`, if a live container pins it, or if a stored container definition names it — that third source is the one easy to miss, because a stopped container has no registry entry at all and collecting its version would leave it permanently unable to start. Refused with `409` while a package job is in flight (a build holds its image rootfs as its container's lowerdir). Versions are enumerated from the **filesystem**, not the recorded history: `IMAGE_MAX_VERSION_HISTORY` caps the list at 256 while `image_record_version()` keeps repointing past it, so a long-lived image can own directories its own history no longer names — precisely the ones most worth reclaiming. `cixctl image gc [--dry-run]` and Preview/Reclaim buttons on the dashboard's Images page complete the three surfaces. **Verified with the discriminating case:** a container pinned to a deliberately *non-current* version protects it, and deleting that container makes the same version collectable — a test pinning only the current version would pass with the reference scan deleted outright, confirmed by deleting it (three assertions fail). `apparent_bytes` is named as such everywhere because on btrfs a version is a snapshot sharing extents, so real reclaimed space is usually well below it.
- **Whole-rootfs image artifacts are dropped; package artifacts are the only published binaries (ADR-0209).** ADR-0123's fast path let a fully-`pinned` image recipe carrying an `image_artifact_sha256=` be applied by fetching one tarball and extracting it as the image's entire rootfs, skipping every per-package build. That is the mechanism that took one contaminated capture and shipped it to every host (#168), and it was a second representation of something a package set plus a manifest already describes completely. The whole tier goes: the fetch, the async job, `POST /v1/images/{name}/apply-recipe`'s 202 branch, `GET /v1/images/recipe-apply-status` and its schema, the `cixctl image recipe-apply-status` command, the dashboard's Apply-status panel, and the `image_artifact_sha256=` field itself — no longer parsed, and removed from the five recipes that still declared one. Applying a recipe is now bulk-declare and nothing else, always `204`. **The test was inverted rather than deleted:** it still builds a real, correctly-named, correctly-checksummed artifact and serves it from a real HTTP server with the artifact config pointed at it, then proves none of that matters — asserting *absence* on disk, because an artifact quietly fetched anyway would still return 204. Confirmed discriminating by planting the payload where a fetch would have put it and watching the assertion fail.
- **The package test suite bootstraps the way a real host does.** No fabricated toolchain: real recipe-built artifacts are seeded into each test daemon's own cache and install as cache hits, needing no build environment at all — with every artifact verified against the checksum in its own recipe, and both refusal paths (tampered bytes, missing bytes) proven rather than assumed.
- **TCC learns `__has_include` (tcc 0.9.27-9).** Upstream 0.9.27 implements none of the `__has_*` operators, and in a preprocessor conditional an unknown identifier evaluates to 0 — so a real `#if __has_include(<stdcountof.h>)` became `0(<stdcountof.h>)`, a call through a non-function, and the translation unit died with `function pointer expected` pointing at a blank line. Not theoretical: util-linux 2.42's `include/c.h` uses it, so **libblkid could not be compiled at all** — and libblkid is what `btrfs-progs` needs, which provides the `mkfs.btrfs` that ADR-0207 makes the platform's storage depend on. Only `__has_include` is added, deliberately: its siblings (`__has_attribute`/`__has_feature`/`__has_extension`) need no compiler support because portable code defines its own fallback for them — util-linux does exactly that a few lines above the line that broke — while `__has_include` is the one that cannot be faked, since any fallback would have to answer the question it asks. Resolution walks the same search list in the same order as a real `#include`, testing only openability. **Proven sufficient, not just necessary:** libblkid now configures and builds end to end with the patched compiler, producing a real 3.2 MB `libblkid.so.1.1.0` exporting 647 symbols — so `__has_include` was the only gap behind it, not merely the first. The patch is applied with `sed` and a heredoc, not `python3`: a composed build environment contains only the recipe's *declared* build tools, and `-8` (which used python) died on the box with `python3: command not found` before compiling a line — recipe versions are immutable once published, so the correction is `-9` rather than an edit. The recipe carries a build-time gate asserting all three answers (existing header present, nonexistent absent, nonexistent quoted absent), matching the do-while gate `-7` already established.
- **Compressed archives no longer need a shell — the real cause of every failed export on an installed host (#164).** GNU tar spawns `--use-compress-program=` through `/bin/sh`, and the Cix control-plane root deliberately has none: nothing in `cixd` uses `popen`/`system`, every subprocess is an explicit absolute-path `execve`. The shell's failed exec was reported by tar against the *compress program*, so it surfaced as `/usr/bin/gzip: Cannot exec: No such file or directory` on a host where gzip was present and ran fine — confirmed by pulling that exact binary off `.95` (ordinary ELF, needs only the staged loader and libc) and by reproducing the failure in a locally-built control-plane root, where adding a shell fixes it. Decompression was never affected (tar handles `-xzf`/`-xf` itself), which is why installs worked while **every** image/artifact export and **every** `pkg_cache_save()` failed silently on every real host. New `daemon/src/targz.c` builds the pipeline directly — `tar -cf -` into a pipe `gzip -c` reads, both exec'd by absolute path — with no shell and no temporary uncompressed copy (an image export is gigabytes; a plain `.tar` first would double peak disk on the partition being exported). Output is byte-identical to before, asserted in the test, so published artifacts stay valid; the `tar`/`gzip` paths now live in one header instead of three places. This also completes issue #125, whose fix removed the bare-`gzip` PATH lookup but left the shell in the path. `test_targz` stages a root with no `/bin/sh` and archives from inside it — a plain call would have passed against the broken code — verified by reintroducing the bug under a full rebuild.
- **Kernel build guide corrected.** It still told operators to run `python3 -m http.server 8901` before a self-hosted kernel build — a step that predates the recipe being pinned to a real Gitea raw URL for its config fragment, and that today serves a port nothing reads. Removed, with a note saying why so nobody reinstates it. The same section now states plainly that `recipes/image/dev` carries neither `gcc` nor `kmod`, so the `--build-image=dev` it used to prescribe cannot actually build a kernel as-published — found while investigating why 192.168.15.95 had no image able to build one.
- **A host missing `mkfs.btrfs` now says so.** `diskformat.c`'s child wrapper collapsed the `mkfs` process's own exit 127 into 1, which made `diskformat_completed()`'s 127 branch — the one message that names the cause, "the control-plane image was built without it" — unreachable for exactly the case it was written for. Confirmed live: a real `fs_type:"btrfs"` format against a control-plane image built without `btrfs-progs` reported the useless "mkfs.btrfs failed" while the specific message sat there dead. The exit code is now propagated. Not covered by a test — this sandbox has no block devices to format at all (the same constraint `test_storage_placement` already documents), so this is a reasoned fix against live evidence, not a test-proven one.
- **Image/artifact export failures now carry the tar child's actual stderr** (`g_artifact_export_errfd`, drained bounded at completion) — found live on `.95` during phase 4: every export failed as bare `tar failed (status 0x200)` with the real complaint written to a stderr nothing captured, the same diagnostic-gap class issues #125/#132 document. The status line and log entry now append the child's own words.
- **Phase 4 (#161), first slice — btrfs becomes the install default.** `cix-install` formats `cix-containers` btrfs (full label now, no ext4 16-char truncation) and `cix-config` btrfs `--mixed` (64MiB is below the separate-profile minimum; mixed block groups are btrfs-progs' documented answer for tiny filesystems). No mkfs-time quota flags — btrfs quota is qgroups, enabled at runtime per container. The installer ISO stages `mkfs.btrfs` (+`libudev`); `mkfs.ext4` stays staged through the transition. Boot (`boot_init`) and `cix-recover` mount the platform partitions btrfs-then-ext4 — a not-yet-migrated ext4 box boots the new build unchanged, and the ext4 branch retires with the rest of ext4 once btrfs has run production. `test_installer` inspection reworked from `debugfs`/`e2fsck` (ext4-only) to `btrfs restore`; the debugfs `-w` marker-injection persistence proof — impossible offline on btrfs — is replaced by the stronger-in-substance check that installer-seeded content survives two real, independent QEMU boots byte-identical and cixd's grouped layout is present on the raw partition afterwards. Partition *resize* remains ext4-only (`resize2fs`) — filed as #163, not a migration blocker.
- **Two pre-existing lifecycle bugs found by the new test's 200ms stop/start cadence, both fixed:** `POST /start` during an in-flight stop returned the idempotent 200 for the *dying* incarnation — acking a start that never happened, leaving the container down while the caller believes it restarted (every restart script had this window; it now returns a retryable 409). And the stop/delete async completion removed its registry entry **by name**, so a same-name container registered in the completion window would be removed — and killed — by its predecessor's teardown (now guarded by incarnation identity: captured pid + started_at). A third gap — the files API on a cleanly stopped container is a race, then a 404, while an *exited* container's files stay accessible indefinitely — is pre-existing, orthogonal, and filed as #162 rather than smuggled into this change.

### Part 210 (in progress): what a real deploy finds that review does not

Five releases went to 192.168.15.95 in one afternoon (v2.1.1 → v2.1.5). Every one of them found something, and **three of the bugs were introduced by fixes made earlier the same day** — which is the substantive finding: on this platform a fix is a hypothesis until a real box runs it.

- **A good update could silently revert two reboots later.** `confirm_boot()` took whichever entry `readdir()` returned first, so with both `cix-a.conf` and `cix-a+3.conf` on the ESP it could "confirm" the already-confirmed one and no-op — leaving the real counter ticking down until systemd-boot gave up on the new slot. The update booted, ran, passed every health check, and was undone anyway. Caught on the real host after a successful cutover. Selection moved into `esp.c` as a rank rather than a first match.
- **The ESP ordering model was wrong, and confidently so.** `will boot:` ignored `sort-key`/`version` and sorted ids ascending, reporting that a correctly staged update would never boot. That answer was nearly acted on — and the obvious response (pinning `default` to one slot) genuinely breaks the *next* update. Settled by extracting a real `bootctl` and asking it. Issue #147, filed on the strength of the wrong model, is closed as invalid.
- **Boot slots can be switched now (#154, `GET/POST/DELETE /system/boot-next`).** Rollback previously meant waiting three reboots for a counter to exhaust, or reinstalling. Uses systemd-boot's `LoaderEntryOneShot`: one boot, then normal selection resumes, so a machine that fails to come back is never left pinned to a broken slot. A slot with no loader entry is refused rather than armed — arming a boot into nothing needs a console to recover from, which is the situation the feature exists to avoid.
- **A fresh install can deploy to itself (#146).** `mkbootroot` fell back to a `/usr/bin/mksquashfs` that exists only on a dev box. The first fix staged it from the bare host — so it worked only where it was not needed, and reproduced the original failure on the real box. Correct source is `cix-hosttools`.
- **A cache-hit hostbuild ran none of the work that follows a build (#144).** The fast path duplicated the post-build follow-up and omitted the bootroot assembly, so `--deploy` reported success and produced no image at all. One `pkg_completion_followup()` now serves both paths.
- **Provisioning became an endpoint (ADR-0205).** `cixctl dns provision` sequenced four REST calls itself — a CLI feature with no endpoint behind it, which the mandate forbids and which would have forced the dashboard to write the same sequence again. Required splitting `handle_create()` so a workflow endpoint creates containers through the same implementation as `POST /containers`.
- **DNS forwarders, provisioning and the ESP reached the dashboard**, and `cixctl update` gained `--image-url=`. Every capability the CLI could reach and the web could not was half-delivered.
- **Two test-methodology corrections**, both found by deliberately reintroducing a bug to check the test caught it. The first `confirm_boot` regression test **passed against the broken code**, because `readdir` order is unspecified and this sandbox returns the opposite order from the real vfat ESP; the decision is now a pure function asserted directly. And `test_dns`/`test_container_restart` leaked host bridges on failure, poisoning the *next* run with cascading errors that read exactly like a code regression — they now enumerate containers rather than naming them.

### Part 209 (in progress): closing the gaps Part 208 could only name

Part 208 ended with a retrospective and eight issues rather than features, because the DNS bring-up had been seven-eighths workaround. This part is the other half: turning those issues into mechanisms. Two of them turned out to be the same shape — a capability that *looked* present, was routed around in practice, and so was never actually exercised.

- **DNS forwarders are configuration now, not argv (#134, [ADR-0203](docs/adr/0203-dns-forwarders-are-daemon-owned-config.md)).** `GET/PUT /v1/dns/forwarders`, persisted with the rest of host config and applied live to every registered server via a daemon-written servers-file plus `SIGHUP`. The old convention — `--server=1.1.1.1` baked into each DNS container's command line — cost three real things: changing a forwarder meant **recreating core infrastructure**, `dns-1` and `dns-2` could **silently disagree** with nothing tying their argv together, and "what does this platform resolve through?" had **no answer at all**, the value living only inside a running process. One `PUT` now updates every replica, and a newly registered server picks up the current list without being told. `dnsmasq.recipe` and both DNS container recipes move to `--servers-file=`.
- **A host can update itself over its own API (#141, [ADR-0204](docs/adr/0204-the-daemon-fetches-its-own-update-image.md)).** `POST /v1/system/update` accepts `image_url` + a **mandatory** `image_sha256`. The endpoint previously took only `image_path` — a file already on the box — but an installed Cix host has no SSH, no shell, no scp target, and the API's 1 MiB cap rules out sending a ~10 MB squashfs as a body. So **the one endpoint whose entire job is updating the control plane could not be used to update it**, and every deploy in this project's history routed around it instead. The checksum is required rather than optional because this call writes a boot slot: an unverified image surfaces its damage at the next reboot, the worst possible moment. The URL is rewritten into the existing `image_path` flow, so slot-writing — the highest-consequence code here — keeps exactly one path.
- **A cache-hit install no longer demands the build tools it is not going to use (#144).** Installing a package whose artifact is already cached ran the build-container setup anyway, so a missing build tool failed an install that was never going to compile anything. The cache-hit branch now roots directly on the target image and skips container setup entirely.
- **Documentation swept for the drift that made Part 208 expensive.** `/dns/forwarders` was in the API README but had **never reached `openapi.yaml`** — precisely the divergence the Documentation Map exists to prevent, found by auditing rather than by it biting. Fixed, along with the README's three now-superseded `--server=` passages, the missing `image_url` contract in both files, four ADRs absent from the ADR index (0201–0204), and six broken intra-document anchors.
- **15 package artifacts rebuilt and re-approved (#130/#139).** Their cached artifacts had been published through `GET /containers/{name}/files`, which returns file **content with no mode** — so every binary inside arrived non-executable, checksummed perfectly, and died at `execve` with nothing naming the artifact as the cause. Each recipe's `pkg_artifact_sha256` now approves a correctly-moded rebuild. The checksum lives in git precisely because the artifact server is not a trust boundary: it serves bytes, the recipe line approves them.

### Part 208 (in progress): DNS on a fresh install, and an honest account of what that cost

`dns-1`/`dns-2` are running on a freshly installed host and answering real queries (`cix.internal` → the host, verified off-box against both replicas). Getting there took eight steps, **seven of which were workarounds** — so the substantive output of this part is a retrospective and eight issues, not a feature.

- **[docs/retrospective/0001](docs/retrospective/0001-why-bringing-up-dns-was-painful.md)** — a new document type, registered in the Documentation Map: *why an entire episode was harder than the work inside it*, for when the pattern matters more than any individual fix. Five root causes: a circular bootstrap (recipes ⇄ git ⇄ DNS), diagnostics that are discarded, failures that present as kernel panics, state that cannot round-trip through the API, and identity-by-manifest silently discarding correct fixes. The common shape: **the platform knew something the operator could not see** — a legibility failure, not a correctness one.
- **Issues #134–#141 filed**: configurable DNS forwarders (they are currently baked into a container's command line); the circular bootstrap; `cixctl dns provision` as one action instead of seven; declarable network address pools (auto-allocation put containers on live LAN addresses — a real hazard on a bridged management network); the `/etc/resolv.conf` bind-mount failure; artifacts losing file modes; OS-disk free space being unusable plus the disk UI inconsistencies; and the absence of any product path to seed a build toolchain.
- **The `/etc/resolv.conf` mystery is root-caused** (#138) and CLAUDE.md's long-standing "a real installed host has no outbound DNS at all" note is **corrected**: it is not missing NSS libraries (A/B tested — both image variants resolve fine) and not the kernel (a faithful rebuild changes nothing). `migrate_one_flat_entry()` returns early when there is nothing to migrate — i.e. on every fresh install — so `STATE_DIR` is never created, the bind mount fails ENOENT, and `PUT /v1/system/resolv` writes where nothing reads. That is why migrated boxes resolve and fresh ones never do.
- **Two traps recorded in CLAUDE.md** after each cost a full debugging cycle: `GET /containers/{name}/files` returns content with **no mode**, so anything built on it silently produces non-executable binaries (a checksum-perfect `dnsmasq` that could not `execve`); and an image version hashes the **manifest, not the content**, so a repaired package reinstalled at the same version is silently discarded (ADR-0155) — the fix "not taking" three times in a row.
- **Operator-facing guidance added** to `docs/guides/installing.md`: installing over a serial console (including MokManager, verified from real captures), what a degraded no-uplink first boot looks like and how to attach the interface live without reinstalling, and the fresh-install DNS limitation with its literal-IP workaround.
- **Documentation map closed**: `docs/README.md` had no owner row — the exact state the map declares invalid — and now has one, alongside the new `retrospective/` type.

### Part 207 (done): the installer gets eyes, and a missing NIC stops killing the box

Three fixes from one real failed install, each pinned by experiment before it was written (#131, #133, and the video mystery). The investigative record matters as much as the fixes, because three plausible theories died on the way.

- **The installer video console works now (`insmod all_video` + `gfxpayload=keep`).** Every EFI install to date was silently serial-only: GRUB printed `no suitable video mode found / Booting in blind mode` and the VGA stayed black forever. The mechanism took three controlled QEMU screendump experiments to pin: `gfxpayload=text` fails (text mode does not exist under EFI) — but so does `keep`, identically, which discriminated the real cause: **grub.cfg never loaded any video driver**, so every mode operation failed and GRUB passed the kernel no framebuffer at all. The menu rendering fine via the EFI *text* console (driver-free) is exactly what kept this invisible. With `all_video` loaded the third screendump shows the full kernel boot and installer prompts live on VGA. Two theories died en route, recorded here deliberately: the kernel config fragment was suspected and proven complete (Phase 18's video block resolves fully under the documented `allnoconfig`+merge procedure), and a freshly built faithful kernel was proven to change nothing by itself — the kernel was never the problem.
- **A missing management uplink degrades instead of panicking (#133).** A fresh install's first boot died with `network_attach_interface failed (13)` → `cixd` exit → PID-1 kernel panic, on a VM whose PCI scan (serial-captured from the rescue entry) demonstrably contained the virtio NIC. The attach failure is now log-and-continue: the management bridge and address already exist by then, so `cixd` binds and serves — including the serial console's interactive `cixctl` shell — and the log names the interface it wanted **and every interface present**. The exact trigger remains unreproduced and is stated so: the same transitional-virtio-behind-PCI-bridges topology was replicated in QEMU against both the shipped and the freshly built kernel, and **both found eth0** — so no speculative retry was added; the new diagnostic makes any recurrence self-explaining instead.
- **`cix-recover` parks instead of panicking (#131's purest instance).** Serial capture showed it doing its job perfectly, printing its summary, exiting 0 — and the kernel panicking with `Attempted to kill init! exitcode=0x00000000`, because it runs as PID 1. Success presented as a crash. Every path now funnels into a clear final banner ("finished successfully / finished with an ERROR — safe to power off or reset") followed by `sync()` and a permanent `pause()` loop.
- **Verified**: each fix by direct QEMU experiment (VGA screendumps before/after; full scripted install to `install complete` on the fixed ISO; first boot of the installed disk on the exact Proxmox-like NIC topology reaching `cixd listening`), plus the full regression suite on the final tree.

### Part 206 (done): the ESP is reachable over REST

**#128: a host could not complete an A/B update, and nothing said why** ([ADR-0202](docs/adr/0202-the-esp-is-reachable-over-rest.md)).

- **The failure.** `POST /v1/system/update` wrote the new control-plane image to the inactive slot and staged a correct loader entry. The machine rebooted into exactly what it was already running. Repeatedly, with no error anywhere. The cause was one line in `loader.conf`: `default thinc-*`, written at install time under the project's previous name. **systemd-boot's `default` is a glob PATTERN, not an entry name** — so it went on matching six stale `thinc-*` entries and outranking `cix-b+3.conf`, the one correctly-staged new one. From the bootloader's view nothing was wrong; from the daemon's view the update succeeded.
- **What actually made it expensive was invisibility.** Every other piece of a running host's state had an endpoint — containers, networks, DNS, PKI, disks, sysctls, kernel modules, routes, logs. The ESP had none, and on a platform with no SSH and no general shell on an installed host, that made `loader.conf` permanently unreachable and one stale line in it permanently fatal to updates.
- **Reporting comes before repair.** The new `GET /v1/system/esp` returns `selected_entry` — the entry systemd-boot would *actually* boot — plus `matches_default` per entry. The daemon computes that rather than leaving an operator to derive it from a glob and a directory listing, which is the step that went wrong. `cixctl esp show` leads with `will boot: <entry>`. This turns #128 from a long investigation into one command.
- **Pattern matching and selection follow the bootloader, not the filesystem.** The entry id is the filename minus `.conf` *and* minus the boot counter (`cix-b+3.conf` → `cix-b`), so `default cix-b` selects it exactly as firmware would; entries with no attempts left sort last, the rest ascending by id, and the pattern takes the **first** match. That last rule was wrong in the first cut — it took the *last* match, which against the real host's entries named a **slot-B** entry while the machine demonstrably boots **slot A**. It surfaced only by checking the computed answer against what the box actually does, and the test now asserts the slot rather than the prefix. A field whose entire purpose is to be believed is worse than useless when confidently wrong.
- **Two guards, both hard refusals rather than warnings**, because anyone using this endpoint is by construction not at the console: a `default` matching **zero** entries is refused with 409 (silent, and strands the host at next boot — the error names what does exist), and the **last remaining** entry for the running slot cannot be deleted. Duplicates of it can be, since clearing accumulated duplicates is exactly what removal is for. Path traversal in an entry name is rejected outright. The second guard **degrades rather than disappears**: it attributes entries to the running slot via the `--slot=` the daemon writes into every entry it creates, so a daemon started without one would otherwise protect nothing — it falls back to refusing the last entry on the ESP at all, and the test starts a second, slotless daemon to prove it.
- **A `loader.conf` rewrite preserves what it does not understand** — `console-mode`, `editor` and friends are copied verbatim rather than the file being regenerated from a template and settings silently dropped.
- **The loader directory is derived from the entries directory, not composed separately**, so the existing `--test-esp-entries-dir=` override governs both; otherwise a test could point entries somewhere harmless while `loader.conf` writes still landed on the real `/boot`.
- **Verified** with `test_esp`, whose fixture is the real host's exact state (a stale pattern, six entries it matches, one staged entry it does not). It asserts the diagnostic first — `selected_entry` must name the stale entry — then the repair, then both guards, path traversal, and that a refused delete really left the file alone. As with the previous part, one assertion was deliberately broken to confirm the checks execute rather than trusting a silent pass.
- **This does not rescue the host that prompted it**, and that is stated rather than glossed: that machine runs a build predating the endpoint, and the endpoint only exists in builds it cannot boot — the catch-22 *is* the issue. It needs hypervisor-side console or disk access, or a reinstall. Every host installed from a build carrying this API is fixable remotely; that one is not.

### Part 205 (done): a built artifact is retrievable, and publishes itself

**#129: hostbuild artifacts had no retrieval route; built packages never left the box that built them** ([ADR-0201](docs/adr/0201-artifacts-are-retrievable-and-self-publishing.md)). Found while push-testing a real artifact cache: `kmod@34.2-2` pushed fine, `kernel@6.18.40-14` could not be extracted at all.

- **The gap, precisely.** `GET /v1/pkg` reported the kernel `installed` with 34 recorded files, every one unreachable: booting a container from `__hostbuild` and reading `/bzImage` returned `no such file` for all 34, and the image showed `manifest: []` with both versions predating the build (`e3b0c442…` being the sha256 of the empty string). None of that is a bug — per ADR-0056 a hostbuild's output lands in a host directory deliberately never made container-visible, so the recorded list describes that directory, not any rootfs. The gap was that **nothing could read it back out**: `artifact_path` was exposed as a path *string*, its only consumers `access()` the files off local disk, and `artifacts` is classified REBUILDABLE so backup skips it and factory reset wipes it. The self-hosted kernel — a ~50-minute build at the end of a four-stage toolchain chain — existed as bytes in one directory on one machine.
- **One export mechanism, two subjects.** The image export state machine (#126) already tarred a tree, reaped the child, reported status and served bounded chunks; a hostbuild artifact needed all of it and differed only in source and filename. Generalized to `artifact_export_*` with an explicit kind rather than duplicated — growing a second near-identical machine would have been a direct No Parallel Implementations violation. New routes: `POST`/`GET /v1/pkg/{name}/artifact/export` and `GET .../export/download`. Handlers match on **both** kind and name, so an image and a package sharing a name can never serve each other's export.
- **A fresh build publishes itself.** `push_enabled` on `PUT /v1/pkg/artifact-config` makes a genuine fresh build upload its own cache tarball — a `PUT` to exactly the URL a puller later fetches from, carrying the bearer token and an `X-Cix-Sha256` header. It never publishes what it did not build (a cache/artifact *hit*'s bytes already came from there); it never becomes a trust boundary (the consumer still verifies against the recipe's git-tracked checksum — the digest header is a corruption check at the door, not a claim taken on faith); it never blocks the event loop (forked child computes the digest and uploads); and it is never silent (every skip reason logged, and the reaper reports what the server actually said — a host that silently publishes nothing looks exactly like a host with nothing to publish, the trap #125 set). **Off by default**: publishing is outward-facing, so it is opted into, never inherited from having a `base_url` set for pulling. Pushes are serialized through a queue, because parallel builds can finish together and dropping the overflow would recreate the very problem being fixed.
- **Cache tarballs are now reproducible**, which is what makes an immutability rule usable rather than noisy. Confirmed by direct experiment rather than assumed: with the previous flags two builds of an identical tree differ, because per-file mtimes ride in the tar headers; with `--sort=name --mtime=@0 --owner=0 --group=0 --numeric-owner` they are byte-identical. (The gzip header timestamp was already zero for an unrelated reason — `--use-compress-program` pipes through gzip's stdin, which has no filename or mtime to record; that fell out of #125's PATH fix and is worth knowing before anyone "simplifies" it back to `-z`.) Without this, every host would produce different bytes for the same recipe version, the first push would win, and every later one would be refused — turning a real integrity rule into permanent background noise.
- **The image export finally has a test.** #126 shipped with none; generalizing that exact code is what surfaced it. `test_artifact_export` covers both kinds: a seeded hostbuild artifact exported and pulled back with its **content** compared (not just its filenames — the class of bug #122 was), the image kind over the same machine, that the two kinds do not cross-match on a shared name, and 404s for an unknown package and for a download with no ready export behind it.
- **Push is tested end-to-end** against a real PUT-accepting receiver in `test_pkg_cache`: a real build must produce a real upload, under exactly the name a puller asks for, carrying the configured bearer token and a digest that matches the bytes that actually arrived — and a subsequent cache-hit reinstall must **not** republish. The assertions were themselves verified by deliberately breaking one and confirming it fails, since a silent-on-success check that never runs is indistinguishable from one that passes.
- **Known consequence, recorded rather than reconciled silently**: `pkg_artifact_sha256` values recorded before this describe non-canonical tarballs. Existing pulls are unaffected — the server still holds the objects those checksums describe — but a checksum regenerated from a daemon-built tarball will differ. Filed separately rather than quietly fixed. Whether `artifacts` should remain in the REBUILDABLE class now that its contents are retrievable is likewise left open, not settled as a side effect.

### Part 204 (done): the project is renamed to Cix

**#121: rebrand to Cix** ([ADR-0200](docs/adr/0200-rebrand-to-cix.md)). "C" for the C language and for containers, "ix" for POSIX and UNIX, pronounced *six*. The owner supplied the full brand system first (`docs/brand/`: guidelines, logo reference sheet, the canonical SVG mark and a 102-icon UI set), so this pass had something to rename *to* rather than a name and a guess.

- **Everything, in one mechanical pass**: 10,570 occurrences across 470 files — binaries (`cixd`, `cixctl`, `cix-install`, `cix-recover`), the `cix_`/`CIX_` identifier prefix, state paths (`/var/lib/cix`, `/etc/cix-tls`, `/etc/cix-ldap`), image and package names (`cix-builder`, `cix-hosttools`, the `cix` self-package), the `X-Cix-Exec-Cmd` header, the PKI's own `Cix Root CA` subject, every document, every recipe, every test fixture. Verified the way a rename of this size has to be: a clean `-Wall -Werror` build (a missed identifier is an undeclared symbol, not a silent behaviour change) plus the full regression suite.
- **Zero occurrences of either previous name anywhere** — the owner's explicit choice over the narrower option [ADR-0192](docs/adr/0192-cix-identifier-prefix.md) took, and it reaches `CHANGELOG.md` and the frozen `docs/mission/MISSION.md` too. Only names changed; no entry's substance, dates, or claims were touched. Where rewriting produced a self-referential sentence (a changelog line describing a *previous* rename now reading as a rename from a name to itself), the sentence was rewritten to describe it as an earlier project rename rather than left as nonsense — six such places.
- **Two ADRs re-anchored rather than left broken.** ADR-0162 (written for the earlier rename) and ADR-0192 (the identifier-prefix rename) had dead names as their entire subject. ADR-0192 keeps its decision — one prefix, and it is the project's own name — described without naming the dead one. ADR-0162 is rewritten to keep the part that outlived the names and genuinely earned its place: *what a rename in this system actually costs* — a Secure Boot certificate's own subject, on-disk state paths, the default instance FQDN, and the image names recorded inside every installed host's database. It is now superseded by ADR-0200, which applied exactly the sequence it describes.
- **The Secure Boot signing key is regenerated, not renamed** — `CN=Cix Secure Boot Signing Key, O=Cix Project`, the same choice ADR-0162 made for the same reason. **Any machine that MOK-enrolled the previous key must re-enroll** (interactive, physical-console MokManager) before a chain signed with the new one is trusted there.
- **The web dashboard gets the real mark.** The header and About panel previously loaded an SVG that was the *previous* project's artwork with a hardcoded cyan fill; both now inline the canonical Cix mark using `currentColor`, so it follows the light/dark theme instead of being painted one fixed colour, and the favicon is the brand set's purpose-built app-icon tile.
- **`docs/brand/` is deliberately excluded** from the mechanical rename. It is the owner's own supplied material, and it names the previous identity legitimately — migrating away from it is that document's own subject (its section 29 is the migration plan). Rewriting those mentions would have made it describe a rename from Cix to Cix.
- **Installed hosts are untouched by design.** The owner chose to defer the live box entirely: this change is repo-side only, so nothing in flight on it — including a multi-hour compiler bootstrap running at the time — was disturbed. Their state paths, image names, and running binaries still carry the old names until a separately scheduled migration, which is an operator action, never a compatibility path in the code.
- **Verified**: clean `-Wall -Werror` build from scratch, **67 of 68** regression tests passing. The one failure, `test_rolling_restart`, was proven pre-existing rather than caused here — 3 runs in this tree and 3 in a clean worktree at the pre-rebrand commit both passed twice and failed on the third, with identical assertions, and every tracked source diffs clean through a reverse-rename. Filed as issue #123: the test allows a fixed 12 seconds for a package install, and this box's filesystem journal stalls for 5-13 seconds under load, which the daemon's own stall watchdog logs.
- Three pre-existing broken documentation links (ADR filenames referenced by names they never had) were found by the link check this pass added and fixed: `0107-image-versioning`, `0076-operator-set-upstream-resolvers`, `0034-no-ssh-on-installed-hosts`.

### Part 203 (in progress): pre-bare-metal quality sprint

**#109: a recipe declares its build tools, and gets exactly those** ([ADR-0199](docs/adr/0199-recipes-declare-their-build-tools.md)). Raised by the operator: *"shouldn't a recipe declare the build tools it requires explicitly? no extras and no less, very explicit, not fungible?"* — and the measurement said yes, emphatically.
- **What the shared sandbox actually was**, measured on the real box: 79,438 files, of which at most **19%** was accounted for by any installed package. **53,535 of them — 67% of the whole thing — were a Rust and Go toolchain** (`/usr/local/cargo`, `/usr/local/go`, `/usr/local/rustup`) that no recipe asks for and no package installs; zero of 200 recipes write to `/usr/local`. The compiler answered to `/usr/bin/gcc`, resolved to a Debian-named `x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc-12`, and reported `gcc (GCC) 4.7.4`.
- **`pkg_build_depends=`** is the declaration, deliberately a *second* field rather than a redefinition of `pkg_depends`: one says what must be present to **build**, the other what the built thing needs at **runtime**. `bison` needs `m4` at runtime; `m4` needs `binutils` to build; `gcc` needs both, and different ones.
- **The build container is composed from exactly those packages' own recorded file lists** — not the image they live in (a union of whatever was installed into it), and not the shared sandbox (the problem). Deliberately the manifest rather than the build cache, though the cache holds the same bytes: a cache is prunable, and the first live attempt proved why — it failed with *"declared build tool `tcc@0.9.27` has no cached build output"* on a box where tcc was installed and working. Files are copied faithfully: mode preserved, symlinks recreated as symlinks. Both halves are then enforced rather than trusted: *no less*, because the build fails naming what is missing; *no extras*, because nothing else is there to depend on.
- **A build that failed at container setup or `execve()` no longer sits in `building` forever.** Three of the five failure branches wrote the error string but never moved the state, so a package whose build container could not be set up — or whose build script could not be `execve()`d at all — reported a real, accurate error next to a state that said it was still working. Every branch now fails the package properly. Found by the test below rather than by a user waiting on a build that was never going to finish.
- **The shared copy-forward path names its failing step.** `image_produce_new_version()` had nine silent `return -1` exits, and two separate investigations this cycle (the flat-sandbox migration, and the first live build-environment composition) each stalled on the same bare "could not produce a new version" with no way to tell which step or which errno. Each exit now logs the step and the errno; the composition path additionally names the exact file and declared tool it failed on.
- **The composition success path is now tested.** Only the refusal path had coverage — a recipe naming a tool that does not exist. A composition that failed for *every* input would have looked green, which is precisely what shipped. The new case declares a tool that really is installed and asserts the build gets far enough to fail on its own merits rather than on composition.
- **A build environment that exists is not a build environment that was filled.** `image_create()` hands every new image a current version straight away, so the "already composed, reuse it" check was answering the wrong question. A composition that failed left the created-but-empty image behind, and the next build accepted it: the daemon logged a composed environment, then the build died at `execve(/usr/bin/bash)` on an environment holding nothing at all. The check now skips an image still at its empty-manifest version — so one poisoned by an earlier daemon heals itself — and a failed composition deletes what it created.
- **The flat build sandbox can migrate again (#40).** It was failing on `File exists`, which turned out to be a merged-`/usr` shape difference rather than a content conflict: the flat sandbox has `/lib` as a symlink to `usr/lib`, the image has a real `/lib` directory, `unlink()` cannot remove a directory, and the `symlink()` after it took the whole migration down. The directory is kept — everything reachable through the symlink is reachable through its target, which the same walk merges anyway — and the decision is logged rather than made silently.
- **A declared build tool resolves to an image that actually exists.** Resolution took the first installed package matching the name, and on the real box `bash` matched a row naming `cix-builder` — an image from this project's previous name that no longer exists, while `bash` sat installed in three healthy images. Candidates whose image cannot be resolved are now skipped, and if that is the only place a tool lives the failure says so by name. The orphaned registry rows themselves are filed as #111.
- **A declared build tool brings what it needs to run.** `zlib` declared `binutils` for `ar`; the environment received binutils' own files and `ar` died with *"error while loading shared libraries: libz.so.1"*. Composition now includes each declared tool's runtime dependency closure as recorded at install time. This is not a relaxation of "exactly what the recipe declares" — a tool that cannot start is not a leaner environment — and no recipe author should have to enumerate the shared libraries of a tool they named. `binutils` 2.42-3 now declares `pkg_depends="zlib"`, which was always true and never written down.
- **A declared build tool resolves to its newest installed version, deterministically.** Resolution took whichever copy the registry listed first, so a build environment depended on install order — the exact non-determinism this is supposed to remove. It failed a real build: `libc-dev` resolved to 2.36, which stages no `libm.so`, while 2.36-3, which does, sat installed in two other images. Versions are now compared the way a person reads them (digit runs numerically, the rest lexically), because plain string ordering puts `2.36-3` before `2.36` and `1.3.2-10` before `1.3.2-9`.
- **Every `libz.so.1` in this catalog had been built by GCC, not TCC — and the recipe said `CC=tcc`.** zlib's configure probes for shared-library support by linking one, with an `LDSHARED` it composes itself ending in `--version-script`. TCC supports `-shared` and `-Wl,-soname` but rejects `--version-script` outright, so the probe fails — and configure does not treat that as an error. It prints "No shared library support" and builds a static library instead. `make`, `make install` and the package install all succeed; the only symptom is a `libz.so.1` that was never created. That shipped: 1.3.2-5 installed cleanly with headers, a pkg-config file and no library, and the next thing to link against it died with *"cannot open shared object file: libz.so"*. It went unnoticed for as long as it did because the shared sandbox's `cc` had quietly become real GCC, which accepts the flag. 1.3.2-6 sets `LDSHARED` without the version script (nothing here needs one) and **refuses to install** if no shared library was built, rather than leaving it for the next consumer to discover.
- **First recipes converted and verified on the real box**: `zlib`, `binutils`, `sed`, `grep` and `make` each build in an environment composed from exactly what they declare. Every list was written by building and reading the failure, which is the intended method — `zlib` learned `binutils` from *"make: ar: No such file or directory"*, `make` learned it from *"no acceptable ld found in $PATH"*, and `binutils` learned `flex` from `ar` refusing to start without `libfl.so.2`.
- **`tcc` had never once compiled itself.** Its recipe reads `CC=tcc`, but tcc's configure is hand-written and ignores a `CC=` environment variable entirely — it takes `--cc=`. So every tcc this project ever installed was built by whatever ambient GCC the shared sandbox carried. In a declared environment the build printed `C compiler  gcc (0.0)` and stopped at `make: gcc: No such file or directory`. 0.9.27-3 passes `--cc=tcc`, and tcc now builds itself.
- **`flex`'s build-time helpers were compiled by an unnamed compiler too.** Its configure runs a *second* probe (`AX_PROG_CC_FOR_BUILD`) which does not read `CC` at all — it looks for gcc, then cc, then cl.exe. With `CC=tcc` accepted and cached a few lines earlier, the same configure still stopped with "no acceptable C compiler found in $PATH". 2.6.4-4 sets `CC_FOR_BUILD=tcc`.
- **`libc-dev` now stages `libdl.a`**, the same glibc ≥ 2.34 gap it already documents for `libpthread`: libdl folded into `libc.so.6`, leaving an 8-byte placeholder archive and no `libdl.so`, while real build systems still pass `-ldl` unconditionally. tcc's own Makefile does, so tcc could not link itself.
- **A real dependency cycle, and the mislabelling that caused it.** `m4` declared `pkg_depends="binutils"`, which was never true — m4 does not shell out to `ar`; it needs it to *build*. The field was carrying build dependencies because there was nowhere else to put them. That became a refusal-to-install the moment anything else was declared honestly: binutils' `ar` genuinely needs libfl, flex genuinely needs m4, and m4 claiming binutils closed the loop. There is no cycle in the real relationships, only in the mislabelled one.
- **Ten packages converted and verified on 192.168.15.95**: `zlib`, `binutils`, `sed`, `grep`, `make`, `tcc`, `libc-dev`, `bash`, `m4`, `flex` — each built in an environment composed from exactly what it declares.
- **The kernel could not run scripts (#114).** `CONFIG_BINFMT_SCRIPT` was never enabled, so `execve()` of any `#!` script returned `ENOEXEC` — and because POSIX makes a shell whose `execve()` returns `ENOEXEC` run the file itself, every shell script kept working by pure coincidence while every script with any other interpreter was quietly handed to bash. Found building `diffutils`, whose bundled `help2man` Perl script produced *bash* syntax errors (`use Text::Tabs qw(expand);` → "syntax error near unexpected token `('"`) with a working `/usr/bin/perl` sitting in the same container. Reproduced in isolation with a two-line Perl script, which is what turned "diffutils is broken" into "this kernel cannot run scripts". Same `allnoconfig` trap the config file already documents above `CONFIG_BINFMT_ELF` — ELF was caught because nothing boots without it; SCRIPT was not, because its absence degrades instead of failing.
- **Our compiler now provides the `__atomic_*` builtins.** TCC 0.9.27 implements neither `__atomic_test_and_set`/`__atomic_clear` nor the `__ATOMIC_*` order macros that GCC and Clang have had for over a decade, so any package using them — libcap's internal spinlock is two lines of exactly that — simply does not compile. They now come from `libtcc1.a`, the compiler's own runtime, which is the same answer GCC gives with libgcc, rather than from a copy in every affected recipe. `xchg` with a memory operand asserts LOCK implicitly on x86, so one `xchgb` is a genuine full-barrier atomic RMW; verified by disassembly and by running the resulting spinlock, and the recipe asserts it at build time.
- **`libcap` is a real package now (#110).** `coreutils` links against it — that is how `ls` shows file capabilities — and had been staging the *build host's* Debian copy, a library no recipe built and no package owned. The alternative was `--disable-libcap` and losing a real feature. A distribution builds its own libraries: `libcap` 2.78-2 builds libcap.so.2, libpsx, and the setcap/getcap/getpcaps/capsh tools under TCC.
- **A declared list that was measured rather than reasoned about.** libcap 2.78 declared `sed`, `grep` and `gawk` on the assumption that a build of its shape must use them; a clean build invokes none of the three. Conversely `diffutils` 3.10-2 deliberately left `gawk` out as an experiment the build environment can settle — and it failed with `config.status: line 2898: awk: command not found`. So awk is genuinely required by any autoconf-generated configure and genuinely not required by a package with no configure at all, and both halves now rest on builds that were actually run. "No extras" is the half of this property nothing enforces, so it has to be checked.
- **A command that fails inside a recipe now fails the package.** Recipes ran as `. recipe.sh; cd src && pkg_build && pkg_install` with no `set -e`, so a command that failed *partway* through either function was simply stepped over — the function carried on and returned whatever ran last. `libcap` 2.78-3 shipped exactly that way: `make install` died with Error 2, the `rm -rf` after it succeeded, and the package was recorded as **installed** with four of its binaries missing. A package that quietly contains less than it should is worse than one that fails, because nothing downstream can tell. The separators matter as much as the flag: POSIX suspends `set -e` for any command in an `&&` list except the last, *including inside functions called from there*, so `pkg_build && pkg_install` would have left every failure inside `pkg_build()` ignored.
- **…and the first thing that rule broke was a `wait`.** `gcc` 4.7.4 builds a background helper loop, kills it when `make` finishes, and waits for it. `kill` on an already-exited job returns 1; `wait` on a job just SIGTERM'd returns 143. Under `set -e` both end the build — so the entire compiler built, `make` returned 0, and the recipe died cleaning up. The daemon then reported exit 143 as *"overlay mount or exec failed: No such process"*, since 143 is both `128+SIGTERM` and `140+ESRCH` in its own encoding: a finished build reported as a container that never started. Fixed with `|| true` on both, and `set -e` is now documented in the recipe guide, which it should have been when it was introduced.
- **Observability: the daemon now says where a build stopped, instead of nothing.** Four gaps closed together, each one having cost real hours this cycle:
  - **A stalled build reports itself.** `last_output_seconds_ago` existed since #58 and nothing ever acted on it, so a build that stopped producing output sat in `building` looking exactly like one that was working — a real gcc build did that for an hour, and the only thing that noticed was a person wondering why the machine was idle. A periodic check now reports any build quiet for 10 minutes, **with what every process in its build container is blocked on**. It reports and does not kill: a long quiet stretch is not always a stall, and killing a build about to finish is worse than handing an operator the evidence. Threshold is `CIX_BUILD_STALL_SECONDS`.
  - **`state` and `wchan` on `GET /v1/system/processes`.** The single field that cracked the gcc deadlock — everything at `do_wait` (waiting for a child, says nothing) except one `cc1` at `__futex_wait` (says everything) — previously required `exec`ing into the container by hand. The daemon collected everything about a process except what it was waiting for.
  - **Exit status 143 is no longer reported as "overlay mount or exec failed".** The `140+errno` encoding and the shell's `128+signal` convention overlap, so a build that compiled an entire compiler and died in cleanup was described as a container that never started. Captured output settles it decisively: the errno encoding is only ever emitted *before* `execve()` succeeds, so one byte of build output proves the setup path was long gone.
  - **`merge_tree()` names the file and the errno.** Eight silent `return -1`s meant "failed to merge installed files into the target image" was the entire diagnosis — the same silence that cost hours on #40 and #109, one function further down (#118).
- **Installing a package file over a symlink wrote *through* it (#118).** `copy_file_simple()` opens the destination `O_CREAT|O_TRUNC`, which follows a symlink — so a package file landing on an existing link wrote to the link's *target* instead of replacing the link. The visible failure was the lucky case: gcc's own `usr/bin/c++` landed on a Debian-alternatives symlink left in the build sandbox (`-> /etc/alternatives/c++`, which does not exist there), so the open failed `ENOENT` and the merge stopped with `failed to merge installed files into the target image` and nothing else. Had that target existed, the install would have **silently overwritten an unrelated file and reported success**. The symlink branch had always unlinked first; the regular-file branch now does too. Found in one attempt once `merge_tree()` named the file — the diagnostic and the bug it exposed shipped together.
- **The exec endpoint silently truncated over-long arguments.** `argv` entries are copied into a 512-byte buffer with `snprintf()`, so a longer one was cut and **run anyway** — a shell script passed to `bash -c` came back as `unexpected EOF while looking for matching quote` and `missing filename after '-o'`, errors that describe the damage and give no hint the request was altered between being accepted and executed. Now a 400 naming the limit.
- **`libcap`, `diffutils` and `elfutils` are honest packages now.** `diffutils` had never once built in this project — its recipe has said `CC=tcc` since it was written and the package was installed in no image at all; it needed a parenthesized-string-literal initializer (a GCC extension TCC correctly rejects) and man-page generation turned off. `elfutils` declared `pkg_depends=""` while its `libelf.so.1` genuinely needs `libz`, `liblzma` and `libbz2` — so the image the kernel builds in has been carrying a libelf that cannot load, which is what surfaced it.
- **`__dso_handle` moved into the compiler, where it belongs.** Seven recipes — `sed`, `grep`, `coreutils`, `m4`, `bison`, `gawk`, `sysklogd` — each compiled and linked their own one-line copy, because glibc's static-destructor bookkeeping expects a symbol GCC supplies from `crtbegin.o` and a bare TCC link has nothing to supply. It now comes from `libtcc1.a`. Strong rather than weak, and that is the trick: a weak definition does not cause archive extraction (which is exactly why those recipes pass a bare object path), while a strong one in an archive is pulled in *only* when nothing else defines the symbol. Both paths verified — a program that needs it links, a program defining its own links with no conflict.
- **`ncurses` had never been built by TCC either.** Its configure is a customised autoconf 2.52-era script that ignores a preset `CC` from the environment: the log said `checking for gcc... gcc` / `using the GNU C compiler... yes`, and every feature test then ran through the compiler that segfaults on ordinary C (#116) — which is why they came back "no" en masse and configure gave up with "getopt is required for building programs". Passing `CC=tcc` as a configure *argument* (authoritative, and recorded in `config.status`) fixes it. Third package in this pattern after `tcc` (`--cc=`) and `flex` (`CC_FOR_BUILD`).
- **`ncurses` now ships the compatibility names.** The build is `--enable-widec`, so everything installed under wide-char names and nothing called `libncurses.so` or `libtinfo.so` existed at all — so `psmisc` stopped with "Cannot find tinfo, ncurses or termcap libraries" against a perfectly good ncurses, and `vim`, `htop`, `screen` and `procps` all link the same conventional names. The links Debian and Fedora ship for the same reason are now shipped here.
- **Fourteen more packages converted and verified**: `gzip`, `tar`, `patch`, `findutils`, `bc`, `psmisc`, `pkgconf`, `xz`, `ncurses` join the earlier set — each built on the real box in an environment composed from exactly what it declares.
- **Detail panels are banded tables instead of a reflowing grid.** Every labelled value on every detail page — a container's Summary, Hardware and Options, a network's addressing, a disk's geometry, zswap, kernel policy, LDAP delivery, package recipes, volumes — now renders as a row: label in the left column, value in the right, alternate rows shaded. All thirteen panels come from one shared helper (`fieldBlock`, 65 call sites), so they cannot drift apart and this was a change in one function plus its CSS rather than thirteen edits. The grid it replaced packed more into the same height, but it rearranged itself at every window width, so a value was never twice in the same place and nothing connected a label to its value across the gap. The label is a real `<th scope="row">`, which is what it is — screen readers announce it as the row's header. Long values (a command line, a capability list) wrap in their own cell rather than widening the page.
- **The composed environment is an image named for the hash of the declared set**, sorted before hashing, so the same set is built once and reused and two sets can never collide. That reuse is what makes declaring tools cheap enough to do everywhere.
- **A declared tool that cannot be provided fails the build, naming it — with no fallback.** Asserted by a test, because it is the whole property: a fallback would let a build succeed against something fuller than it declared, and would teach everyone the declaration is decorative.
- **Proven end to end on the real box** before any of it was written. zlib built in a declared environment (the `dev` image) instead of the shared sandbox: first attempt failed with `tcc: command not found` → `configure: Missing or broken C compiler`; declaring that one package produced `configure: OK`, `make: OK`, `libz.a` 197,450 bytes — with `/usr/local` absent entirely and one unambiguous compiler. `zlib` 1.3.2-4 now carries the declaration, with a line per tool saying why it earns its place.
- **Stated plainly rather than implied**: sufficiency is enforced, minimality is not — declaring a tool you do not need still builds, and review is the only check. And `pkg_depends` across the existing catalogue is inconsistent *necessarily*, because the word meant two things; splitting it is what makes "accurate" definable, and auditing the set is the work that follows.

**#40: the build sandbox is an ordinary image now, not a second mechanism beside images** ([ADR-0198](docs/adr/0198-build-sandbox-is-a-real-image.md)). It lived at a flat `<images_dir>/pkgbuild/rootfs` with no version, no manifest and no history, seeded straight to disk and then grown silently by every successful install. Its content was a function of one box's entire install history, expressible nowhere and comparable to nothing — which is why a recipe that built once could stop building with no visible change anywhere, exactly as `gcc/4.7.4` did while working #55, blocking a ready fix.
- It is the **`cix-builder`** image now, resolved with the same two calls the hostbuild path three lines above was already making. Operator's choice over a separate name, with the real consequence stated rather than discovered: `cix-builder` is grown by *every* ordinary install now, so a hostbuild's inputs move when unrelated things are installed — which is precisely what the version history exists to make visible, and roll back.
- **The trap this walks into**: an image's version identity is a hash of its *manifest* (ADR-0108), and folding a package into the sandbox adds no manifest entry — so the naive implementation hashes to the same version, discards the staging copy as already-produced, and reports success while losing the merge. ADR-0155's same-manifest trap from the other direction, and silent. Fixed with an identity chain — `v(n+1) = H(manifest, v(n), pkg@version)` — used by this one caller and NULL for every other.
- **Verified by breaking it on purpose**: with the identity chain removed, `test_pkg` does not fail gently — packages get stuck in `building`, because later recipes no longer find what earlier ones installed. The regression test asserts the sandbox version actually *advances* across an install, not merely that the install succeeded.
- **Migrated, not dropped.** Resolving the image instead would have silently discarded everything already accreted — turning a structural refactor into an unannounced content change. An existing flat directory is folded in as a real version at startup and then **set aside rather than deleted**, renamed with the version it produced. What the sandbox contains is unchanged; only how it is tracked changes.
- **If the migration fails, builds keep using the flat directory** — a safety net added *because the first version lacked it*. On the real box the migration failed, builds silently switched to the image's declared content, and the very next install died on `sed: command not found`: `sed` had only ever accreted into the flat sandbox and was never in the manifest. Exactly what this issue is about, biting the migration first. The box was rolled back within minutes, the fallback added, and the deployed version left at v1.95.0 until the migration itself is fixed.
- Still open, and honestly so: the manifest lists only what was installed into the image directly, so the accreted union is real content without a declared list — and that content is **load-bearing**, not incidental. That is the remaining half of #40, now possible because the versioning exists to hang it on.

**DHCP: a self-contained service** ([ADR-0197](docs/adr/0197-dhcp-served-by-the-dns-server.md)). Requested by the operator: ranges per network, an enable switch, static reservations, all API-driven, "play nice with DNS" with the entry appearing on the fly — then corrected three times as it took shape, each correction making it more contained rather than more clever.
- **Containment is the constraint**, and it came from the operator directly: services stay self-sufficient because they may become loadable plugins. So DHCP registers its **own** servers, owns its own ranges and reservations, and every endpoint lives under `/v1/dhcp`. It reads no other service's registry and nothing DHCP-shaped hangs off `/v1/networks`. The first version had both wrong in ways that read as elegant integration and were actually coupling: it *required* a DHCP server to be a registered DNS server, and hung the range off the network resource.
- **The pairing with DNS survives as a reported fact.** dnsmasq answers for the names of clients it has itself leased addresses to, so registering the same container as both makes a lease resolve the instant it is issued. `resolves_leases` says whether that is true for each server — the same information enforcing it would have given, at no structural cost.
- **A lease is not a DNS record.** A record is durable operator intent; a lease is short-lived state owned by its server. Mirroring leases into the record store would put two writers in one namespace and leave a record pointing at an address another machine now holds. Leases are read from each server's own lease file, every time.
- **Redundancy is split scope, because with dnsmasq it has to be.** It implements no failover protocol — no peer relationship, no shared lease database. A range names the servers that serve it (one, three, more — an operator's decision), and Cix divides it into one **disjoint slice** each: all answer, a client takes whichever offer arrives first, and no two servers hold the same address. Any one alone keeps serving from its own slice. Order is preserved because it is the slice order — a derived order would move every client's address whenever something unrelated changed. What this does *not* give is an ISC-dhcpd-style hot standby knowing its peer's leases; that needs a server implementing a failover protocol.
- **Found on the real box, and it was the bug that mattered**: dnsmasq reads its conf only at startup, and a restart re-stages the container's creation-time `files[]` — so the rendered conf written into the *running* container was overwritten by the empty placeholder on the very next restart, and the range silently never took effect. The exact failure this design exists to refuse, hiding inside the mechanism meant to prevent it. The render is now staged into the container **at creation, before its process starts**; the test restarts the server and re-reads rather than trusting the write.
- **One place to configure each thing.** Reservations had ended up on three surfaces at once — the network page, the service page, and the menu. Creating now happens only from the Services menu and listing only on the page, the rule ADR-0184 already set for the rest of the dashboard. The DHCP service page (Servers / Ranges / Reservations / Leases) owns configuration; a network's own page shows the leases on it and nothing else.
- **Static reservations are live; range changes are not, and that difference is honoured.** dnsmasq re-reads reservations on `SIGHUP`; ranges only at startup, so a range change restarts the servers that serve it — through the same jittered rolling-restart timer a rolling image update uses, and only those whose own conf actually changed.
