There *was* already a remembered fs_type (`diskrole_set_fs_type()`, persisted) but only for disks carrying a role, so nothing could answer the question for the OS layout or a freshly-partitioned disk -- exactly where an operator most needs it, since a partition with no reported filesystem reads as empty whether or not it is. The device is the truth; the remembered value is a cache for choosing a mount type. Read directly rather than by shelling out to `blkid`, because this project has just spent a release with partitioning silently broken by a compiled-in binary path that was never staged (#9) and adding another would be the same mistake with a different binary. Only what this platform produces or boots from is recognised, and anything else reports `""` rather than guessing -- a blank partition reported as ext4 is worse than one reported as unknown. `role` is joined into the same response rather than leaving every client to fetch `GET /diskroles` and match by name, which is what every client was doing.
- Verified against crafted superblocks at their real offsets, plus a blank device and a missing one, because the real path **cannot run in this sandbox at all**: it has no block device nodes. `/sys/class/block` is fully visible -- which is why enumeration cheerfully lists `sda`, `nvme0n1` and 70+ `dm-*` here -- but `/dev/sda` does not exist, confirmed with `ls` and `dd` as real root, so every `open()` returns ENOENT. Recorded in `CLAUDE.md`; it is a *different* restriction from the loop-device gap already noted there.
- **#91, the page shape.** The Disks page was three storage-placement forms stacked on one flat table with no `is_partition` filter, so `vda`, its five partitions, `sda` and `sr0` were eight peers in one list. Now: **Disks** lists whole disks only, identity and state, no actions -- nothing destructive one stray click away in a list. Each name links to its own **disk page** with three tabs: Overview; **Partitions** (per-partition role/format/unmount/delete, add a partition, write a fresh GPT table, both `confirm()`-guarded, with `has_mounted_partition` surfaced as the *reason* a rewrite is refused rather than a bare 409); and **Whole disk** -- giving the entire device a role and format with no partition table, its own tab rather than a footnote, because a single-purpose data disk usually wants exactly that and burying it pushes people into partitioning they do not need. The OS disk offers no destructive action anywhere and says why.
- **Storage Placement** becomes its own page holding state/log/rebuildable placement. Backup-config and swap placement are **linked, not repeated** -- both already have homes, and one setting with two places to change it is one that drifts.
- Stated rather than quietly omitted: there is **no partition resize**. The API has create-table, append and delete; sfdisk is driven in append and delete modes only. Growing or moving a partition in place is a data-bearing operation that needs its own design, so the page offers create and delete honestly instead of implying a resize that does not exist.

**#9: partitioning had never once worked, and the first real run found a data-loss bug.** The issue body said this was "deliberately not started"; it shipped as Part 148. What had never happened is a partition being created by the daemon on real hardware, because Part 148 had no safe disposable disk to try it on. 192.168.15.95 now has one (`sda`, 100GB, no role, never written).
- **`sfdisk` was never staged into the control-plane image.** `mkbootroot.c` stages openssl, curl, tar, unsquashfs, rm, mkfs.ext4 — not sfdisk. So `execve()` hit ENOENT, the child exited 127, and every partitioning call on every installed host has always returned `500 "sfdisk failed"`. Two things hid it: this build sandbox has a rich `/usr` where sfdisk always resolves, and `cix-install.c` drives the same sfdisk at install time from the ISO, which also has it. Only the installed host lacks it, and only at runtime. Fixed by staging it plus the three libs nothing else already pulls in (libfdisk/libsmartcols/libreadline). `test_mkbootroot_firmware` now asserts **every** binary the daemon has a compiled-in path for is staged — the class, not the instance — and was confirmed to catch this by removing the staging line alone.
- **execve-failed and sfdisk-refused reported identically.** On a host with no shell (ADR-0034) the error string is the only diagnostic there is, and "sfdisk failed" pointed nowhere. Exit 127 now says sfdisk is not installed and to update the image; a real rejection now describes what an operator can act on. Same lesson Part 193 learned adding per-step diagnostics to `mountns_pivot()`.
- **Then the real sequence ran**: GPT table on `sda`, a 20GiB `sda1`, an 80GiB `sda2` from the omitted-size "rest of disk" path, both enumerated correctly with `is_partition`/`parent_disk`, a `container-storage` role assigned to the **partition**, and ext4 formatted and mounted on it. Guard rails checked first, before anything destructive: OS disk `400`, a partition `400`, wrong/missing `confirm_disk_name` `400`, unknown disk `404`.
- **And it surfaced a data-loss bug.** `fill_mount_status()` mapped every mounted device to its **parent** whole disk. That was right while only whole disks were enumerated and became wrong the moment ADR-0158 put partitions in the same array: a genuinely mounted `sda1` reported `mounted: false` while `sda` reported `sda1`'s mountpoint as its own. `diskpart_delete()` reads that flag to refuse deleting a partition in use — so it never fired. Confirmed live rather than reasoned about: with the role removed (allowed while mounted) and `mounted` false, `DELETE /v1/disks/sda/partitions/sda1` returned **204 and deleted a partition whose ext4 was mounted and live**, leaving the kernel holding a device the on-disk GPT no longer describes. The same misattribution also refused `POST /disks/sda1/unmount` on the genuinely mounted partition while accepting it on `sda`, and would have broken container storage placed on any partition (every placement lookup asks "is *this* device mounted").
- Fixed by separating the two questions: `mounted`/`mount_path` are now strictly about **this** device, and whole disks carry a new `has_mounted_partition` for "something on this disk is in use" — which is what the repartition guard actually wants, and is now reported so an operator with no shell can see why a `409` happened. The attribution logic was split behind `disk_fill_mount_status_from()` so a test can drive it from a synthetic `/proc/mounts` (the real one cannot be arranged to order, and this sandbox has no loop devices to mount anything on); `test_diskpart` asserts all three symptoms and was confirmed to reproduce every one against the old code.

**Volumes, answering four questions the user asked while using them.** Each one turned out to be a real gap, not a misunderstanding.
- **"We should show volumes on the container? I am unsure how the mapping between container and volume ownership and volume mounting happens."** The model was under-surfaced, which is why it was unclear. A container's Hardware tab now lists the volumes it mounts (name, path, read-write/read-only), and the Volumes page gained a **Mounted by** column showing the reverse. That reverse direction is the whole answer: **containers reference volumes, never the other way round** -- nothing owns a volume, a volume does not know who uses it, several containers may mount the same one, and it outlives all of them. There is no ownership field to show because there is no ownership; the column is cross-referenced client-side against the container list, the same way the network detail page does "containers on this network". "not currently mounted" is deliberately not an error state -- a volume outliving every container that used it is the point, and is exactly when its data is most at risk from someone assuming it is dead weight. A container with no volumes now says so explicitly ("everything this container writes is lost when it is deleted") rather than showing an empty table.
- **"Volume additions should go under Create, right?"** Right, and the inline form on the Volumes page was the same inconsistency Routes already had fixed under ADR-0138 -- volumes are a top-level creatable resource, so creation belongs in the header `Create` menu and the shared modal. Moved.
- **"I want to be able to backup volumes, right?"** This found a real bug rather than a missing feature. Container definitions reference volumes by name and an unknown name is a hard 400 by design -- so a bundle carrying the definitions but *not* the volume registry restores onto a box where **every container with a volume fails to start**. That is a broken restore, not a partial one. The registry (which volumes exist, and their disk placement) is configuration and is now in the bundle; volume *contents* are workload data and stay out, which is the boundary ADR-0033 actually draws (it excludes image content on identical grounds). ADR-0183's own "not in the backup" line conflated those two things and has been corrected in place. `test_system_backup` now asserts the registry is present, with the failure message stating the consequence rather than just the absence.
- **"I want to be able to take backups of files as well (files we attach to containers)."** Already true and verified live against 192.168.15.95's real bundle rather than assumed: `container_defs` persists each container's entire create request verbatim (ADR-0025), so every `files[]` entry is in the backup **with its content inline** -- `jump`'s nine, including the 1488-byte `/etc/profile`. The real gap is narrower and worth naming: a file written live via `PUT /containers/{name}/files` is explicitly ephemeral and is *not* in any backup, so anything meant to last belongs in the definition's `files[]` or on a volume.
- Honest note on a non-bug: a container detail page appeared to render blank on a deep link, and a fix for the "race" was written before an A/B check showed the page renders fine -- the URL used to test it was simply wrong (`#container/` for `#containers/`). Reverted rather than shipped; a fix for a problem that does not exist is still a change that can break something.

**#88 follow-through: `jump`'s `/home` is now actually on a volume, a write-only read-back gap closed, and #89's ROADMAP drift fixed.** Three things the first volumes commit left open, all found by using the feature rather than by reading the diff again.
- **The jump box actually uses it.** Applying the recipe recreates the container, so its `/home` went one last time and stops going after that. Verified end to end on 192.168.15.95, not just accepted at 201: a real LDAP SSH login lands in a `/home/osakka` created by `pam_mkhomedir` **on the volume** (`df /home` reports the real containers partition, not the overlay), a file written there survived a full `stop`+`start`, and the container read back a file written earlier by a completely different, since-deleted container. Two blocks of recipe prose that this made false were corrected in the same change rather than left to mislead -- `/etc/skel/.bashrc` carried a "HEADS UP: this does not survive a recreate" warning, and `/etc/profile` explained per-user files as living in the writable layer. Both were accurate when written; a stale warning is worse than none, because people act on it.
- **`volumes` was write-only.** The API accepted it and `GET /containers/{name}` never echoed it -- caught immediately by looking at the recreated container's own read-back, and exactly the gap Part 163 had to close for `memory_max`/`cpu_max`/`pids_max`. Now echoed for both running and stopped containers, by the volume **name** rather than the resolved host path (the name is what makes a read-back useful), through one shared `containerdef_write_json_volumes()` used by both writers so the two can never render the same field differently. Sourced from the persisted body rather than mirrored onto either struct, for the same reason `image` already is: a second copy of a field is a second thing that can disagree with it. `test/test_volume.c` now asserts on it.
- **A stale duplicate on the real box.** Two container recipes existed for the same thing -- `jump` (canonical, matching the repo) and `jumpbox` (an orphan defining a container that does not exist and is not in source control). Applying the wrong one would have produced a second, volume-less jump box on the same IP. Removed; the box now has exactly 9 recipes for exactly 9 containers.
- **#89 closed**: `ROADMAP.md`'s headings stopped at Part 181 while this file ran to Part 203 -- 21 parts shipped with a changelog entry and no matching roadmap heading, which is a Documentation Map violation, not a cosmetic gap: ROADMAP's job is the per-part *verification* record, a deliberately different thing from this file's chronological narrative, and for 21 parts it no longer answered the question it exists to answer. All of 182-202 backfilled, each written as what shipped and **how it was verified** -- including the parts where that record is the interesting half: the hypotheses ruled out before the real root cause in #34, the option checked and rejected before building `keep_on_failure`, the positive swap-placement path deliberately left for the real box after the dev sandbox's disks turned out to be shared Proxmox storage, and the folio-split-race theory recorded honestly as an open question rather than a conclusion.

**#88 done (ADR-0183): persistent volumes -- storage whose lifetime is independent of any container.** Raised by the user asking a plain question about the jump box: *"when I login the bash has no prompt; if I create one in my home dir, then it will get deleted on restart or recreation of the container, right?"* -- correct, and worse than it sounds. Everything a container writes lives in its overlay upper layer, which `DELETE` removes (ADR-0106), and `jump` has `follow_rolling: true`, so an ordinary image rebuild recreates it automatically -- it was recreated roughly a dozen times during a single working session, taking every shell history, dotfile and scratch note with it, silently, with nothing anywhere indicating that would happen.
- **A volume is a named directory that outlives its containers.** That is the whole point, so it follows that deleting one is explicit and separate -- and refused (409) while **any container definition** references it, not merely while one is running: a stopped container will come back and expect its data, so removing it underneath would be a data-loss bug that only surfaces later. The error names the container holding it.
- **Not a second storage story**: placement reuses the same disk-role mechanism container overlays already use, so a `container-storage` disk serves both and there is one answer to "where does container data live". A volume's data sits alongside `containers/` rather than inside it -- nesting storage that deliberately outlives containers *under* container storage would be the wrong lifetime association.
- **Two failures are deliberately fatal.** A volume that fails to mount kills the container (exit 125) rather than starting without it: a container silently running without its persistent storage would write to the overlay upper layer instead, look perfectly healthy, and lose that data on its next recreate -- the exact failure volumes exist to prevent, made harder to notice. Same for `read_only`, which fails the start rather than coming up writable, because a guarantee that silently isn't one is worse than none.
- **An unknown volume name is a hard 400, never an implicit create** -- a typo silently producing a fresh empty volume is precisely how someone loses data and then concludes persistence "didn't work".
- Mechanics: new `daemon/src/volume.c` registry + `POST/GET/DELETE /v1/volumes[/{name}]`; `container_spec` carries resolved host *paths*, never volume names, so the runtime library never learns the registry exists; the bind mount happens child-side, between `clone3()` and `pivot_root`, so nothing accumulates on the host.
- Surfaces per the API-First Mandate: `cixctl volume ls|create|show|rm` plus `container run --volume=NAME:/path[:ro]`, and a **System > Host > Volumes** dashboard page (filed beside Disks, not under Monitoring -- it is storage management, and shares Disks' own role mechanism).
- Verified by `test/test_volume.c` against real containers, asserting on real data rather than on the API returning 201: a container writes into a volume, is **deleted entirely**, and a *different* container mounting the same volume reads the data back -- plus every guard rail (path-escaping name refused, unknown volume refused, in-use delete refused, delete succeeds once nothing references it). That discipline earned its keep immediately: the create-time parse initially ran *before* `container_spec`'s own `memset()`, so `volume_count` was zeroed and containers came up with no volume and **no error at all** -- invisible to any test that only checked the response code.

**#73 done (ADR-0181, supersedes the one `restart:"no"`-is-ephemeral decision of ADR-0027)**: every container is now persisted at create time, and `restart` governs only auto-restart, never existence -- closing a real reported surprise where `POST .../stop` on a default (`restart:"no"`) container made it **vanish entirely** (no def to fall back to), i.e. `stop` silently behaving like `delete`. Now: `stop` always keeps a container (it reappears as status `"stopped"`), a container that exits on its own is retained as status `"exited"` with its real exit code (Docker `ps -a` semantics -- observable, and its name stays reserved so a duplicate create still `409`s), `restart:"no"` means "kept but never auto-restarted" (not at boot, on exit, or by a rolling update), and only `DELETE` ever removes a container -- *stop is stop, delete is delete*. `POST .../start` now also brings an `"exited"` container back (it clears the stale exited record first, rather than silently `200`-ing it). The nine infra containers and every `always`/`on-failure`/`unless-stopped` workload are byte-for-byte unaffected. Mechanics: create-time persist made unconditional; `containerdef_autostart_all()`/`apply_rolling_container_restarts()`/the crash-restart exit path all skip `restart:"no"`; the list's persisted-but-not-running fallback (`containerdef_write_json_inactive_list`) no longer keys on the `stopped` flag but on an injected `registry_name_is_live()` liveness predicate, keeping `containerdef.c` free of a back-dependency on the registry. Verified end-to-end (test_daemon: a `"no"` `c1` observable as `"exited"`/`exit_status=5`, name stays reserved; test_container_restart: an `on-failure` clean exit stays down as `"exited"` and is startable again with a fresh live pid, every crash/always/unless-stopped/backoff scenario still green). openapi.yaml + api/README.md restart/stop/start/delete semantics updated in the same change; ADR-0027 annotated as partially superseded; ADR index gained its missing 0180 + new 0181 rows.

**Real operator tooling on the jump box (user request), and four TCC gaps closed to get it there.** `procps`, `mtr` and `vim` now genuinely work on `jump`, alongside the `screen` it already had -- 18 tools total (`ps free kill pgrep pkill pidof pmap pwdx tload uptime vmstat w watch slabtop sysctl vim screen mtr`), each verified by running it over a real SSH login rather than trusting `pkg` state.
- **procps 4.0.6-6** took four new gaps beyond the seven its recipe already documented. (8) `configure` died with "cannot make tcc report undeclared builtins" -- self-inflicted: gap seven's own `-D__GNUC__=0` made glibc's `limits.h` take its `#include_next` GCC branch, which TCC can't satisfy, so autoconf's probe program failed to compile and the probe reported failure. Fixed by also defining `_GCC_LIMITS_H_`, glibc's own "GCC's limits.h is already included" marker; verified by compiling AND RUNNING a probe (`INT_MAX`/`CHAR_BIT` correct), so nothing is lost. (9) TCC 0.9.27 has **no `__thread` support at all** -- confirmed with a standalone probe, not inferred. Defining it away is only safe in single-threaded programs, so `grep -l pthread_create` was run across the whole tree: only `src/top` matches. So everything **except top** is built, and the omission is stated rather than hidden -- shipping `top` with shared-instead-of-per-thread caches would be a real data race dressed up as a build fix. (10) `undefined symbol '__dso_handle'` -- the catalog's own known CRT gap, fixed with the established weak-stub-object-in-LIBS pattern. (11) `unsupported linker option '--version-script'` -- dropped (symbol-versioning metadata nothing here consumes) while keeping `-version-info`, so the library still installs as `libproc2.so.1`.
- **mtr 0.96-3**: `configure: error: cannot find working error printing function`, alongside `checking for fcntl... no` -- `fcntl` obviously exists, so the giveaway was that autoconf's *link* probes were all failing: the same `__dso_handle` gap as procps' tenth. Same stub fix. Then a second, more important catch: mtr installed cleanly and **did not run** (`libresolv.so.2: cannot open shared object file`) -- found by actually invoking it. Now stages the library it needs. Noted in the recipe as a general gap, not an mtr quirk: the image baseline stages libc/libm/libtinfo/libgcc_s/libnss_files and nothing before this needed name resolution.
- **jumpbox image recipe 1.4.0** declares the real set. It also *removes* five packages 1.3.0 declared but which had never actually installed (the image carried 13 while the recipe named 19) -- a recipe that names packages the image does not have reads as a guarantee and silently is not one.
- **Still failing, tracked rather than papered over**: `htop` (two real gaps -- ambient-gcc contamination per issue #37 picking gcc over tcc despite `CC=tcc`, then a `NAN` constant-initializer difference between this project's own two TCCs) and `btop` (no recipe; C++). Deliberately left out of the image recipe until they genuinely build.

**#85 + #86 (a real incident and its two fixes).** Deploying #2's re-enabled build limits and then launching four concurrent package builds for the jump box made 192.168.15.95 **unreachable** -- the kernel stayed perfectly healthy throughout (ping 0% loss, 0.26ms) but `cixd` stopped answering, and since a real install has no SSH and no shell (ADR-0034) that removed every way in short of a hypervisor reset.
- **#85, the structural bug**: `pkg-build-config`'s `cpu_max`/`memory_max` read like a build-subsystem budget but were applied **per build container** (`pkg.c`), while `max_concurrent_jobs` defaults to 10 -- so the configured ceiling silently multiplied by concurrency (1.5 CPU x 4 builds = 6 CPUs demanded on a 2-CPU box). There was no safe value to pick, because the real bound depended on a different setting. Fixed with a real aggregate budget: new `cgroup_create_parent()` creates one parent cgroup carrying the configured limits and delegating controllers to its subtree, and every build container is now created as a leaf beneath it (`cix-pkgbuild/<name>`) with no ceiling of its own. N concurrent builds can never collectively exceed the budget, whatever N is, and the number finally means what it says. The parent's limits are re-applied on every build so a runtime config change takes effect instead of leaving a stale ceiling.
- **#86, the hardening**: the incident's real lesson is that on this platform the control plane *is* the only management channel, so it must be hard to starve regardless of what caused the load. `cixd` now sets itself to nice **-20** and `oom_score_adj` **-1000** at startup -- best-effort by design (a dev run as an ordinary user simply won't be permitted, and must not fail to start over it), reporting anything it could not do rather than failing silently. Verified: the daemon really does run at `ni=-20` with `oom_score_adj=-1000`.
- Honest note on why #2's own verification missed this: it proved "no deadlock" using small packages that each settled in ~20s, never holding a CPU ceiling long enough to contend. Proving "no deadlock" is not proving "no starvation".

**#81 done (ADR-0182): registered-server health / heartbeat, as ONE primitive for all four subsystems.** Cix let an operator register redundant LDAP/DNS/NTP/syslog servers but only ever tracked *that* one was registered, never whether it was serving -- which is exactly how #80 stayed invisible (a registered LDAP pair, running and listening, that could not resolve anything under the configured base DN, breaking every login with nothing anywhere reporting a bad server).
- **One module** (`daemon/src/serverhealth.c`), not four parallel ones: each kind contributes only an enumerator and a probe target to a table in `main.c`; adding a fifth subsystem is one row. Three of the four registries gained the `*_list_containers()` enumerator LDAP already had, making them uniform.
- **The probe is a non-blocking `connect()` on the daemon's own reactor** -- load-bearing, not incidental: a blocking probe against an unreachable server would stall the single epoll loop, the exact failure ADR-0180 exists to prevent. `serverhealth.c` performs no I/O at all and is pure state; in-flight probes are timed out by the next sweep rather than left to the kernel's multi-minute TCP timeout.
- **The probe reports what it actually did**: `tcp:PORT` (the server accepted a real connection) vs `process` (only that the container is running). NTP and syslog are UDP, where a TCP connect would be a meaningless check dressed up as a real one, so they get the honest weaker check and the API says so plainly.
- **Asymmetric transitions**: one success restores health immediately; several *consecutive* failures are needed to declare a server unhealthy, so a single dropped probe never pulls a working directory server out of service while recovery is never delayed.
- **Drain is persisted, health is not**: draining is operator intent that must survive a restart (like a container's `stopped` flag); observed health would be a lie if replayed from disk, so it always starts `unknown`.
- **Not-in-service servers are withheld from generated client config** -- the point of the mechanism: an unhealthy or drained LDAP server stops being handed to `ldap_login` containers. Two safety rules bound it so filtering can never itself cause an outage: a never-yet-probed server counts as in service, and if filtering would leave *nothing* the unfiltered list is used instead.
- Surfaces per the API-First Mandate: `GET/PUT /v1/system/server-health...`, `cixctl server-health [ls] | drain | undrain`, and a **System > Monitoring > Server Health** dashboard page with a per-row Drain/Undrain button. Verified locally: drain survives a real daemon restart while health correctly resets to `unknown`; the web view screenshotted. openapi.yaml + api/README.md + cli-reference.md + web-dashboard.md updated together.

**#77 done (surface parity: every delivered REST capability now has a CLI and web surface)**. An audit found **five** features that were REST-only with zero client surface -- two more than the issue listed (`capture_output` and `term_signal` were missed):
- **CLI**: `container run` gains `--userns` (ADR-0179 user namespaces), `--ldap-login` (server-staged nsswitch/nslcd from the daemon's LDAP config) and `--capture-output` (keep the container's own stdout/stderr -- the first thing to reach for on a silent crash-loop). New top-level `kmsg [--tail=N]` renders the kernel ring buffer in dmesg's own `[   ts] level message` form. `container ls`/`inspect` now render a signal death as `exit_status=sig9` rather than a bare `9` (issue #78) -- folded into the existing column rather than spending a new one.
- **Web**: three new toggles on the create-container form (user namespace / LDAP login / capture stdout+stderr); a new **System > Monitoring > Kernel Log** view alongside the Log Store, with a tail field and Refresh, which degrades gracefully when `/dev/kmsg` isn't readable; the container detail pane now shows `Exit status` as "exit code N" vs "killed by signal N" plus the real `Exit reason`.
- **Lifecycle (#73) reflected in the web**: the container action menu only ever knew running/paused/stopped, so an `exited` container (retained since ADR-0181 instead of vanishing) offered a useless "Stop" and no "Start". Start is now offered for anything revivable (stopped **or** exited) and Stop only for something actually alive; the transient `stopping`/`deleting` states correctly offer neither.
Verified live on 192.168.15.95: `--capture-output` captured a container's real stdout, `--userns` produced a genuine `/proc/1/uid_map` of `0 493216 65536`, `kmsg` rendered real kernel lines, and a real signal death rendered as `exit_status=sig9`. Web views screenshotted via headless Chromium. `ldap_client` (#76) stays on `ldap_login` until that rename lands. cli-reference.md + web-dashboard.md updated.

**#61 part 2 done + a host-file-disclosure bug found doing it**: `GET /containers/{name}/files` on an exited container falls back from its overlay upper to its read-only lower layer -- but it RECONSTRUCTED the lowerdir path from `image`/`image_version`, which only works for an ordinary container. A build container (`__pkgbuild-N`) is registered under the synthetic image name `"pkgbuild"` with an empty version, so both reconstruction branches missed and it fell through to an **empty path prefix** -- turning the read into a bare `open()` of the requested path on the **daemon host's own filesystem**. That both 404'd real lowerdir content (the reported symptom: `/usr/bin/gcc` missing on a preserved build container while `/build/*` worked) and, far worse, served host files through a per-container endpoint. Confirmed live, not theorised: with the old code `GET /v1/containers/__pkgbuild-0/files?path=/etc/os-release` returns **200** with the host's own file. Fixed by recording the container's REAL lowerdir on its registry entry at create time (copied verbatim from the `container_spec`) and using it for the fallback -- simpler than the reconstruction it replaces, correct for every container kind, and ADR-0107/0108's pinned-version guarantee is preserved byte-for-byte (for an ordinary container the recorded lowerdir IS the pinned image-version rootfs). An empty lowerdir (userns containers, which use a per-container rootfs and no overlay) correctly means "no fallback". Regression test in `test_pkg` asserts both halves against a real preserved build container -- lowerdir content reads back, and a host-only path (`/etc/os-release`) must 404 -- and was verified to catch the bug (reverting the fix reproduces the 200). Part 1 of #61 (directory listing) is untouched and stays open.

**CRITICAL regression fixed (ADR-0181 loader half): a daemon that had ever created a default `restart:"no"` container refused to boot again.** Chasing what looked like a "pre-existing `test_ldap` restart flake" found a real, severe bug introduced by #73: ADR-0181 made the daemon *write* `restart_policy:"no"` definitions, but `parse_persisted_entry()` still enforced the pre-ADR-0181 invariant and rejected `"no"` as corruption -- so on the very next restart the daemon aborted loading its own state file (`container_defs.json: invalid entry at index N`) and **never came back up**. Every restart-heavy test that created a plain container hit it; it would have bricked any real box on its next reboot once a default container existed. One-line fix (accept `"no"` alongside the other three) plus a real regression guard in `test_container_restart`: a `restart:"no"` container is now created immediately before the suite's real daemon restart, and asserted afterwards to be known (200) and `"stopped"` (persisted, never autostarted). The guard was verified to actually catch the bug -- reverting the fix reproduces `invalid entry at index 8` / "restarted daemon never accepted connections", restoring it passes. `test_ldap`, `test_daemon`, `test_container_restart`, `test_system_backup`, `test_container_lifecycle`, `test_rolling_restart` all green.

**#80 follow-ups (base_dn One Source of Truth + bind-account auto-provisioning) + a web edit-modal bug**, all flowing from the #80 investigation:
- **base_dn drift closed**: `/v1/ldap/config`'s `base_dn` was a second, independently-settable copy of the canonical `hostauth_ldap_base_dn()` (ADR-0148) -- exactly the copy that drifted to `dc=cix,dc=local` and broke jump login. `ldap_config_get()` now overlays it with the canonical value on every read, so every consumer (the nslcd/nsswitch `ldap_login` auto-staging, the `{{LDAP:BASE_DN}}` recipe token, and `GET /v1/ldap/config`) always sees what the servers actually serve and can never drift again. Empty (unconfigured) leaves a stored value untouched, matching ADR-0148's own posture.
- **bind account auto-provisioned**: Cix no longer needs an operator to hand-create the nslcd service/bind account and type its DN/password into the config (the other half of what broke #80). New `ldap_ensure_service_bind_account()` -- called from the `ldap_login` staging path, the moment a client container needs the config -- idempotently ensures a well-known `svc-nslcd` account exists (a service group + a `can_search` user with a fresh random secret) and records its real DN + secret as `bind_dn`/`bind_password`. A no-op once provisioned, and a no-op if an operator deliberately configured a different bind account. Reuses the proven task-#727 provisioning pattern (`ldap_uid_alloc`/`ldap_gid_alloc`/`ldap_generate_secret`); `ldap_user_create`/`ldap_group_create` push to the running glauth servers themselves.
- **web edit-modal bug**: the dashboard's Edit button for LDAP users (and, same root cause, LDAP groups and DNS records) sent `POST` (create) instead of `PUT` (update), 409-ing on the existing name -- the edit-name state was set *before* `openModal()`, which calls `closeModal()` and resets it to null. Fixed all three by setting the edit-name after `openModal()`. Reported live: an LDAP password change via the UI failed with `409 already exists`.

**#80 done** (LDAP login to the jump box was completely broken): root-caused live on 192.168.15.95. Every service ran and the client modules were present, but the `jump` recipe **hard-coded** its LDAP client files (`/etc/nslcd.conf`, `/etc/ldap-authkeys.conf`) with a legacy `dc=cix,dc=local` base DN and a `cn=svc-nslcd,ou=service-accounts,dc=cix,dc=local` bind account -- while glauth actually serves `dc=cix,dc=internal` (the canonical `hostauth_ldap_base_dn()`, ADR-0148) and no `svc-nslcd` account had ever been created. So nslcd searched a subtree glauth doesn't serve, binding as an account that doesn't exist -- no user ever resolved. A leftover an earlier project rename (ADR-0162) missed, in the one place a base DN was still typed by hand.

Fix (One Source of Truth, per user direction): the jump recipe now uses **`ldap_login: true`** -- the daemon auto-stages `nsswitch.conf`/`nslcd.conf` from the central `/v1/ldap/config` -- instead of baking literal client files; `/etc/ldap-authkeys.conf` (the sshd `AuthorizedKeysCommand` helper, not covered by `ldap_login`) now derives its values from `{{LDAP:URI/BIND_DN/BASE_DN/BIND_PASSWORD}}` tokens rather than hard-coded strings. `recipes/container/jumpbox/1.0.0/container.json` carries the fix (no stale base DN left in the repo). On .95: created the missing `svc-nslcd` bind account as a real `--can-search` LDAP user, corrected `/v1/ldap/config` (base_dn `dc=cix,dc=internal`, bind_dn `cn=svc-nslcd,ou=users,dc=cix,dc=internal`), and re-applied the recipe. Verified end-to-end: binding as `svc-nslcd` finds `osakka` in glauth, the auto-staged nslcd.conf carries the correct base/bind, and `id osakka` inside the jump box resolves `uid=10000(osakka) gid=10000(wheel)` through its own NSS->nslcd->glauth chain -- the previously-broken path now works. (Residual, noted on the ticket: `/v1/ldap/config.base_dn` is still a copy of `hostauth_ldap_base_dn()` that can drift; a client base_dn the registered servers can't resolve should be flagged -- ties into #81.)

**#78 + #79 done** (container exit-status reporting & logging clarity, both found while verifying #73 live on .95): a container killed by a signal no longer masquerades as an exit code, and a deliberate stop/delete no longer logs like a crash.
- **#78**: `container_wait()` stored `waitid()`'s `si_status` raw, without checking `si_code` — so a `SIGKILL` (signal 9, how stop/delete terminate a container) was indistinguishable from a real `exit 9`. Added a companion `term_signal` field, plumbed through the registry entry and surfaced in every container GET (`0` = exited normally so `exit_status` is a real code; nonzero = the signal that killed it). `exit_status` itself is unchanged (still raw `si_status`, so every `== 0` clean-check and existing test is byte-identical), and `container_decode_exit_status()`/`exit_reason` now reads `"killed by signal 11 (SIGSEGV)"` instead of `"exited with status 11"`. New `test_container_restart` scenario proves it end-to-end (a NULL-deref SIGSEGV container, retained `"exited"` by #73, reports `term_signal:11` + the named reason) — SIGKILL-via-stop can't be self-inflicted by a container's own PID 1 (the kernel force-delivers only synchronous faults to namespace init), so that path stays covered by the live .95 verification.
- **#79**: `registry_mark_exited()` logged *any* nonzero exit at `error` severity, so every routine stop/delete (SIGKILL → nonzero) produced a crash-looking error line. Now it branches on `teardown_kind`: `STOP`/`DELETE` log an `info`-level "container X stopped/removed (...)", and only a genuinely unprompted abnormal exit stays at `error`. openapi.yaml + api/README document the new `term_signal` field in the same change.

**#74 done**: every container operation now lives under one `container` namespace (`container ls`/`run`/`inspect`/`start`/`stop`/`pause`/`unpause`/`rm`/`stats`/`console`/`files`/`migrate-storage`), matching the `<noun> <verb>` shape every other resource (`network`/`image`/`dns`/`ldap`/`pki`/…) already had -- the redundant bare top-level verbs (`ps`/`run`/`rm`/… as their own commands) are gone, per the user's "drop them, but don't lose any in the reshuffle". The dispatch change shipped in an earlier commit; this completes it by bringing its own regression test (`test_cli`) and every operator doc into sync: `test_cli` drove the old bare `run`/`ps`/`inspect`/`rm` (it went red the moment the verbs moved) and now drives `container run`/`container ls`/`container inspect`/`container rm`; `docs/guides/cli-reference.md`'s Containers table and every `cixctl run|inspect|console|stats|rm|stop|start|pause` example across administration/networking/quickstart/remote-development/security guides were copy-paste-broken and are corrected. (One incomplete commit's leftover -- caught here rather than shipped: the code landed without updating its own test or the guides.)

**#60 done**: `{{REPO_TOKEN}}` in a `pkg_source` URL is substituted at fetch time with the daemon's own stored repo auth token (`pkg repo-config set --token=`). A recipe that self-fetches from the private Gitea is now committable in its final, working form -- eliminating the live-token-substitute-before-first-sync-then-revert-and-delete dance every kernel/cix re-pin needed (done ~10 times this sprint alone; documented at length in remote-development.md, now rewritten around the placeholder). Token never touches the catalog or logs; no-regression verified across the full pkg suite.

**#70 done**: per-network auto-IP allocation window (`alloc_start`/`alloc_end`, dotted IPs; `cixctl network create --alloc-start/--alloc-end`) plus a safe default -- a management network (bridged onto a real LAN) now skips host-part `.1` in auto-allocation even with no window set, since `.1` is by convention the real gateway. Caught live during the ADR-0180 canary test, when the allocator handed a container `192.168.15.1`. Explicit container IPs are unconstrained by the window (auto-allocation only). Persisted, serialized, migration-safe (absent = full-range default), and regression-tested (a container on a windowed network lands on the window's first host-part, not `.1`). -- limits fully visible + strict (#48/#49/#68/#69 done), LDAP centralization and user namespaces next

Wave 1 of the user-directed sprint ("hammer through the low-hanging features; LDAP, user namespaces, and all the limits sorted before the bare-metal box arrives"):

- **#49 done**: `cpuset_cpus` (live from the real cgroup, like memory/cpu/pids already were) and `disk_quota_bytes` (mirrored from the creation request -- a project quota has no per-container kernel file to read back through a kept fd) now appear in every container GET. The write-only gap that made the jump container's own quota unverifiable is closed.
- **#68 done**: unknown top-level fields in a container create or recipe body are a 400 naming the offender -- at recipe ADD time too, so a typo'd limit can no longer sit latent in the catalog until an apply silently drops it. Daemon-internal replay paths (autostart/rolling/migration) stay deliberately lenient so an upgrade can never strand an existing definition.
- **#48/#69 done**: `cixctl ps` grows `cpuset=`/`disk_quota=`/`caps=` columns; the dashboard's container Hardware tab now carries the full resource envelope (memory/CPU/pids/cpuset/quota/capabilities) alongside devices/interfaces/networks, instead of scattering it on the overview.
- **#58 done**: `last_output_seconds_ago` on every building pkg row -- the daemon stamps each byte it drains from the build-output pipe, so hang-vs-slow is a one-glance answer instead of the load-average guesswork that caused one mistaken kill of a healthy build and one unnoticed wedge. **#56 done**: rows loaded in fetching/building at daemon startup settle to failed ("interrupted by a daemon restart") -- the stranded-`building`-row half; the leaked-chain-slot half was fixed incidentally by ADR-0180 (operator deletes of build containers now route through pkg_build_completed()).
- **#66 DONE (full)**: `ldap_login: true` on a container create/recipe now stages `/etc/nsswitch.conf` + `/etc/nslcd.conf` server-side, rendered from `/ldap/config` -- the container carries none of the LDAP client values itself. The URI is the configured `client_uri` or, when unset, auto-derived from the live IPs of containers registered via `ldap server register` (so registering the servers is the only step). Refused unless base_dn + an effective URI are resolvable; the container still owns its own PAM/service/startup wiring. This plus the earlier `{{LDAP:*}}` token support and centralized config fully closes #66 -- the jump login container's recipe collapses from nine hand-rolled files (with a duplicated URI list, base DN, bind DN, and a hand-passed bind secret) to its own baseline + `ldap_login: true`. Verified end-to-end in test_daemon (refused-then-accepted, nslcd.conf rendered with the daemon's own bind values).
- **#66 (earlier, same issue)**: the daemon's LDAP config (`GET`/`PUT /ldap/config`, `cixctl ldap config`) now stores the client login settings -- URI list, base DN, bind DN, and a write-only bind credential (never echoed; `bind_password_set` only) -- and container recipes reference them as `{{LDAP:URI}}`/`{{LDAP:BASE_DN}}`/`{{LDAP:BIND_DN}}`/`{{LDAP:BIND_PASSWORD}}` tokens, resolved at render exactly like `{{SECRET:KEY}}`. A recipe needing LDAP login now carries zero copied values and needs zero per-apply secrets (proven end-to-end in test_container_recipe: a token-carrying recipe applied with an empty body renders the real nslcd.conf inside a real container). Remaining on #66, deliberately: the full `ldap_login: true` auto-staging flag and URI auto-derivation from registered servers.
- **#29 Phase 1 done** (ADR-0179): the subordinate-ID range allocator (`daemon/src/subid.c`) -- a persisted `identity-key -> host-UID/GID range` table, floor 100000 / width 65536 (the Docker/Podman/systemd conventions), first-come per key, with active both-direction collision checking against real LDAP uidnumbers (the allocator steps past a colliding range; `ldap_user_create`/`update` reject a uidnumber inside a committed range). Wired into boot init and validated by a new `test/test_subid.c` (idempotence, non-overlap, floor, persistence-across-reload). `container_spec` carries the `userns_*` fields; nothing enables them yet.
- **#29 Phase 2a built** (`CLONE_NEWUSER` + parent-side map handshake): `POST /v1/containers` accepts `"userns": true` (opt-in during verification, so the platform's running containers are untouched until the path is proven on real hardware; the ADR flips it default-on afterward). When set, `create_container_from_body()` allocates the container a subordinate-ID range (`subid_lookup_or_assign`, keyed on the container name for now — the ADR's host-auth-off fallback key) and adds `CLONE_NEWUSER` to the clone flags. `container_create()` gains a blocking userns sync pipe: the cloned child blocks on it before any privileged step (overlay mount included — an incomplete map would run those with the wrong credentials); the parent writes `/proc/<pid>/{setgroups=deny,gid_map,uid_map}` (the documented ordering) then releases it, SIGKILL+reaping on any failure. Every new codepath is gated on `userns_enabled`, so non-userns creates are byte-identical (verified: clean `-Wall -Werror` build + `test_harness` container-create pass). New child exit code 121 (+ the previously-undecoded 120) added to `container_decode_exit_status`. **Verified live on .95** (kernel + this cixd both deployed, one A/B reboot each): a `"userns":true` container was created and reached `overlay_create` — proving `CLONE_NEWUSER` and the map handshake both work on the real VM — then **failed `EACCES` mounting the overlay *inside* the userns** (`exit 153`, `"child: overlay_create: Permission denied"`): the mapped root (host uid 100000) can't write the host-uid-0-owned upperdir/workdir. This is the direct empirical confirmation of ADR-0179's own design call — the overlay must be mounted **parent-side before `clone3`**, not by the child. Phase 2b (parent-side overlay mount + id-mapped presentation) is the remaining work; the 9 running infra containers were untouched throughout (opt-in gating). The `USER_NS` kernel is now live on .95 (both A/B slots).
- **#29 Phase 2b built** (parent-side overlay mount): for a `userns_enabled` container, `container_create()` now mounts the overlay itself — in the parent (cixd, init user namespace, full privilege) *before* `clone3` — marks it `MS_PRIVATE`, and lets the child inherit it through its `CLONE_NEWNS` snapshot and merely pivot into it; the child-side `overlay_create` is skipped for userns (guarded, non-userns path byte-identical). After releasing the child, the parent drops its own transient copy with `umount2(MNT_DETACH)` (safe/non-propagating — the child's copy is a separate mount object over the same refcounted superblock). This directly fixes the phase-2a `EACCES`: because cixd (host uid 0) is the overlay's *mounter*, the kernel's mounter-credential model runs every upperdir/workdir operation as root, so the mapped-uid container reads and writes normally — no id-mapped mount or chowned upperdir needed. Clean `-Wall -Werror` build; `test_harness` + `test_overlay` (non-userns) both pass. **Verified live on .95** (a userns container now runs with a correctly mapped root — `/proc/1/uid_map` reads `0 100000 65536`), after two further live-found userns fixes committed alongside: **(a)** `pivot_root` rejects a `MNT_LOCKED` new root and mounts inherited into a userns-owned mount ns are locked, so the child bind-mounts `merged` onto itself first (unlocked) before pivoting; **(b)** an unprivileged userns may only mount proc/sysfs when a fully-visible instance already exists, so `mountns_pivot()` now detaches the old root *after* the fresh proc/sys/run/devpts mounts, not before. **Still read-only — Phase 2c (id-mapped mounts) is required next:** every writable target (rootfs, `/run`) is host-uid-0-owned and thus outside the container's mapped [100000,165536) range, so the container gets `EOVERFLOW` touching it (confirmed live). Id-mapped mounts (`mount_setattr(MOUNT_ATTR_IDMAP)`) shift the presented ownership into range; tracked under #29, userns stays opt-in until then.

- **#29 Phase 2c first cut + live constraint found**: implemented the detached-clone id-mapped-overlay plumbing (`open_tree(OPEN_TREE_CLONE)` → `mount_setattr(MOUNT_ATTR_IDMAP)` with an inverse idmap userns `"<base> 0 <len>"`, parent-built and inherited by the child, which `move_mount`s it in — replacing the 2b self-bind, which would strip the idmapping) plus a race-fixed `create_idmap_userns_fd` (a ready-handshake so the parent never writes the helper's map before the child leaves the init userns — that race gave intermittent `EPERM`). **Live finding: `mount_setattr(MOUNT_ATTR_IDMAP)` on the *merged* overlay mount returns `EINVAL` on 6.18** — overlayfs supports id-mapping only its *layers*, not the merged mount. So the working path is id-mapped lower/upper layers via the fd-based mount API (`fsopen`/`fsconfig`); substituting that for the merged-mount `mount_setattr` is the remaining 2c work (its own iteration — verification is a per-attempt deploy+reboot on the shell-less VM). A `"userns":true` create currently fails `EINVAL` at this step; userns stays opt-in. Create failures now also surface `container_create_last_error_step()` (was errno-only) — a general diagnostic win.
- **#29 Phase 2c layer-idmap built, two walls found**: implemented id-mapped layers via `fsopen`/`fsconfig`/`fsmount` — the overlay now mounts and is writable (no more `EINVAL`). Remaining, and blocked on not being able to read `dmesg` on the shell-less box: id-mapping only the shared lower leaves copy-up of existing host-0 lower dirs owned host-0 in the non-id-mapped upper (`mkdir /dev/pts` EACCES); id-mapping upper+work too (one id-mapped base mount, since overlay requires upper+work on the same vfsmount) mounts read-only via `ovl_make_workdir`, reason hidden in a kernel `pr_warn`. Kernel facts confirmed from 6.18 source. Next unblock: a cixd kernel-log (`/dev/kmsg`) endpoint. userns stays opt-in; no working userns container yet.
- **`GET /v1/system/kmsg?tail=N`** — tails the kernel ring buffer (`/dev/kmsg`) as JSON: dmesg-class kernel diagnostics (mount failures, driver probes, OOM) over the REST API, the only kernel-log window a shell-less installed host has. Immediately used to close the #29 phase 2c diagnosis.
- **#29 Phase 2c root cause found via kmsg**: the all-layers-idmap overlay went read-only because `overlayfs: failed to create directory /work/work (errno: 13 EACCES); mounting read-only` — **cixd mounts the overlay from *outside* the userns (host-0), but on the id-mapped upper/work it's a non-owner, so overlay's own `work/` creation (done as cixd) is denied** (confirmed not a mode issue — `chmod 0777` didn't help). The fix is the standard rootless pattern: **mount the overlay from *inside* the userns** — parent id-maps only the shared lower and chowns the per-container upper/work to `base`; the child (now the mapped root that owns upper/work) does `fsopen`/`fsconfig`(idmapped lower fd + plain upper/work + `userxattr`)/`fsmount`. Building blocks are all in place; this is the remaining 2c restructure. userns stays opt-in; no working userns container yet.
- **#29 Phase 2c mount-from-inside done, fundamental wall reached** (commit 49438ec): the child now mounts the overlay from inside the userns (owns the chowned upper/work + the id-mapped shared-lower fd) and reaches `fsconfig(CMD_CREATE)`, which fails `EACCES` (kmsg: `overlayfs: upper fs does not support tmpfile`). Confirmed against 6.18 source: `ovl_make_workdir`'s O_TMPFILE/whiteout/xattr probes need privilege over the **layer filesystem's** `s_user_ns` = init (Cix's persistent upper/work are on host ext4), which the mapped-root child lacks. This is the same reason rootless overlay needs the upper on a fs mounted inside the userns (or fuse-overlayfs). **So id-mapped overlay with a persistent host upper + shared host-0 lower is not achievable from this architecture on 6.18 — it's now an architecture tradeoff (per-container rootfs copy; or a non-persistent tmpfs upper inside the userns; or keep userns experimental).** The mount-from-inside code is correct and stays. userns remains opt-in.
- **#29 Phase 2 real blocker found + unblocked** (corrected framing -- an earlier draft of the Phase 1 note above wrongly said Phase 2 was "gated on the incoming bare-metal box"): the true prerequisite was that the deployed kernel was **never built with `CONFIG_USER_NS=y`** (the config fragment carried `NAMESPACES`/`PID_NS`/`NET_NS`/`UTS_NS` but not `USER_NS`), so `CLONE_NEWUSER` returns `EINVAL` on the current kernel regardless of environment. Enabled it in `image/kernel/qemu-part1.config` (with the post-merge `=y` survival check the file's own history mandates), triggering a kernel rebuild. Once that kernel is on .95, Phase 2's `mount_setattr(MOUNT_ATTR_IDMAP)` verification runs on the **.95 Proxmox VM** (which owns its own guest kernel -- a fully faithful environment for kernel-VFS behaviour), **not** bare metal; bare metal is only needed for the orthogonal hardware-passthrough work #29 doesn't touch. Confirmed directly here that the privileged-nested-LXC dev sandbox blocks the very first step (`uid_map` write -> `EPERM` at the LSM layer even for the always-permitted `0 0 1` self-map), which is exactly why verification cannot happen in this sandbox. ADR-0179's Status corrected in the same change.
- Regression coverage in test_daemon (unknown-field 400 + cpuset read-back; quota read-back excluded there deliberately -- the test env's fs has no prjquota -- and verified against the real box instead).

### Part 202 (done): async container teardown (ADR-0180) -- a delete/stop can never freeze the daemon again (issue #67)

Root-caused and fixed the control-plane-wide wedge the user hit independently and this project hit twice in one day (both needed hard host resets): `DELETE`/`stop` of a running container ran `registry_remove()`'s synchronous SIGKILL + `waitid()` inside the single epoll loop -- unbounded when a child sticks in uninterruptible D-state (SIGKILL only *pends* there). The evidence had narrowed it precisely: the wedged delete mutated nothing (container row/DNS record/cert all survived the reset), and stop-then-delete-while-exited worked flawlessly -- the wait was the whole story. `registry_remove()`'s own comment had even deferred the async design as "not warranted for a v1 skeleton."

Now (ADR-0180): durable intent lands synchronously (containerdef removal + service-ownership forgets for delete; the stopped flag for stop), `registry_begin_kill()` thaws-unconditionally + SIGKILLs without waiting, and the existing crash-detection reactor completes teardown (registry release, disk cleanup, pkgbuild bookkeeping) when the pidfd actually fires. Transient `"deleting"`/`"stopping"` statuses are visible; same-name creates 409 during the window; a truly unkillable child now costs one visibly-stuck container instead of the whole daemon. The stale-`paused`-flag freezer hazard is fixed everywhere (thaw is unconditional in the synchronous paths too). Storage-migration finalize and the rolling-restart timer keep the synchronous primitive deliberately (tracked for phase-2 conversion on #67).

Contract change documented in `openapi.yaml` + `docs/api/README.md` in the same commit: responses mean "intent durably recorded + kill sent," and clients chaining on full teardown settle-poll first (the concrete case: network delete right after deleting its last container can transiently 409). Verified across the real suite -- test_container_lifecycle, test_daemon, test_container_restart, test_cli, test_networks (all updated from immediate-expectation to bounded settle-polls, 5s cap), plus test_web/test_container_files/test_container_stats/test_console_exec/test_rolling_restart/test_pkg unchanged-and-green.

### Part 201 (done): kernel 6.18.40 rebuild DELIVERED (issue #1 closed) -- via a full toolchain-lineage investigation, then a deliberate decoupling

**The resolution (2026-08-21):** after a week of the self-hosted-gcc chain holding the kernel hostage, the two were deliberately decoupled (user-approved): kernel 6.18.40 built in the dev sandbox with its known-good toolchain from the current config fragment (`CONFIG_CFS_BANDWIDTH` #1/ADR-0166 + `CONFIG_BLK_CGROUP`/`CONFIG_CGROUP_WRITEBACK` Part 199, `CONFIG_SMP`, EFI stub -- all verified in the final .config), QEMU-boot-tested (test_boot PASS, cixd reached as init), transferred via the documented LAN-serve scratch-recipe flow, staged to slot b, rebooted, and **functionally verified live**: cpu_max+memory_max+pids_max container creation succeeds (ADR-0165's exact failure), memcg limits apply and read back, and per-container disk I/O accounting works for the first time (32MiB written in a container -> `write_bytes: 33554432` in its stats). A tracked exception to self-hosting, not an abandonment: the gcc chain continues as a data-driven background track (local isolation experiment), and the kernel recipe pins (6.18.40-12/-13) stay ready for the self-hosted rebuild once the chain lands. Also fixed en route: `/proc/cgroups` no longer lists controllers whose v1 interface is compiled out (CONFIG_MEMCG_V1 unset) -- a display change of the legacy file, not a regression, confirmed by functional probes.

What started as "rebuild the kernel with the Part 199 config fixes and reboot into it" became a deep toolchain investigation. Every step below is committed (see `recipes/package/{gcc,zlib,elfutils,libc-dev,kernel,probe-gcc-headers}/*/build.sh` -- each version's own header comment carries its full evidence trail):

- **Real dev-image gaps found and fixed via the kernel build's own failures**: `bc` (kconfig's `timeconst.h`), `elfutils`/libelf for objtool (`0.192-6`, libelf-only, `CC=gcc` since TCC cannot parse `__thread` at all -- confirmed by minimal probe), `zlib/1.3.2-3` (TCC's shared-library link never auto-adds its own `libtcc1.a`, leaving `__va_start`/`__va_arg` genuinely undefined in `libz.so.1` for any gcc-linked consumer -- statically resolved into the library), `libc-dev/2.36-3` (no `libm.so` dev script staged at all; and this project's older ld treats `AS_NEEDED` as mandatory, so the staged script references only `libm.so.6`).
- **The real syslimits.h root cause** (supersedes kernel/6.18.40-8's cruder wholesale-replace): gcc/12.5.0-10's installed `include-fixed/syslimits.h` is a byte-identical copy of `limits.h` instead of the chaining wrapper, so glibc's real limits.h is never reached (`MB_LEN_MAX`/`PATH_MAX`/`UCHAR_MAX` all break differently downstream). Proven via probe-gcc-headers v3-v6; scoped fix in `elfutils/0.192-5+` and `kernel/6.18.40-9+`; permanent gcc.recipe fix is issue #55.
- **gcc-12.5.0 has a deterministic C-frontend ICE on the rotate idiom** (`rol64`/`ror32`: `(x << s) | (x >> (-s & mask))` in a return statement), at *every* -O level -- confirmed by isolated probes; pervasive in kernel source, so 12.5.0 genuinely cannot build the kernel.
- **Three gcc-16.2.0-from-12.5.0 bootstrap attempts failed three different ways**: the `btree_destroy` corrupted `rex.W jns` jump-into-padding infinite loop (root-caused via gdb on the real crashed binary, `keep_on_failure` + files API), the same signature one level deeper after a scoped `-O0` fix, then an unrelated dlopen-self conftest hang.
- **User-directed pivot to the Live-Bootstrap chain**: TCC (this project's own trusted seed) built **gcc-4.7.4-6** directly (`c,c++`, single-pass) -- fully validated on-box: real C and C++ programs compile, link, *run correctly*, and the rol64 case compiles clean. Genuine milestone: a working GCC with no ambient compiler anywhere in its lineage. gcc-16.2.0 then confirmed to *require* a C++14 bootstrap compiler (its own configure probe), which 4.7.4 predates -- **gcc-6.4.0** chosen as the bridge; its build (seeded by 4.7.4-6) fixed two more real gaps (empty `include-fixed/` needing the complete glimits.h/syslimits.h pair -- a bare passthrough loses `LONG_MIN` et al) and then **hung**: its own freshly-built `cc1` stuck 50+ minutes on a trivial conftest.
- **Where it stands**: the user suspects an accumulated platform-level fault rather than N independent toolchain bugs -- the anomaly list supports it (the box's own `tar` silently truncating multi-file archives; the deployed kernel's confirmed binfmt_script ENOEXEC bug; repeated hangs of freshly-built binaries on trivial input; identical byte-level "miscompile" from two different seed compilers). Isolation experiment in progress: the same gcc-6.4.0 build, same tarballs, same seed lineage, run in the dev sandbox (ordinary Debian kernel, no Cix runtime) -- if it builds clean there, the platform is implicated, not the compilers. `docs/guides/remote-development.md` gained a "Debugging a remote build in depth" section documenting the full operational workflow this investigation established (tail-capture limits + make.log redirect, keep-on-failure + files-API post-mortems, live build-log streaming, hang-vs-slow detection, the pkg-sync per-version cache trap, and the private-Gitea live-token flow).
- **Web dashboard, user-reported gap**: a package's Versions tab rows were dead ends -- no way to view a specific historical version's recipe content, and nothing marked which version a plain install/rolling rebuild would actually resolve to. Each row now carries a real "View…" action (a version-scoped `GET /pkg/recipes/{name}?version=`, opening the existing recipe modal pre-filled with that exact version's content -- which doubles as a working restore-old-version path, since saving republishes as a new version) and the newest row is labeled "(rolling candidate)" (the same newest-created_at resolution ADR-0107 applies to an omitted ?version=).

### Part 200 (done): GCC 12.5.0 genuinely self-hosted -- issue #32 closed, real root causes down to disassembled machine code

`gcc/12.5.0-10` built, bootstrapped (all 3 stages), and installed on 192.168.15.95, confirmed live: `state: "installed"`, 1005 files merged into the `dev` image, zero kernel oopses across the full ~4h run at `-j6`. The real, working conclusion of issue #32, continuing directly from Part 199's own kernel investigation.

Two more real bugs found and fixed along the way, both via direct evidence, not guessing: `url_basename()` (`daemon/src/pkg.c`) never stripped a URL's query string, breaking every `pkg_source` entry using the git-raw-file `?ref=<commit>` pattern -- found the first time that mechanism was ever actually exercised end-to-end (ADR-0178, new regression test verified to genuinely catch the bug by reverting the fix and confirming the test alone failed). And `--with-build-config=` (empty) turned out to silently do nothing at all -- GCC's own real `./configure` script only special-cases literal `yes`/`no`, confirmed by reading it directly -- which led to a bigger discovery: *disabling* `bootstrap-debug` was the wrong move outright, since it swaps GCC's own real `contrib/compare-debug` tool (which correctly tolerates debug-info-driven differences) for a naive `cmp`, and a fresh disabled-bootstrap-debug run failed far worse (hundreds of files differing, not 4).

The one remaining, narrow mismatch -- exactly 4 `libiberty` object files, deterministic across three separate attempts regardless of `-j` level -- was root-caused down to real disassembled machine code and ELF relocation symbols (stage2 compiles `lrealpath()` as `realpath()+strdup()`, stage3 as `canonicalize_file_name()`, both individually correct, just non-reproducible) and fixed using GCC's own real, upstream-sanctioned exception mechanism: the top-level Makefile's own `compare` target already carries a `case` statement treating `gcc/cc*-checksum.o` as a known-benign warning instead of a fatal failure (it legitimately differs by design, since it embeds a hash of the compiler binary itself) -- extended with the same real pattern for the 4 confirmed files, not a workaround.

Also confirmed live: `-j6` is completely safe on this 2-core box when run from a clean state (steady ~190%+ CPU, zero pressure stalls, full responsiveness for hours) -- two earlier apparent "crashes" both traced to killing an actively-compiling build container and immediately spawning a new one in the same breath, not to the parallelism level itself.

Unblocks: issue #1 (kernel rebuild, needs a real GCC -- `kernel/6.18.40-3`'s own `CONFIG_BLK_CGROUP` fix from Part 199 can now actually build) and issue #30 (WiFi AP, transitively blocked on #32). Also produced ADR-0179 (full user-namespace design for issue #29, written and revised during the wait -- three real design flaws caught and fixed in direct review: a self-contradicting chown fallback, a UID-collision gap in the sub-range allocator, and a cross-container isolation gap when host-auth is disabled) and five new backlog issues (#50-#54: KSM, zswap, cgroup swap accounting, cgroup hugetlb, overlayfs metacopy) plus two capability-visibility gaps found investigating the container model (#48, #49).

### Part 199 (done): kernel blk-cgroup/cgroup-writeback + a real `pkg_source` query-string basename bug (ADR-0178), found live diagnosing an overnight gcc stall

An overnight `gcc/12.5.0-4` (`-j1`) bootstrap on 192.168.15.95 silently hung after ~9 hours -- two real kernel Oopses (`filemap_get_folios_tag`, hit by `jbd2` and a writeback `kworker` 23 seconds apart on the identical address) left a `ranlib`/`sync` pair permanently stuck in D-state. Root-caused as far as directly possible without a live kernel debugger: this kernel's config had `CONFIG_MEMCG=y` but no `CONFIG_BLK_CGROUP`/`CONFIG_CGROUP_WRITEBACK` (all writeback funnels through the global/root bdi path, a less-tested configuration -- also the direct cause of a separate, already-known gap where per-container disk I/O stats always read 0) and zero memory-debugging instrumentation compiled in (no way to catch the actual corruption event at its origin). Real-world research found "folio-split races corrupting xarray state during writeback" is a genuine, recurring class of upstream kernel bug (hit XFS and shmem at different points, fixed at different kernel versions) -- no exact match found for this specific ext4+overlayfs combination, an honest open question, not a confirmed root cause. Recovered via a user-initiated Proxmox hard reset (a graceful `POST /system/reboot` was attempted first but risked hanging too, given a `sync` call was already stuck).

Added `CONFIG_BLK_CGROUP=y`/`CONFIG_CGROUP_WRITEBACK=y` to `image/kernel/qemu-part1.config`, cut as `kernel/6.18.40-3`. Deploying it via `pkg hostbuild` was the first real end-to-end exercise of this project's git-raw-file `pkg_source` mechanism (`kernel/6.18.40-2` had only ever been committed, never actually built) -- which surfaced a real, previously-latent daemon bug: `url_basename()` never stripped a URL's `?ref=<commit>` query string, so the config file staged as `qemu-part1.config?ref=<40 hex chars>` instead of plain `qemu-part1.config`, breaking the recipe's own `cp` reference. Fixed (ADR-0178), with a new regression test verified to actually catch the bug (reverted the fix, confirmed the new test alone failed, restored it).

Also published `gcc/12.5.0-5` (adds `--with-build-config=`, disabling GCC's own auto-selected `bootstrap-debug` compare pass -- found via `config.log` while explaining to the user why the bootstrap was running well past the usual 1.5-4h) for whichever rebuild starts fresh next; not applied to the in-flight `12.5.0-4` attempt itself. Confirmed the box's guest kernel only ever brought up 2 CPUs (`smpboot: Total of 2 processors activated`, identical across three separate boots) despite an expectation of 8 -- a Proxmox-level VM vCPU allocation question, not a guest-side or daemon issue.

### Part 198 (done): `pkg resume` -- continue a kept-on-failure build in place, no fetch/extract restart (ADR-0177, issue #46)

Prompted directly by the user, mid-investigation of issue #32's gcc bootstrap: "why don't we continue compilation from where it broke, rather than start from the beginning again?" Every recipe fixup iteration on `gcc.recipe` was paying for a full `reset_build_container_dir()` (`rm -rf` the whole build container) + `extract_tarball()` (re-untar gcc/gmp/mpfr/mpc) + a build restart from `configure`, even when only one line in the recipe's own `pkg_build()` changed between attempts.

Before writing any code, the real mechanics were confirmed by reading, not assumed: `overlay_create()` already tolerates a pre-existing upperdir/workdir; `registry_remove()` never touches disk (confirmed directly in `registry.c`); `struct pkg_entry` already retains its own `build_lowerdir`/`build_upperdir`/`build_workdir`/`build_merged`/`build_container_name` from the original attempt; `pkg_build_container_chain_index()` already parses a build container's own chain slot back out of its name. Every precondition for "reuse the exact same overlay" already existed.

New `pkg_resume_build()` (`daemon/src/pkg.c`) + `POST /v1/pkg/resume` (`daemon/src/main.c`, `cixctl pkg resume`): given a `failed` entry with a non-empty `kept_build_container` (ADR-0175), stages a (optionally newly-published) recipe version over the old one in the existing build container's own upperdir, resets only the previous attempt's partial install destination, and leaves the already-extracted source tree completely untouched -- no fetch subprocess at all, synchronous, reusing the exact same chain slot the original attempt used (never a freshly allocated one, since `pkg_build_completed()` looks it up by that same index). `pkg_fetch_completed()`'s own container-spec-building tail was extracted into a shared `start_build_container_spec()` helper so the two entry points don't duplicate that sequence.

Verified end-to-end with a new `test_pkg` step 19: the first (deliberately failing) build leaves a marker file in `/build/src`; the resumed recipe's own `pkg_build()` fails loudly if that marker is missing -- proof this is a genuine reuse, not a disguised restart (a real `extract_tarball()` re-run would never reproduce it). A real use-after-free was found and fixed along the way (the handler freed its parsed JSON body before a later read-back still needed `name`/`image` from it), caught by the test itself, not by inspection. See ADR-0177.
